items.title: Staggered age of consent to be discussed after Brand case, minister says
items.summary: A woman who alleges she was raped by the jailed comedian when she was 16 is campaigning to see relationships between 16-and 17-year-olds and adults made illegal.

scraped.title: Age of consent: Pat McFadden says changes to law will be discussed after Brand allegations
scraped.description: A woman who alleges she was raped by the jailed comedian when she was 16 is campaigning to see relationships between 16-and 17-year-olds and adults made illegal.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Staggered age of consent to be discussed after Brand case, minister says
scraped.body_text:
Brand was jailed this week after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault

A discussion over a staggered age of consent is to take place, the work and pensions secretary has said, as the government faces calls to change the law following the case against Russell Brand.

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Pat McFadden said that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" have emerged this week.

A woman who alleges she was raped by jailed comedian Brand when she was 16 is now campaigning to see the law changed so that relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal.

Questions over a staggered age of consent have "been raised and will be discussed" McFadden said, adding: "[I] can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."

Adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, under UK law.

Mia Latter, who has waived her right to anonymity, told the Sunday Times that she wants the age of consent to be staggered.

Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

At Southwark Crown Court on Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years imprisonment after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, involving four women between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

Latter said she was 16 when she met the comedian, then 30. She told the Sunday Times: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power].

"I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other.

"If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to.

"But...if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."

Latter told the Sunday Times the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but police wanted her to be part of "subsequent" proceedings.

She told the paper she was "devastated" by the decision and that police had said they didn't want the trial "to become 'the Alice show'", a reference to her pseudonym in the stories published in 2023.

It is understood the Met Police has apologised for the language officers used in a meeting with Latter about her case.

A Met spokesperson said: "This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence."

Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, said bringing in a staggered age of consent was about addressing a "power imbalance" in relationships involving 16 and 17 year-olds and adults. She urged ministers to commit to such a change.

Stone, a child protection social worker, told the BBC that 16 and 17 year-olds were seen as children in "every single framework of the law" and "we don't believe [they are] old enough to consent to having sex with much older adults".

Close the Consent Gap is proposing that 16 year-olds would not be able to have a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and that someone aged 17 would be prohibited from a relationship with anyone older than 20.

Further allegations of sexual misconduct in the entertainment industry came in the same week Brand was convicted.

ITV News and the Guardian published a story alleging that comedian David Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

One woman said she now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour when he was a judge at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

Walliams said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Metropolitan Police said on Friday it has launched an investigation into Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences", after the ITV News and the Guardian story. The Met said that the allegations it is investigating are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian but that it was "also proactively reviewing that reporting".

Speaking to Sky News, the work and pensions secretary said: "I do think that between Russell Brand, David Walliams, what's been put out there, people are looking at these issues in a new light."

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told the BBC that questions over a staggered age of consent have "been raised and will be discussed"

Helen Whately, the shadow work and pension secretary, told Kuenssberg that it was worth debating a change to age of consent laws.

Whately said she has teenage daughters and would be concerned if they brought home a man many years older than them.

"I think any parent would look twice," she said, adding: "Let's have the debate."

Anna Edmundson, director of policy and social change at the NSPCC charity, said 16 and 17-year-olds can be particularly vulnerable to grooming by some adults and laws have been changed in recent years to prevent more people in positions of trust from having sexual relationships with children of such an age.

She said "other laws are failing to prevent them from being sexually exploited", adding: "Even though they are over the age of consent, young people are still entitled to be protected from harm."

items.title: Man and woman die and four arrested after police pursuit crash in Leeds
items.summary: Four people have been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving, police say.

scraped.title: Two die in Leeds car crash after police pursuit
scraped.description: Four people have been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving, police say.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Man and woman die in police pursuit crash
scraped.body_text:
This video can not be played

Four arrested after two killed in Leeds crash

Two people have been killed after their car was hit by a vehicle fleeing from police in Leeds.

West Yorkshire Police said it happened at 00:44 GMT, when a blue BMW 123D failed to stop for officers in Gelderd Road and then crashed into a white Volkswagen Scirocco.

The driver of the Volkswagen, a 22-year-old man, died at the scene. His passenger, a woman, 23, died later in hospital. Both were from York.

The occupants of the BMW, a 39-year-old man from Harrogate, two boys aged 16 and 17 and a 16-year-old girl, have been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

The 39-year-old is also being held on suspicion of driving while over the prescribed limit for cannabis, the force confirmed.

The teenagers in the BMW were taken to hospital for treatment to injuries that were not considered life-threatening.

A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said a referral had been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which confirmed it had started an investigation.

Officers are appealing for anyone who witnessed the crash to get in touch

The crash happened in the early hours of Sunday morning

A spokesperson for the IOPC said it had launched an independent investigation at about 02:30 and sent investigators to the crash scene to "begin gathering evidence".

The spokesperson said that inquiries were "at a very early stage".

A police scene and road closure remain in place in Gelderd Road, and drivers are advised to avoid the area and seek alternative routes. A steady stream of cars is being directed by officers to turn around at the cordon.

The area is made up of business units and car dealerships and was very quiet on this cold Sunday morning, with very few people about.

A dark car can be seen a short distance away from a very badly damaged white Volkswagen just outside a used car dealership.

Anyone who saw the vehicles before or during the crash and may have information or footage is urged to contact police.

Your Voice

Listen to highlights from West Yorkshire on BBC Sounds , catch up with the latest episode of Look North .

items.title: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
items.summary: The Ukrainian president says restrictions are still in place and making it difficult to stop Russian attacks.

scraped.title: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
scraped.description: The Ukrainian president says restrictions are still in place and making it difficult to stop Russian attacks.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
scraped.body_text:
Restrictions have affected Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian missiles and drones

A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.

The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military military-grade Starlink service owned by Elon Musk and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks.

Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said.

US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says

Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace.

The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.

Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".

It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.

The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.

Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.

On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".

"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.

Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.

Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.

It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.

Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.

Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.

Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.

Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.

"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.

"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."

Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.

In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.

Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.

Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.

The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try and carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.

"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

items.title: New Orleans port sues owners of tanker involved in Mississippi crash
items.summary: Officials are seeking at least $1 million in damages from the owners of the tanker that hit a cruise ship last week. The incident was dubbed "the miracle on the Mississippi" after no one was killed. Officials are seeking at least $1 million in damages from the owners of the tanker that hit a cruise ship last week. The incident was dubbed "the miracle on the Mississippi" after no one was killed.(Image credit: Gerald Herbert)

scraped.title: New Orleans port sues owners of tanker involved in Mississippi crash
scraped.description: Officials are seeking at least $1 million in damages from the owners of the tanker that hit a cruise ship last week. The incident was dubbed "the miracle on the Mississippi" after no one was killed.
scraped.h1: New Orleans port sues owners of tanker involved in Mississippi crash
scraped.body_text:
By

Ava Pukatch

The American Heritage river cruise paddleboat is seen on its side after being struck by the Atlantic Asphalt tanker ship in the Mississippi River, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, in New Orleans. Gerald Herbert/AP hide caption

New Orleans port officials filed a lawsuit against the owner and operator of the tanker that crashed into a docked cruise ship in the Mississippi River on Friday.

The Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans is seeking at least $1 million in damages from people connected to the tanker, which is called Atlantic Asphalt. The lawsuit also names the tanker's owner, Nave Shipping SA and its management company Thome Ship Management as defendants.

The lawsuit states that at 12:30 p.m. Friday, the Atlantic Asphalt tanker crashed into the American Heritage river cruise paddleboat which was docked at the Thalia Street terminal for disembarkment of passengers.

There were almost 200 people on board the American Heritage at the time of the crash, which left the ship on its side and partially submerged. All passengers and crew survived, including more than 100 who were rescued from the river, leading New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno to dub the incident "the miracle on the Mississippi."

There were 32 people brought to the hospital, none with critical injuries.

The port commissioners said as a result of the collision, the Thalia Street terminal had significant damage.

"The extent of said damage remains under investigation, but physical damage is currently estimated to exceed [$1 million], with additional substantial direct, indirect and consequential damages anticipated," the lawsuit reads.

The lawsuit also states that the port expects to incur additional costs, including clean-up, surveys, repair, replacement and salvage costs.

On Friday, port officials requested the tanker be seized and sold to cover costs of the damage. A federal judge approved the seizure request.

Officials claimed that the collision occurred "as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness" by Atlantic Asphalt, Nave Shipping SA and Thome Ship Management.

The American Heritage river cruise paddleboat is seen on its side after being struck by the Atlantic Asphalt tanker ship in the Mississippi River, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, in New Orleans. Gerald Herbert/AP hide caption

As of Saturday, eight people remained in the hospital, two in serious condition.

Mayor Moreno said Saturday that the Atlantic Asphalt had been towed away from the site, but noted it could take weeks to fully remove the American Heritage.

Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said that operations were now focused on fully reopening the river and safe removal of hazardous material on board the American Heritage. Burnham said it is estimated there are 160,000 gallons of fuel on board the ship.

"We're going to have divers in the water so they can do a full assessment on what's the right path to be able to remove it," Burnham said. "We also have teams that have been deployed throughout the entire area, the river system to monitor the area for any pollution."

Burnham said there are restrictions in place for boat traffic along the Mississippi River.

The exact cause of the crash is unknown, though Burnham said the tanker appeared to have an issue with steering. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the crash.

John DeLeeuw, board member with the NTSB, said during a Saturday briefing that the tanker's voyage data recorder was recovered.

"The voyage data recorder essentially is going to provide the data," DeLeeuw said. "It's like a flight data recorder on an aircraft. We can look at speeds and all kinds of information. It's essentially covering speed all kinds of maneuverings that was done on the ship."

A preliminary report by the NTSB is expected within 30 days, with the final report on probable causes and safety recommendations coming in 18 to 24 months.

items.title: New Mexico wanted free childcare for all. This is what's worked — and what hasn't
items.summary: A year ago in November, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to every eligible family, regardless of income. A year ago in November, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to every eligible family, regardless of income.(Image credit: Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR)

scraped.title: New Mexico wanted free childcare for all. This is what's worked — and what hasn't
scraped.description: A year ago in November, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to every eligible family, regardless of income.
scraped.h1: New Mexico wanted free childcare for all. This is what's worked — and what hasn't
scraped.body_text:
By

Julie Depenbrock

Children wearing Halloween costumes play on the playground of Kids Campus in Santa Fe, N.M. Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR hide caption

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

It's a hazy August morning, and Judyn Martinez is dropping her daughter off at Kids Campus, a sought-after childcare center in Santa Fe that is now free for any eligible family in New Mexico.

"It's an amazing school so far. She loves it. I love it," Martinez said. "Everyone's nice. She's learning, growing already."

A year ago this month, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to every family, regardless of income. To qualify, families must be residents of New Mexico and adults in the house must be working, looking for work, in school or unable to work.

Many parents, including Martinez, told NPR that it's been life-changing.

"I'm really grateful for universal childcare because I wouldn't have been able to send her," Martinez said.

There's just one drawback for families: Right now, the state doesn't have the capacity to meet the demand, which has left some families waiting without childcare. Martinez said it took her about a year and half to get off the waitlist for Kids Campus — a waitlist that, today, has nearly 700 children on it.

When she first spoke with NPR in September, Lilia Doyle said her 2-year-old son was on six different waitlists.

"I'm 97th on a multi-hundred person waitlist. I'm 75th on something. And some, I'm not even getting calls back," Doyle said.

Doyle, a children's librarian with a background in early childhood education, lives in Santa Fe. She acknowledged that she's selective when it comes to childcare. Still, she said, it should be easier.

"I have great belief in this program, but as it currently stands, I think the rollout needs a lot, a lot of help."

Kids Campus is a sought-after childcare center, with a waitlist nearly 700 children long. Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR hide caption

According to the state, New Mexico has about 67,000 children 5 and under, and about 50% of them are enrolled in the universal childcare program. Some of the remaining families participate in other free public programs, like New Mexico PreK and Head Start.

But many children aren't enrolled in any public, free childcare program, and it's hard to know exactly how many are in Doyle's position, unable to access universal childcare because of limited capacity. New Mexico officials acknowledged to NPR that the program needs to expand.

In order to work for every family, the program will have to overcome both a shortage of childcare workers and childcare slots — two challenges that are also playing out at the national level.

Because of that, across the country, policymakers and childcare advocates are keeping a close eye on this Southwestern experiment.

Cynthia Osborne, who leads Vanderbilt University's Prenatal-to-3 Policy Impact Center , said New Mexico is "going to provide lessons that the rest of the states are going to have to pay attention to."

"If New Mexico can show us how to build the infrastructure, I think other states will say that's an investment that we should make."

But the challenges to building that infrastructure – and keeping costs under control – are very real.

The program has built-in safeguards in case economic downturns make it harder to pay for – and one of those safeguards was recently triggered: The annual Consumer Price Index rose above 3%, which means wealthier families – who make more than $198,000 for a household of four – will soon have to start making a copayment. According to the state's Early Childhood Education and Care Department, ECECD, that copay won't exceed $148.50 a month. The department says this change will affect about 10% of enrolled families, and will remain in effect through the fiscal year.

Like many states, New Mexico previously offered childcare subsidies to low-income families, and free childcare to the lowest-income families. For a while, the state was raising the income limits for those programs.

Kids Campus has capacity for about 130 children. "Nobody questions a wealthy family sending their kids to public school and it should be the same for early childhood," said Catron Allred, who oversees Kids Campus and the early childhood program at Santa Fe Community College. Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR hide caption

Families, providers and grassroots organizers had also been campaigning to do away with those limits entirely. One of the big sticking points was how to pay for it, and the answer came in 2022, when New Mexicans voted to dedicate a portion of the state's Land Grant Permanent Fund to early childhood education. Much of that fund consists of taxes and royalties on the state's vast oil and gas production, and it's large enough to provide hundreds of millions of dollars to support childcare every year.

Then, in September 2025, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced a plan for free, universal childcare and prekindergarten, which would begin Nov. 1 of that year. After it launched, the program was approved by the Democrat-majority state legislature and was officially written into law in March 2026.

Any licensed or registered childcare provider in New Mexico can participate in the program. The state offers higher reimbursements for centers that pay workers higher wages and operate a minimum of 10 hours, five days a week.

"I think childcare is a gamechanger for every single thing that a state ought to deliver for its families," Lujan Grisham told NPR.

The governor said this year is going "stunningly well."

"I can't go anywhere in New Mexico… where I don't have a parent tell me that this is life-changing and transformative," she said.

But she knows more capacity is needed.

"We need to keep growing," Lujan Grisham said. "It is not a stagnant set of opportunities."

In 2025, ECECD set a goal to create 12,000 new childcare spots in the first few years of the program, but did not share a specific deadline with NPR. According to the department, they are more than halfway there.

It was no surprise that accessibility would be an issue for a program like this.

Nearly half of all U.S. children, ages 5 and under, live in a licensed childcare desert, where demand for care outpaces availability, according to the Center for American Progress , a left-leaning think tank.

Olga Grays, a childcare provider for more than 20 years, said she fields messages every day from desperate parents who she isn't able to give slots to. That's one reason she's part of a group chat that includes over 40 childcare providers in her area.

Olga Grays operates Mrs. Olga's Daycare out of her home in Las Cruces, N.M. Bree Lamb for NPR hide caption

"Every time somebody calls me, you know, I put their name and the age of their kids in that group. And I'm like, 'Does anybody have openings?' You know, but the sad thing is that not a lot of people have openings, especially for infants."

Grays, a single mother of five, operates out of her home in Las Cruces, in the southern part of the state.

At Mrs. Olga's Daycare, the living room has been transformed into a classroom, with cushioned, fall-safe floors. The outdoor space is part children's playground and part garden oasis.

"[The children] can play with water, with dirt, grass. They ground themselves. It makes a world of a difference," Grays said.

She wishes she didn't have to turn any children away.

At Mrs. Olga's Daycare, the living room has been transformed into a classroom, with cushioned, fall-safe floors. Bree Lamb for NPR hide caption

"I think that's one of our biggest issues right now, is making sure that we have enough spots available for everybody coming in," Grays said. "And I think that's one of the flaws that perhaps other states can learn from."

According to the Center for American Progress, rural areas especially struggle with childcare deserts — and New Mexico is very rural.

"It's not a lack of funding, it's a lack of providers," the state's speaker of the house, Javier Martinez, told NPR. He's a Democrat and an advocate for universal childcare. "We have communities that are miles from any type of population center. Hundreds of miles sometimes. And so there are communities where that market isn't quite there to support a business."

The program's current operating budget is almost $600 million.

But there's concern among some state lawmakers that it's projected to be about $50 million over budget this year.

"By calling it universal, all we've done is add the wealthier folks," said state Sen. Steve Lanier, a Republican representing the northwest corner of New Mexico.

Lanier sued to stop the governor's universal childcare initiative — a lawsuit that was ultimately unsuccessful .

He told NPR that the steep price tag for this program is why he only supports childcare assistance for some.

"My daughter's a school teacher. She has two young boys. She gets free childcare. So, from a personal view, I see where it is needed. I mean, that helps her and her family immensely," Lanier said. "But somebody that's making $450,000, $600,000, do they really need that assistance?"

Catron Allred, who oversees the early childhood center at Santa Fe Community College, doesn't see it that way.

"To me, I think it's a mentality of early childhood as a public good," she explained. "Nobody questions a wealthy family sending their kids to public school and it should be the same for early childhood."

While New Mexico is the only state with free, universal childcare right now, other states and cities have made progress in that direction, including Oregon, Connecticut, Washington, D.C., New York City and Vermont, which has tapped into payroll taxes for funding.

In New York City, which already has free prekindergarten for 3- and 4-year-olds, Mayor Zohran Mamdani recently rolled out free daycare for thousands of the city's 2-year-olds.

As in New Mexico, "Both the biggest challenge and opportunity in New York City is our scale," explained Emmy Liss, executive director of the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education.

Children eat breakfast at Mrs. Olga's Daycare. Grays said she fields messages every day from desperate parents who she isn't able to give slots to. Bree Lamb for NPR hide caption

"We know that every family's childcare needs are different. We know that our diverse landscape of childcare providers offer a really wide mix of services that families value," Liss added. "But to build a system that incorporates all of those different providers and meets the needs of all of our families is a complex challenge."

Liss said the goal is to have free pre-k for every 2-year-old by the end of the mayor's first term. But instead of expanding access to everyone all at once, as New Mexico has done, she said the city is growing capacity "in parallel" with access by creating more slots and matching them with families.

"We are working to build the infrastructure, the workforce, the physical capacity and the support to providers to ensure that we can continue to scale access to care here," Liss told NPR.

She said her office has been in conversation with leaders in New Mexico, and has had the chance to learn from them. But ultimately, she said, "Our realities are different."

"I think we're making slightly different choices in how we are implementing expanded access to care, which is good. I think we should be making different choices, responsive to the needs we hear from New Yorkers."

Veronica Ramirez lives in Ohkay Owingeh, a federally recognized tribe and pueblo in northern New Mexico. She said she learned about universal childcare when it was in the news last year and decided to enroll her 2-year-old daughter.

"For my daughter, I think it's really opened doors for her," Ramirez told NPR.

"Just being able to be around other little human beings that are her age...I've seen her go up to other little kids in public and say hi or just start playing with them. And I'm like, 'Oh, well, she's social now. She's not clinging to mom only.' "

Olga Grays, a childcare provider for more than 20 years, reads to children at her daycare. Bree Lamb for NPR hide caption

For Ramirez, having consistent childcare has enabled her to do more nonprofit work, including as an outreach coordinator at a birth center that primarily serves indigenous clients in nearby Española. It helps that her 7-year-old son is in school for the same hours as her daughter is in daycare.

"Now I'm able to work more and make more money and support my family a little bit better," Ramirez said.

The childcare help has opened other doors for her, too.

"I'm trying to get my bachelor's. I had my son when I was 19, right when I graduated high school," Ramirez said. "It's taken me a little bit longer, but I'm getting closer to getting a degree."

A new paper from Arizona State University found that lower-income mothers in New Mexico have seen significant gains since free, universal childcare was enacted, with full-time employment increasing by 23%.

The outdoor space at Mrs. Olga's Daycare is part children's playground and part garden oasis. Bree Lamb for NPR hide caption

But for Lilia Doyle, in Santa Fe, working full-time won't be an option until she gets her son off a waitlist and into consistent childcare. When she first spoke to NPR in September, she said she and her family are living on her husband's income.

"Hopefully our finances will be able to absorb it," she said. "We'll buckle down, and we'll make it through, but … it's not ideal."

Then, in October, Doyle got some news: A childcare center told her they found a spot for her son – but it wouldn't open up until August 2027.

scraped.body_text:

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent joins 'Sunday Morning Futures' to discuss the Trump administration's economic sanctions against Iran, predicting a swift collapse of the regime's economy. Bessent also addresses the Iranian death threats that forced his family to relocate to a military base and weighs in on the compliance failures at Nvidia amid its ongoing espionage probe.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused the WSJ's editor-in-chief of "reckless journalism" for authorizing a photograph of his Washington, D.C., home that he said exposed its location.

During an appearance on "Sunday Morning Futures," Bessent declined to say whether he had faced an assassination attempt but said the threats were serious enough to force his family to relocate to a military base.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent gestures while speaking at the U.S.-China Relations Gala Dinner on Nov. 10, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Frank Franklin II)

"Obviously, it's a high threat level for us to move," he told Larry Kudlow. "And sadly, one of the reasons we had to move is because Emma Tucker, the news editor at The Wall Street Journal, authorized a photo of our house the day we bought it that had a geolocate on it. And so you can go on the Internet and see our beautiful residence [where] we made our home here in D.C. because of reckless journalism."

TRUMP'S TOP OFFICIALS RETREAT BEHIND MILITARY GATES AS EX-FBI DEPUTY POINTS TO WHAT'S FUELING THREATS

Threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage" amid reported Iranian assassination threats, a senior administration official told Fox News Digital.

Threats against top Trump officials have prompted several high-ranking members of the administration and their families to move to military bases for protection. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Bessent is the latest senior administration official to relocate to a military installation, joining a growing number of top Trump officials living behind military gates as federal authorities confront security threats that extend well beyond the White House.

ANOTHER TRUMP HEAVYWEIGHT REVEALED TO BE LIVING ON MILITARY BASE AS CABINET ROSTER GROWS

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth have reportedly taken up residence at Fort McNair in Washington, D.C., while White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other administration officials have moved to military installations or protected government housing. Attorney General Todd Blanche also moved to a military base earlier this year, a source familiar with the arrangement told Fox News Digital.

The relocations have not all stemmed from the same threats. Some followed concerns about domestic political violence, while Bessent's move comes amid reported threats linked to Iran.

The recent Iranian threats against Bessent come amid a documented history of alleged Tehran-backed assassination plots targeting senior U.S. officials.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Justice Department charged a member of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in 2022 in an alleged murder-for-hire plot targeting former Trump national security advisor John Bolton, while prosecutors disclosed in 2024 that another Iranian operative had allegedly been tasked with developing a plan to assassinate Trump.

Fox News Digital's Ashley J. DiMella contributed to this report.

Max Bacall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital covering media, culture and comedy.

scraped.title: Duffy: Investigators examining 2 routers after nationwide FAA ground stop, no signs of foreign cyberattack
scraped.description: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says two routers from FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas are being tested after the nationwide ground stop that halted flights for hours.
scraped.author: Stephen Sorace
scraped.h1: Duffy: Investigators examining 2 routers after nationwide FAA ground stop, no signs of foreign cyberattack
scraped.body_text:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. Market data provided by Factset . Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions . Legal Statement . Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG .

Fox News correspondent Alex Hogan reports from the White House on the travel chaos resulting from a massive nationwide ground stop. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy also joins 'Fox News Sunday' to detail the latest on the investigation as he asks Congress for additional funding to modernize the agency's telecommunications network.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that two routers from FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas are undergoing extensive testing as investigators examine whether faulty equipment or an installation problem triggered the nation's longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years .

Appearing on "Fox News Sunday," Duffy said that investigators have found no indication of a foreign cyberattack, although the FBI and other federal law enforcement partners remain involved in the probe.

"We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said. "But we're open, if we see something else, we're gonna continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement."

FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, right, with Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford, left, speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Tom Brenner)

In an update posted on X, Duffy said contractor L3Harris had secured the two routers from remote FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas and was conducting "deep diagnostics testing" at its headquarters in Florida, with engineers from the FAA, Juniper and Cisco assisting.

The investigation follows Friday's nationwide ground stop, which halted air traffic for more than four hours and contributed to disruptions affecting roughly 15,000 flights Friday and Saturday.

The fallout continued Sunday, with 3,798 flights delayed and another 1,638 canceled within, into or out of the United States as of noon ET, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware. Among the hardest-hit airports according to the provided data were Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport, with 376 delays, and Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, with 363 delays and 195 cancellations.

The shutdown occurred as L3Harris was replacing aging copper wiring with fiber-optic technology in the FAA's communications system. The work led to intermittent communications and radar gaps, prompting officials to halt flights nationwide .

Duffy said President Donald Trump convened federal officials on Friday as the administration investigated whether the disruption could have involved malicious interference.

"President Trump actually had the whole of government on the phone on Friday," Duffy said. "Was anyone seeing footprints? Was anyone hearing chatter? Was this a cyber attack from a foreign nation?"

"We have no indication that that was at play here," he added.

4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Duffy defended the decision to issue the nationwide ground stop, emphasizing that passenger safety takes precedence when problems emerge in the FAA's communications network .

"When we have inconsistencies in our network we're going to shut it down," Duffy said.

Passengers wait at boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington, D.C. on Nov. 13, 2026, after the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop at all airports due to a communications problem. (Zina DESMAZES / AFP via Getty Images)

The transportation secretary also warned that the FAA's communications infrastructure remains outdated despite ongoing efforts to replace copper wiring with fiber-optic technology.

"We're still using an old 1980 architecture for telecom," Duffy said. "I need a brand new telecom system."

BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS

Duffy said AT&T, Verizon and Lumen are prepared to help build a replacement network, but additional congressional funding is needed to move forward.

The request has drawn scrutiny from congressional Democrats, who argue the administration has yet to spend billions already allocated for air traffic control modernization. Duffy countered that the existing funds were designated for specific upgrades, including radar, radios and electronic flight strips, rather than a new communications network.

Travelers wait at LaGuardia Airport in New York, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide. (AP Photo/Ryan Murphy)

Meanwhile, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that "the worst is behind us," with air travel expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023 and only the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks .

scraped.title: Wyatt Hammond makes kayak fishing history with third straight national title and KBF record
scraped.description: Wyatt Hammond completed a historic three-peat at the KBF National Championship on Lake Guntersville, also claiming the Challenge Series title and Angler of the Year honors.
scraped.author: Amber Harding
scraped.h1: Wyatt Hammond makes kayak fishing history with third straight national title and KBF record
scraped.body_text:
In an interview with OutKick OutDoors recorded before his historic third consecutive KBF National Championship, Wyatt Hammond discusses his pursuit of more titles, his rivalry with Ewing Minor and the tournaments he's looking forward to in 2027.

When I caught up with professional kayak angler Wyatt Hammond on Wednesday, he was in Guntersville, Ala., preparing for a pretty big weekend at the Kayak Bass Fishing (KBF) National Championship.

"I've won it the past two years. I'm trying to see if I can do it three years in a row," Hammond told OutKick OutDoors.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

Well, folks, mission accomplished.

Wyatt Hammond took home the 2026 KBF Challenge Series Championship on Lake Guntersville, Ala. (Mark Cisneros)

Not only did Hammond complete the historic three-peat on Friday, but he also claimed the 2026 KBF Challenge Series Championship, earned Angler of the Year honors and set a new KBF record for the highest three-day total.

Not too shabby.

Hammond, who also won the 2025 Bassmaster Kayak Series National Championship, now has four national titles on his résumé. And his latest victory might have been his most impressive yet.

Hammond wasted no time getting to work at the KBF Championships on Lakes Guntersville and Wheeler.

He opened Wednesday's Challenge Series Championship with a 106-inch five-fish limit, building a commanding 9.75-inch lead over the rest of the field.

Watch Wyatt Hammond's full interview with OutKick OutDoors here :

For those unfamiliar with competitive kayak fishing , anglers are scored by the total length of their five longest bass rather than weight. Fish are measured, photographed and released instead of being transported to a traditional weigh-in.

On Thursday, Hammond followed up with another impressive limit of 102.25 inches, bringing his two-day total to 208.25 inches.

That was enough to win the Challenge Series Championship by a whopping 15.75 inches over runner-up Jody Queen.

But the biggest prize was still up for grabs.

FISHING IS BIG BUSINESS, AND FXR FOUNDER SAYS THE SPORT'S GROWTH IS ONLY GETTING STARTED

For Friday's KBF National Championship , the leaderboard reset to zero, meaning Hammond's massive lead from the previous two days meant absolutely nothing. He would have to do it all over again.

And that's exactly what he did.

Hammond landed another five-fish limit totaling 101.75 inches, narrowly edging out Rus Snyders, who finished with 100.50 inches. Abby Abbondanza took third with 99.25 inches.

Just 1.25 inches separated first and second place.

A 7 pound largemouth bass is held against a backdrop of cypress trees. (Getty: JLFCapture)

The victory made Hammond the first angler in KBF history to win three consecutive national championships.

And if that weren't enough, his combined total of 310 inches over the three days established a new KBF record. That's 15 scoring bass averaging more than 20 inches apiece.

What makes Hammond's latest accomplishment even more remarkable is what happened just a few weeks earlier.

In October, he came within two inches of defending his Bassmaster Kayak Series National Championship at Lake Murray in South Carolina .

Hammond told OutKick OutDoors that a slow start on Day 1 ultimately cost him, despite recording the largest single-day limit of the tournament on Day 2.

"I kind of got in my own head and kind of spun myself out," he explained.

Wyatt Hammond is a three-time kayak fishing national champion. (Mark Cisneros)

But after settling down and sticking to his game plan, he finished strong. It just wasn't quite enough to catch eventual champion Ewing Minor.

During our conversation Wednesday, Hammond also opened up about the pressure that comes with being a national champion and how that pressure nearly burned him out on fishing altogether.

"I was really putting a lot of stress on myself. Like, I have to do well because, you know, I won a national championship," he said. "I have to continue doing well."

Eventually, Hammond realized he needed to stop worrying so much about the results and get back to enjoying the sport.

"I did a lot better whenever I enjoyed what I was doing," he said.

Judging by this week's results, that approach seems to be working out pretty well.

When I asked Hammond about his goals for 2027, he already had his sights set on another familiar rival.

"I'm gonna see if I can take something from Ewing [Minor] next year. I can't let him win everything all over again," he joked.

Hammond said winning Bassmaster's Angler of the Year award would be a dream, and he's particularly excited about upcoming tournaments at Lake Champlain and Sam Rayburn Reservoir.

Wyatt Hammond fishes from his Old Town Sportsman AutoPilot 136 motorized kayak. (Carson Krenske)

But first, he can enjoy making history.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Three consecutive KBF national championships. Four national titles overall. A Challenge Series championship, an Angler of the Year award and a new KBF record.

Bravo, Wyatt.

Love all things fishing and outdoors? Follow OutKick OutDoors on Instagram , TikTok and YouTube !

Amber Harding is a writer for OutKick.

Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is likely to win Alaska’s Senate race, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis , as vote-counting continues in the state.

Peltola has expanded her narrow lead over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan with each new batch of votes reported this week. A “likely” characterization indicates that the NBC News Decision Desk has at least 95% confidence that Peltola will win the race.

See live results here.

Alaska’s is the only remaining 2026 Senate race in which the NBC News Decision Desk has not yet made a projection.

If Peltola wins, Democrats will have a 56-44 majority in the Senate next year.

The race remains uncalled a week after polls close as votes continue to be counted. Alaskans vote heavily by mail and ballots postmarked by Election Day are counted as long as they arrived by Nov. 13 — and a few days later than that for valid overseas voters.

In a race with such a narrow margin, these final votes are important, especially given Alaska’s ranked-choice rules.

If no candidate wins a majority of the vote on the first ballot, the lowest-placed candidate is eliminated and second-choice votes from that candidate’s supporters are counted. The process then repeats until someone gets a majority.

Ben Kamisar is a national political reporter for NBC News

items.title: UPS plane, passenger jet collide on Miami airport taxiway
items.summary: A UPS cargo plane and a Copa Airlines jet carrying 172 people collided while taxiing at Miami International Airport, leaving two passengers with minor injuries.

scraped.title: UPS cargo plane, Copa Airlines jet carrying 172 people collide while taxiing at Miami International Airport
scraped.description: A UPS cargo plane and a Copa Airlines jet carrying 172 people collided while taxiing at Miami International Airport, leaving two passengers with minor injuries.
scraped.h1: UPS cargo plane, Copa Airlines jet carrying 172 people collide while taxiing at Miami International Airport
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 15, 2026 / 2:18 PM EST / CBS Miami

A UPS cargo plane and a Copa Airlines passenger jet carrying 172 people collided at Miami International Airport on Saturday night, leaving two passengers with apparent minor injuries and prompting a federal investigation, officials said.

The collision involved a UPS Boeing 767 and a Copa Airlines Boeing 737-800NG, according to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue.

According to the Federal Aviation Administration, the wingtip of the Copa Airlines jet struck the nose of the UPS cargo plane around 9 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 14.

Copa Airlines said its flight from Panama City, Panama, landed at MIA around 9 p.m. and was taxiing toward the terminal when the collision occurred. The UPS plane was preparing to depart for Bogota, Colombia, and air traffic controllers had instructed its crew to give way to the Copa flight, according to the FAA.

Air traffic control audio captured the moments surrounding the collision, including a voice saying, "Somebody hit us."

In another exchange, a voice asked, "Did you hit that aircraft?"

"Yeah, we went too far, and he clipped us with the wing," came the response.

"At approximately 9:15 p.m., an arriving aircraft and a departing aircraft made contact with each other at the intersection of two taxiways," Greg Chin, communications director at MIA, said in a statement to CBS News Miami. "Flights are being directed to other taxiways, so there is no impact to airport operations at this time."

The Copa Airlines flight was carrying 166 passengers and six crew members. Two passengers were evaluated by airport paramedics for apparent minor injuries, the airline said. Neither required transportation to a hospital, according to Chin.

Passengers aboard the Copa Airlines flight described frightening moments after the plane had already landed.

"We had already landed. Everything was calm when a woman next to me started screaming that we were going to crash," passenger Jesús Salon said in Spanish.

Another passenger said the collision was particularly frightening for those seated near the wing.

"It affected all of us, especially us. We were sitting next to the wing where the collision happened," the passenger said in Spanish.

A third passenger claimed his wife suffered a spinal injury during the incident.

"My wife and I were sitting right by the wing, and my wife suffered an injury to her spine," he said in Spanish.

The extent of the woman's reported injury was not independently confirmed.

An announcement heard over an aircraft's public address system sought to reassure passengers following the collision.

"Danger has been ruled out. There is no immediate danger," the announcement said.

The airline said the aircraft reached the terminal and all passengers had deplaned. The remaining passengers and crew members were reported to be in good condition.

UPS Flight 358 was scheduled to depart Miami for Colombia, while Copa Airlines Flight 427 was arriving from Panama City.

"The safety of our passengers and crew is our top priority, and we will cooperate with authorities as they investigate the incident," Copa Airlines said in a statement.

The FAA said it is investigating the circumstances surrounding the collision.

The collision came as MIA continued to experience flight delays and cancellations following a rare nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned Friday night that flight operations would take time to return to normal as airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crews.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that U.S. flight schedules were expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday.

Federal officials said Friday's outage was linked to problems with aging air traffic control technology , including switches and routers that became overloaded with data, causing inconsistencies in radar and communications systems.

items.summary: The company denies wrongdoing after accusations that it smuggled Nvidia's AI chips into China.

scraped.title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left company in 2025, denies wrongdoing amid Nvidia scandal
scraped.description: The company denies wrongdoing after accusations that it smuggled Nvidia's AI chips into China.
scraped.h1: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left company in 2025, denies wrongdoing amid Nvidia scandal
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 15, 2026 / 2:10 PM EST / CBS News

The Singapore-based company at the center of the scandal that brought down Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Sunday that suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang left the company in 2025. It also denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business."

In a statement to CBS News, Megaspeed International said Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, left the company in August 2025 and has no current role. It did not comment on the allegations that Alice Huang is a suspected Chinese spy.

"Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.

Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed and is the woman with whom Jensen Huang was having an affair. She is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security , which China denies. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO last week.

U.S. investigators say Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China.

In the past three years, Megaspeed has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.

Now the company, which began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to the Nvidia chips, is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips into China.

In a statement to CBS News on Sunday, the company said that recent assertions about its business, supply chain and global operations are "not supported by verifiable evidence."

"Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," it said.

It added: "The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation."

President Trump said last week the FBI was investigating the romantic and business ties between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who are not related.

CBS News reported on Friday that Singaporean authorities seized Alice Huang's passport in June 2025 while trying to engage the U.S. government to support their investigation into the suspected smuggling of Nvidia chips to China, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.

The source added that the Singaporean government received no meaningful help from Washington at the time.
