items.title: Satellite limitations imposed by Musk's SpaceX pose danger for Ukraine, Zelenskyy says
items.summary: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that limitations on the Starshield satellite system, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, could weaken defences around Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of the winter months, when Moscow has repeatedly targeted the power grid.

scraped.title: Zelenskyy warns Starshield restrictions threaten Ukraine's energy defences ahead of winter | CBC News
scraped.description: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that limitations on the Starshield satellite system, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, could weaken defences around Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of the winter months, when Moscow has repeatedly targeted the power grid.
scraped.h1: Satellite limitations imposed by Musk's SpaceX pose danger for Ukraine, Zelenskyy says
scraped.body_text:
Restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield satellite communications system are hindering its ability to intercept Russian drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.

He warned that limitations on the system, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, could weaken defenses around Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of the winter months, when Moscow has repeatedly targeted the power grid.

Ukraine's interceptor drones continue to lose contact with their operators when flying faster than 161 km/h along the front line and over Russian-occupied territory, leaving them unable to catch Russian Shahed drones, Zelenskyy said.

"We are counting on these restrictions to be lifted," he wrote on social media. "The protection of lives and Ukrainian energy infrastructure before winter depends on this. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defense, and the President's Office have been instructed to work closely with the American side and SpaceX.

"It is important to be on the right side of history. We need to help Ukraine."

Zelenskyy questioned Saturday whether the problem was technical, saying the restrictions appeared to have been imposed by SpaceX despite earlier assurances from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Starshield was more under U.S. government control.

Meanwhile, a Russian strike on Chornomorsk, a port city in Ukraine's Odesa region, injured six people and damaged energy infrastructure, regional head Oleh Kiper said Sunday on Telegram.

The blast and falling debris also damaged a gas pipeline and nearby residential buildings, while two parked cars caught fire.

European security plan floated by U.S. would benefit Putin, Zelenskyy says

The strike hit a facility operated by DTEK Odesa Electric Networks, temporarily leaving about 41,000 customers without power, Kiper said.

A woman walks at the site of a building damaged during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in the city of Chornomorsk, Odesa region, on Nov. 15, 2026. (Nina Liashonok/Reuters)

Overnight Russian airstrikes on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured another six people, including a two-year-old boy, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Sunday.

Russia launched more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 guided aerial bombs and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week, Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian drone strikes damaged two electrical substations in Russia's Rostov region, killing a chief engineer, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said Sunday.

Four people were injured when drone debris fell on their cars, Slyusar wrote on social media. A fifth person was wounded when debris struck a "production facility" in the village of Troitskoye, he said.

Ukrainian forces also targeted Russia's Tatarstan region, officials said. Radmir Belyaev, mayor of Nizhnekamsk, the region's third-largest city, said a "large-scale and prolonged attack" damaged its industrial zone.

Six people were injured, and heating and hot water supplies were disrupted in parts of the city, he said.

Ukraine's General Staff said it had hit two sites in Nizhnekamsk: Nizhnekamskneftekhim, one of the largest petrochemical complexes in Europe, and a production site operated by petrochemical company Sibur. An oil refinery in the area was also hit, it said.

Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces shot down 533 Ukrainian drones overnight across 13 Russian regions, the Russian-annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.

Romanian Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said Sunday that three commercial vessels in the Black Sea were struck by drones overnight, the latest in a string of attacks that have raised fears of the war spilling over into NATO territory.

"Once again, maritime security in the Black Sea has been threatened," Niculescu wrote on X.

Romania's Ministry of National Defense said a Greek-flagged oil tanker was struck by a drone, sparking a fire that was extinguished by the crew. Two more ships were later struck by drones, and their crews also extinguished fires onboard, the ministry said. No casualties were reported and the ministry did not state the origin of the drones.

Black Sea sailors thought a rescue boat was racing toward them. Instead, it was a drone that sank their ship

"These incidents are unacceptable and constitute a violation of international law," Niculescu said, adding that they "reflect the deteriorating security situation caused by Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine."

A rescuer works at the site of an apartment buildings damaged by a Russian air strike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Nov. 14, 2026. (Reuters)

Last month, a string of cargo ships and tankers were struck by aerial or naval drones near the Bulgarian and Romanian coastlines. At least 30 sailors on commercial ships were confirmed dead or reported missing.

"We will continue to take all necessary measures, alongside our Allies, to strengthen security in the Black Sea," Niculescu added. "This remains a key priority for the Government, in close co-operation with our regional partners and NATO."

Estonia's government said Sunday it would close all border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1, after the Baltic country's prime minister accused Moscow of attempting to sabotage an Estonian drone company a day earlier.

The government said an attempted attack had been carried out early Saturday against Threod Systems in Viimsi, north of the capital, Tallinn, "with the aim of causing an explosion and setting the building on fire."

"If Russia continues its hybrid operations in Estonia, and we know that Russian intelligence services exploit border crossings to exert influence over people, we must be prepared to reduce the risks we face," Prime Minister Kristen Michal said in a statement.

"Closing the border would reduce the threat to people in Estonia and send a clear message that attacks on Estonia's defense industry and defense capabilities are unacceptable," Michal added.

National broadcaster ERR reported Sunday that eight Latvian nationals have been detained after the attempted break-in.

items.title: SA Health investigates medication errors at youth detention centre
items.summary: SA Health says three medication errors at the state's youth detention centre have been investigated since January 2025, with a watchdog repeating a call for a dedicated all-hours health service at the site. Three medication errors have been investigated at the Adelaide Youth Training Centre since the beginning of 2025.

scraped.title: SA Health investigates medication errors at youth detention centre
scraped.description: SA Health says three medication errors at the state's youth detention centre have been investigated since January 2025, with a watchdog repeating a call for a dedicated all-hours health service at the site.
scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/stephanie-richards/102388052
scraped.h1: Three medication errors investigated at SA youth detention centre since last year
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Stephanie Richards

Topic: State and Territory Government

Three medication errors have been investigated at the Adelaide Youth Training Centre since the beginning of 2025. ( ABC News )

Three medication errors at South Australia's youth detention centre Kurlana Tapa dating back to January 2025 have been investigated by state health authorities.

A watchdog is concerned that a recommendation to implement a 24/7 health service is yet to be introduced.

The Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service is aiming to have 6.75 full time equivalent clinical staff on site.

South Australian health authorities have investigated three medication errors at the state's youth detention centre since the start of last year, amid ongoing concerns about the lack of a 24/7 health service at the site.

The errors were reported between January 2025 and October this year and involved a "chemist dispensing error with an incorrect dose", a young detainee accessing another detainee's over-the-counter medication, and a "documentation error".

An SA Health spokesperson said the errors did not cause harm.

"All incidents were thoroughly investigated and appropriate follow up action [was] taken," the spokesperson told the ABC.

While SA Health operates a clinical in-reach service at Kurlana Tapa Youth Justice Centre six days per week, operational unit staff are responsible for administering medication to the children in custody.

Last year, SA's Chief Psychiatrist and the Youth Training Centre Visitor raised concerns about the lack of a 24/7 health service at the site , writing in a joint report tabled in state parliament that the absence "undermines timely and appropriate clinical care".

Kurlana Tapa Youth Justice Centre is located at Cavan. ( ABC News )

They wrote there were 10 medication errors reported at the Kurlana Tapa centre between January 2024 and January 2025.

"Clinical incidents reviewed by OCP [Office of the Chief Psychiatrist] found instances where youth workers had administered medication to residents that had not had a medical officer review nor was the medication ordered for the resident and blank paper used to document medication administration times," they wrote.

"Medication charts are handwritten, and systems are fragmented, with medication ordered through local pharmacies and managed manually by operational unit staff.

"Medication management lacks clinical oversight, raising risks related to accuracy, safety, and appropriate administration of psychiatric and general medications."

Acting Training Centre Visitor Sue Macdonald told the ABC medication errors at the centre were concerning, given some young people were on psychotropic or other "strong" medications.

The watchdog said the reported incidents could be partly attributed to human error and to the fact that medication was administered by operational staff, not health workers.

"While any medication error is a problem, I think the bigger problem is the access to healthcare for young people in the centre," she said.

Ms Macdonald said one young person at the centre had spoken to her office about being administered the wrong medication, which prompted her office to provide feedback to centre staff.

Sue Macdonald is concerned about access to healthcare for those in youth detention. ( ABC News: Ben Pettitt )

She said since the joint report by her office and the chief psychiatrist was handed down last year, the centre had improved its systems, but it still lacked a 24/7 health service — a key recommendation of the report.

According to SA Health, clinicians at Kurlana Tapa provide centre staff with "regular medication chart reviews, including clear instructions for administration".

A department spokesperson said several improvements had been made since the joint inspection report was handed down, including improved prescribing and blister pack checking processes, updated medication management procedures, and ongoing education and visual alerts to support workers in administering medication.

"This has contributed to a reduction in reported [medication error] incidents," they said, adding that "medication errors very rarely occur within the health centre".

"The external commercial pharmacy (contracted by Department for Human Services) has solid systems in place to quickly identify and rectify potential errors to ensure the safety of consumers."

SA's Chief Psychiatrist, Associate Professor Melanie Turner, said the forensic Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service (CAMHS) offered "ongoing care" for children at Kurlana Tapa to support medication review and changes, alongside a visiting GP and nursing staff.

"CAMHS provides specialised mental health support for children and young people and is well-placed to support the centre," she said.

Melanie Turner says the forensic Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service is "well-placed" to support young people at Kurlana Tapa. ( ABC News )

Ms Turner said she supported efforts by CAMHS to fill vacant clinician positions at Kurlana Tapa.

After recent hires, the centre will employ 5.2 full-time equivalent clinicians by mid-November.

Women's and Children's Health Network CEO Julie Waddington-Powell said the network was recruiting to bring the centre to its "full capacity" of 6.75 full-time equivalent clinical staff.

But she said recruitment was challenging, due to a national shortage of mental health clinicians.

"In addition to the CAMHS in-reach and specialist assessment support, the centre is supported outside of the CAMHS hours by the Women's and Children's Hospital through the emergency department and SA Ambulance Service," she said.

"Other CAMHS specialist allied health staff provide assessments as required for speech pathology, occupational therapy and advanced clinical psychology."

items.title: Regional Victorians look for health funding ahead of election
items.summary: Regional Victorians are calling for political candidates to consider health inequality ahead of the state election, with one health alliance saying Victorians outside of Melbourne continue to experience a reduced life expectancy. Kai Coff is accessing gender-affirming care via an interstate provider.

scraped.title: Regional Victorians look for health funding ahead of election
scraped.description: Regional Victorians are calling for political candidates to consider health inequality ahead of the state election, with one health alliance saying Victorians outside of Melbourne continue to experience a reduced life expectancy.
scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/grace-marshall/105562980
scraped.h1: Victorian health services seek funding support ahead of November election
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Grace Marshall

ABC Wimmera

Topic: State and Territory Elections

Kai Coff is accessing gender-affirming care via an interstate provider. ( ABC News: Grace Marshall )

Regional Victorians and healthcare providers are advocating for improved access and funding to reduce health inequality ahead of the November state election.

Victorian Alliance of Rural and Regional Community Health (ARRCH) chair Sean Duffy said population health data across the country shows people living in rural and regional areas have a lower life expectancy.

"People living in remote Victoria are living somewhere between five and seven years less than people in Melbourne," he said.

The alliance said this inequity in life expectancy was due to a delayed healthcare response in the regions.

"I think it's a difficult conversation to confront," Mr Duffy said.

"Whether it's access to emergency departments or ongoing treatment of a chronic condition, people in rural and regional Victoria are disadvantaged."

Factors such as higher rates of chronic diseases including diabetes, respiratory conditions, cardiac conditions and higher rates of obesity were leading to shorter life expectancies, the alliance said.

"We know that with the available supports in rural Victoria, it's near or impossible for people to access specialist support," Mr Duffy said.

He said he was advocating for a separate funding model which "could see a reduction in the inequity between life expectancies".

"It is so much more expensive to deliver services, and it is so much harder to recruit the professions," Mr Duffy said.

"Less than 1 per cent of the total health budget in Victoria is spent on community health.

"If we shifted that to say 3 per cent, we will stop people going to hospital.

"And we will improve the lives of people."

Sean Duffy says your life expectancy decreases the further from Melbourne you live. ( Supplied: ARRCH )

For people experiencing homelessness, a regional postcode only adds to the inequity in health outcomes.

"The smaller health problems can quickly escalate," Council to Homeless Persons chief executive Deborah Di Natale said.

"It's harder to keep appointments if you don't have a phone or reliable transport.

Deborah Di Natale says health care is often not a priority for those experiencing homelessness. ( ABC News: Jesse Thompson )

According to the 2021 Census, approximately 30,000 Victorians were without a home.

The Council to Homeless Persons said it was advocating for a Victorian homelessness strategy.

"That's because homelessness creates severe physical and mental health impacts.

"I would like all political parties to commit to a Victorian homelessness strategy that would enable us to approach homelessness as an all-of-government response.

"Every Victorian deserves the dignity of a home."

In Central Victoria, Bendigo Community Health Services (BCHS) said it was seeing success in a trial program that supports people sleeping rough with access to mental and physical health care.

BCHS chief executive Mandy Hutchinson said at least four lives had been saved as a result of the program in the initial months of the trial.

"People that are sleeping rough are getting to their appointments now," Ms Hutchinson said.

"It's been a real win for people getting better access.

"We're putting in our own resources to try and get a better system in place because the system's currently failing."

To learn more about the key electorates, candidates and swing seats in the coming election, head to this guide from the ABC's Chief Elections and Data Analyst Casey Briggs.

A complex health system is made more difficult when English is a second or third language.

Ethnic Council of Shepparton and District case manager Abdullah Naveed spends his spare time supporting migrants and refugees through the health system.

Mr Naveed immigrated to Australia in 2014 and speaks five languages, including Afghan languages Dari and Pashto as well as Persian and Urdu.

Interpreting is not his job, but Mr Naveed said he received "many many calls whilst people are with GPs requesting interpreting via the telephone".

"They don't have any other facilities."

Abdullah Naveed is translating important health care information to refugees and migrants in his spare time. ( ABC News: Rhiannon Tuffield )

Mr Naveed said low literacy and language barriers impacted migrants' ability to access healthcare.

"When the patient can't understand the doctor about the medication, about the next appointment or any other advice, then the patient suffers," Mr Naveed said.

"I try my best whenever I can, even when I receive calls at midnight."

Analysis by Patricia Karvelas

Analysis by Patricia Karvelas

Topic: State and Territory Elections

Topic: Prisons

Topic: Young People

In north-west Victoria, people accessing gender-affirming care have limited options.

When trans man Kai Coff first started looking for access to gender affirming care in Mildura, he could not find it.

After a recommendation from a trans friend, Mr Coff is now accessing gender affirming care via telehealth from a Queensland GP.

"This gender clinic was recommended to me by another trans person, and that was the only experience I had with outside help," he said.

But Mr Coff would prefer something local and close to home.

"If they say yes, good. If they say no, then find someone else.

"That's really all I've got at the moment."

Kai Coff's family has been extremely supportive in helping Kai navigate a complex and overwhelming health system. ( Supplied: Kellie Coff )

Findings from a 2023 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare study found easy access to gender affirming care was associated with lower psychological distress and suicidal thoughts.

Participants who were able to easily access gender-affirming care when needed were less likely to experience suicidal thoughts.

LGBTIQA+ Victoria commissioner Joe Ball said that all services were under pressure in regional Victoria but "to be LGBTIQA+ it's another pressure".

" There's a reduced number of services like GPs etc. in regional Victoria already," he said.

"LGBTIQA+ people might only have a small selection of people to choose from, so it's a compounded pressure that they're experiencing."

Mr Duffy acknowledged how difficult access to care was in regional and rural Victoria for trans people.

"It's impossible for transgender people to access specialist support right across regional Victoria," he said.

"More often than not, people have to travel, and they have to travel extensive distances.

"And there's extensive wait lists."

Joining a local Mildura theatre group was where Kai was first able to feel accepted. ( Supplied: Kellie Coff )

An uplift in funding for the community health sector in regional and rural towns would be transformational, Ms Hutchinson said.

"If we had an uplift we could be responding even better to what's happening in the community," she said.

"Our greatest hope is that we get some commitments from potential Governments to better support community health.

"The whole idea of our work is to try and keep people out of the health system if we can."

Mr Duffy said increasing the funding was a "no-brainer".

"Let's be proactive, let's intervene early," he said.

"We will stop people going to hospital."

In its campaign launch, Labor committed to slashing surgery waitlists by half, and a spokesperson said the party had delivered record health funding while in government and was aiming to also slash emergency wait times by 20 per cent.

Shadow health minister Georgie Crozier said the coalition would incentivise health professionals to work in regional Victoria through incentives of up to $10,000.

items.title: Millions to swelter as new Sydney airport turns into summer 'heat sink'
items.summary: In a suburb that has previously recorded peaks of 50.1C on extreme heat days during summer, the new airport could essentially act as a "heat sink", heating up millions of surrounding homes. The new Western Sydney International Airport could make nearby homes hotter this year, according to one academic.

scraped.title: Millions to swelter as new Sydney airport turns into summer 'heat sink'
scraped.description: In a suburb that has previously recorded peaks of 50.1C on extreme heat days during summer, the new airport could essentially act as a "heat sink", heating up millions of surrounding homes.
scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/miriah-davis/105680756
scraped.h1: Summer to turn Western Sydney airport into 'large heat sink', academic says
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Miriah Davis

Topic: Urban Development and Planning

The new Western Sydney International Airport could make nearby homes hotter this year, according to one academic. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )

In Western Sydney, oppressive heat is part of everyday life when summer rolls around, with temperatures in some suburbs regularly exceeding 40 degrees Celsius.

The sprawling 1,780 hectare Nancy Bird Walton Airport site is located in Badgerys Creek, a suburb that has previously recorded peaks of 50.1C on extreme heat days during summer.

Sebastian Pfautsch, a professor of urban planning at Western Sydney University who has spent years gathering data on the effects of urban heat, is concerned the region's new airport could act as a heat sink making nearby homes even hotter.

The Badgerys Creek area has previously hit temperatures in the 50s. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )

A heat sink is a term that refers to a localised area that absorbs lots of solar radiation and then re-radiates it making the environment around it warmer, he explained.

Nearby suburbs, like St Marys, have hit 48.9C, the same temperature that made Penrith the hottest place on Earth on a day in 2020 .

Professor Pfautsch said the airport conditions could impede southerly winds for Penrith, which normally produce a cooling effect during extreme heat in the summer.

"Everything we know points towards the airport being a very large heat sink, so we have masses of unshaded black tarmac that, of course, acts like a local island that absorbs heat during the day and makes the air warmer," he said.

"The cooling that naturally would occur from the south towards the north, so into Penrith, St Marys, Emu Plains, that area, that is now reduced because of hot air being produced around the airport and that's from the tarmac."

Sebastian Pfautsch from the University of Western Sydney. ( Supplied )

Summer temperatures in Western Sydney can be between 8C and 10C hotter compared to eastern and coastal areas, where there are sea breezes and higher annual rainfall.

A spokesperson for Western Sydney International Airport (WSI) said climate change risk assessments were carried out at every phase of the airport's design and construction.

"We mitigated every high and severe risk for climate change scenarios to 2090, implementing measures to protect airport operations from heat-related disruption," the spokesperson said.

"This work was independently verified by the Infrastructure Sustainability Council and/or the Green Building Council of Australia."

An abundance of dense concrete , lack of shade and housing with dark roofing in the region are additional driving factors for hotter conditions, as hard surfaces retain more heat than in spaces with vegetation.

A "shocking" warning that heatwave deaths could skyrocket brings the issue of urban heat back into sharp focus, particularly in the city's west.

Professor Pfautsch said a massive infrastructure project like WSI, in what already was historically the hottest part of Sydney, required offset measures.

"We're accelerating heat because of all the additional activity," he said of the 24/7 airport.

"There's lots of lots of dark surfaces that absorb heat, lots of additional car traffic, big trucks, lots of workers. All of that produces heat. Where are the offset measures for that?"

Professor Pfautsch says the activity at the new airport will impact workers and local residents. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring )

He said tree canopies and blue infrastructure such as lakes and canals or using reflective tarmac paint for runways could mitigate the urban heating effect of the new airport.

"There's so much that we could do to actually inform how this whole airport aerotropolis area in central south-western Sydney could operate better during our hot summers," he said.

"We really need to do something for the people that still live there and work there."

ABC meteorologist Tom Saunders said the average mid-summer maximum temperature at WSI was about 30C, while Sydney Airport's mean maximum was 26.7C.

He said WSI could be up to 8C warmer than Sydney Airport depending on the wind direction and this summer was "looking particularly hot".

He said according to climatological data, days where temperatures exceed 40C typically arrive from December, and the region averaged about three days per year above 40C.

Summer temperatures in Western Sydney can be between eight and 10 degrees hotter. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )

Jason Middleton from the School of Aviation at the University of New South Wales said hotter temperatures affected engine performance and made take-offs and landings more challenging.

"The air becomes less dense at higher altitudes, and aircraft performance [both aerodynamic lift needed to take off, and engine thrust needed to take off] are lower in less dense air," he said.

Professor Middleton said thinner air density meant the landing distance and the take-off distance would be much longer than usual, although this was likely to impact larger aircraft.

For example, an Airbus A380 at maximum take-off weight would require a take-off distance far in excess of the available runway, if the temperature was over 35C and winds were light, he said.

"Such a flight would need to reduce payload in order to make a safe take-off within the available runway."

He said he did not expect medium-passenger or smaller aircraft, like the A320 and Dash 8, to be affected by hot days at WSI but said he observed some instances extreme heat grounded the aircraft at airports in regional Queensland.

"In Queensland, in the summer, they couldn't take everyone who was booked because it was so hot," he said.

"The fuel and the weight of the passengers and their baggage, they were too heavy to get off on the limited runway length at the airports."

During extreme heat planes need extra runway length. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )

Professor Middleton said turbulence from crosswinds could also prove challenging for flights landing at WSI.

"When you get very strong south-westerly winds, which you do typically get in August, you get west to south-westerly winds and they create turbulence and Western Sydney International Airport is basically in a position where it's susceptible to that."

He said days when turbulence is predicted to be severe "could be a real problem", as flights may be diverted to the heavily congested Sydney Airport.

"I can see potential problems happening down the road there where the overload from when [WSI] is not able to be used … the aircraft will have to go to Sydney Airport and Sydney will get bogged down."

Unsurprisingly, following the scandal involving now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy, Congress is looking to further restrict exports of AI chips. Both Democrats and Republicans have voiced support for various measures and bills that would tighten rules and have demanded that Huang and other Nvidia leaders testify before Congress.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has already said that Huang and the Trump administration need to answer to Congress . Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has also sent letters to both Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick calling on them to publicly testify to the committee.

Bills such as the Remote Access Security Act , first introduced in the House in April 2025 but stalled in the Senate, are receiving renewed interest. While that specific bill might not become law, House Speaker Mike Johnson has said there is “growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China,” according to Reuters . Johnson has also said that he personally supports efforts to restrict China’s access to powerful AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

Apple’s smart glasses are among the worst-kept secrets in the tech world. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says the company’s first model, which will lack augmented reality features , will be announced at June’s WWDC next year. They likely won’t ship right away, however, with Gurman saying only that “glasses shipments would begin before the end of the year.”

Key to their success will be the newly revamped Siri AI, which is adding fine-grained control over apps . By adding those features now and letting developers add support on the iPhone first, it’s hoping that its smart glasses will be able to hit the ground running.

The prototypes, dubbed N50, are currently running a pared-down version of visionOS and a new processor based on its older smartwatch chips. They also have a MagSafe-like charger Gurman describes as “flat, rectangular” and “roughly the size of a Tic Tac,” which can be used even while still wearing the glasses.

In addition to Apple putting an emphasis on style , privacy , and audio quality, the company is also hoping that Wi-Fi connectivity will grant them a certain amount of freedom, despite relying on an iPhone to actually execute many tasks:

The glasses have Wi-Fi, allowing certain functions outside of third-party apps to continue working when the iPhone isn’t nearby. Users could theoretically keep listening to audio over Wi-Fi after walking away from their phones, for instance, though the eyewear won’t operate as a fully independent device. Apple is also emphasizing the sound quality, which employees have said is industry-leading, with support for phone calls, music playback and FaceTime audio communication.

scraped.title: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause
scraped.description: COVID-19 lockdowns cut global fire activity by 12.3 percent.
scraped.h1: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause
scraped.body_text:
COVID-19 lockdowns cut global fire activity by 12.3 percent.

Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.

Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.

A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.

Fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without big fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.

Weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.

Human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.

The double-sided role of humans in fire also adds to the difficulty. Humans do start fires, but they also put them out. Firefighters contain fires that could have gone worse if no action had been taken and can keep them from spreading. Humans can also take preventative actions, such as clearing flammable material.

Sometimes the line between starting fires and preventing them becomes blurred. One way to clear out flammable material is to intentionally set fires to make future fires more manageable. However, these fires are hard to distinguish from other fires through satellite monitoring.

An experiment is one way to find out how humans affect wildfires. If everyone stayed home under the same weather, their impact on fires would be revealed. This is why Wang’s research team focused on the COVID-19 era. It was what’s called a “natural experiment,” in which experimental conditions arose without any action by researchers.

Wang explained: “Human activity and climate normally vary together, because seasons, farming calendars, and weather all shape both fire and human behavior. The early-2020 lockdowns produced an abrupt, large-scale drop in human mobility, and the timing differed across countries while the weather did not change in the same way. This gave us a natural experiment.”

The researchers defined the period of restricted mobility by checking regional lockdown orders and mobile phone location data. Data from NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Suomi NPP satellite helped the team track fires. Its VIIRS sensor detects heat signatures from fires at a spatial resolution of 375 meters. Each hot spot the satellite detects counts as an active-fire detection, meaning one large fire can appear as multiple spots. However, the satellite records both wildfires and prescribed burns without distinguishing between them. As a result, the intent behind each fire remains unknown.

In the study, detections during the 2020 restriction periods were compared with those from the same weeks in 2013–2019. Weather conditions weren’t exactly the same as in past years, which was accounted for.

The results show that areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the recent-past average. The drop varied by vegetation type. In forests, fires decreased by about 27.7 percent, while grasslands decreased by 8.4 percent. Shrublands, savannas, and croplands didn’t show much difference. The researchers interpret this to mean that humans are a major cause of fires in forests and grasslands.

Controlling for weather factors was important in the study. Without adjustments, the drop was only 5.8 percent, which was not statistically significant. After controlling for weather, however, the estimated decline increased to 12.3 percent. If weather in 2020 were more favorable to fires than in previous years, it might have masked some of the human impact.

The 12.3 percent decrease in fire detections doesn’t mean that humans directly caused this share of fires. Restricting human activity shrank both humans’ impact on starting fires and likely limited their impact on extinguishing them. The 12.3 percent figure is the net effect after these two opposing forces partly cancel out.

Wang said, “The 12.3 percent is a net effect, not the share of fires caused by humans; opposing changes in ignition and suppression mean it does not capture the full magnitude of human influence.”

In regional data, some areas experienced a considerable increase in fire after human mobility was restricted. Most of South America, southern Africa, and northeast Asia saw an increase in fire during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Notable increases include 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India, and 70.7 percent in Honduras.

There are no direct field data showing why this occurred. The researchers inferred that diminished fire suppression capacity resulted in more fires in these locations, but Wang acknowledged, “It is an inference, not a direct observation.” That inference was based in part on earlier studies that suggested that weaker fire management in Colombia and Madagascar contributed to increased fires.

One line of evidence is how fires reacted to different levels of mobility loss, based on fire counts in 0.5-degree grid cells. In countries with fewer fires, fire declined in almost a straight line as mobility decreased. But countries that experienced more fires showed a slow increase that leveled off at about 27 percent on average as mobility fell. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that different mechanisms were at work. The steady decline fits fewer human-driven ignitions, while the gradual rise points to weakened suppression. But Wang mentioned that there could be other reasons, such as changes in local land use.

Mobility restrictions may also have disrupted fire management activities, which could mean that fewer fires were set for management purposes. The researchers examined 12 countries with records of prescribed burning. The area burned by prescribed fires in 2020 decreased by about half compared to the 2013–2019 average. Of course, the locations and sizes of prescribed burns also shift from year to year with fire return intervals and land-management cycles, which complicates this analysis.

When areas subjected to prescribed burning were excluded in those 12 countries, the decline in fires there shrank from 45.3 percent to 27.8 percent.

This research has limits partly because it relied on mobile phone data to track human movement. This kind of data might not capture human activity in rural areas where coverage may be limited. Also, the analysis focused only on the first half of each year, so the impact on regions where fires happen more frequently in the latter half of the year, such as the western US, may not have been fully captured.

Wang explained that this quasi-experimental design provides strong associational evidence but is not a controlled experiment.

Wang emphasized that the study is not an evaluation of fire policies. The analysis does, however, suggest that there’s no single ideal policy response. Where fires decreased, human ignition seems to dominate. In those areas, reducing accidental ignitions through public education and maintaining beneficial prescribed burning can be important. On the other hand, areas where fires increased might need to address reduced monitoring and suppression. Maintaining firefighting and patrol capacity during disruptions can be important there.

Wang added, “Overall, a uniform policy is unlikely to work, and strategies should be tailored to local human-fire relationships.” Fire-risk projections might benefit from accounting for human behavior. That way, more accurate fire projections can be made even as weather and society change.

Cell Reports Sustainability, 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.crsus.2026.100860

scraped.title: With Starship catch, SpaceX still shows it can dazzle the world
scraped.description: It felt like stepping into the future.
scraped.h1: SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there’s a catch
scraped.body_text:
It felt like stepping into the future.

STARBASE, Texas —The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.

Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.

Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.

This was a breathtaking feat; a brilliant technical achievement that required the best engineering minds to think through a million different, difficult problems. And on Saturday evening, following a handful of practice runs into the Indian Ocean, they did it before the entire world.

Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power, and be captured by the tower.

It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before, by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks.

Nevertheless, it happened.

Humans have built reusable spacecraft that flew into orbit before. In the 1970s, flush with confidence after the triumphant Moon landings, NASA designed and built several Space Shuttles. They had solid rocket boosters that were fished from the ocean and reused. The large orange external tank was not recovered after each flight, but the orbiters went to space for two weeks, or even longer, before returning to Earth and landing on a runway.

The shuttles were engineering marvels. But during the return to Earth they acted as gliders, not igniting their engines. And their heat shields were delicate flowers, requiring painstaking refurbishment after each flight. At the outset of the shuttle program, the space agency contemplated sending dozens of humans into space at a time, and carrying cargo at a cost as low of $25 per pound.

Reality never matched these rosy projections. The crew space capped out at seven astronauts, and the cost-per-pound was closer to $25,000. Each orbiter cost an extraordinary amount of money to build; NASA only ever built five that went to space.

SpaceX has five Starships in an advanced state of development at Starbase today; and its factory houses the components for a dozen more. The company can currently manufacture a Starship upper stage in its South Texas Starfactory every three weeks. The factory was sized to produce a ship every three days. When SpaceX founder Elon Musk discussed these build targets in an interview five years ago, he sounded mad. But he no longer does.

The Space Shuttle was nearly a fully reusable space launch system, but it fell far short of low-cost, rapid launch. Over 30 years the vehicle made 135 flights. Within a few years SpaceX aims to fly 135 times a year, then thousands of times.

Such was the significance of Saturday. SpaceX aspires to fundamentally change the relationship between humanity and the heavens. The first step is to get the entire rocket back. SpaceX has now returned both elements of a Starship rocket safely to its launch tower. It will take time to reach a high rate of success with such landings, but Saturday’s safe return offered a proof of concept.

The landings will come with increasing frequency; and so will the launches. Over time SpaceX will perfect the heat shield that is likely to be the most difficult aspect of rapid reuse. And eventually, as difficult as it may be to believe, what we experienced with amazement this weekend will become routine. One day, we will take this all for granted.

But not today.

scraped.h1: Flaming Hydra’s new Kickstarter campaign rethinks e-book ownership and digital lending

Here’s a big promise: A new Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.”

That’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project , an initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra . If you back The Phoenix Project, you’re supporting three things — a one-off print magazine designed to celebrate “the values and fun of the early internet,” a new e-book service for libraries, and a newsletter subscription/archiving program that’s also designed for libraries.

To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.”

Bustillos told me that these issues have been highlighted on Flaming Hydra itself, for example when Tal Levin wrote about finding countless AI-generated clones of his book on Amazon. By “creating an ecosystem that is based in people working together, who are offering their stuff in a context that is controlled and doesn’t allow” others to create and sell AI-generated clones, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra is “part of the human project.”

“AI is not this unstoppable force,” she added. “If people just set up publishing pipelines and networks and organizations that are dedicated to the human internet, people who want to read stuff can go to them, and it’s actually completely isolated from mechanistic interference.”

The Phoenix Project fits into this vision by making the work of human writers more accessible to libraries.

Back in 2020, Bustillos wrote about the e-book systems dominating libraries and schools. In one example, instead of just buying a book, a school had to pay $27 per student per year for continued access to copies of “The Diary of Anne Frank.”

This is symptomatic of a broader system that treats true ownership of e-books and other digital media as a thing of the past. Instead, we “license” these e-books from their publishers, and they can be altered or removed at any time.

“E-books are books,” Bustillos said. “They’re not some other thing. They are books, and people should be able to own them, and libraries should be able to own them, and media should be able to be owned. All digital media should be able to be owned.”

In her view, ownership boils down to a simple question: “If you are at the mercy of somebody who can shut the book off, you do not own it.”

So even beyond the question of ongoing payments, there have also been examples of e-books being altered or removed from readers’ devices long after their purchase. Bustillos acknowledged that for individual pieces of media, this distinction may not seem like a big deal, “but if it’s all the textbooks for everybody, if it’s all the books,” then it’s a real problem.

Flaming Hydra and The Phoenix Project seek to solve this by letting libraries truly purchase and own e-books. They can then lend those e-books to their patrons through a new, open source “library in a box” system called Lenny for Libraries .

The Phoenix Project is starting by offering five new e-books from Flaming Hydra writers, including collections of writing from The Awl, and of essays by Tom Scocca and Bustillos herself. That might sound like a relatively small start, but Bustillos said she’s talking to library consortiums and author groups, and the goal here is to “change the conversation” around e-books and digital archiving and lending. So The Phoenix Project could be paving the way for other initiatives that follow a similar model.

Similarly, The Phoenix Foundry Archive is designed to make paywalled newsletter content available to libraries. Bustillos noted that “so much of the best journalism, criticism, essays” is now being published in paywalled newsletters that are inaccessible to libraries (as well as the Internet Archive).

With Phoenix, newsletter writers (starting with those who use Ghost, with support for additional newsletter platforms coming in the future) will be able to offer subscriptions to libraries, similar to the way libraries can subscribe to newspapers and magazines. Once it’s set up, Phoenix will automatically convert whichever newsletter posts the writer wants into EPUB documents, which are then sent to libraries for digital lending.

Flaming Hydra has been working on all this even before launching the Kickstarter, and Bustillos said she was grateful for the financial support from backers like Anand Raganathan, Brewster Kahle, and Paul Ford. But by turning to crowdfunding, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra can better protect the work, ensuring that it remains sustainable and independent.

“We don’t have to be at the mercy of anybody, and it also protects editorial independence,” she said. “Those things go hand in hand.”

Flaming Hydra seeks to raise $30,000 for The Phoenix Project , with the campaign ending on November 27.

Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility !

I am traveling through Portugal now that Web Summit has wrapped up, so please enjoy this shortened edition.

Web Summit leaned heavily into Chinese founders and companies this year. The opening remarks from Web Summit co-founder Paddy Cosgrave drove the point home when he said the superstars of the future are coming from China, not California. He also gave a strong endorsement of China and open source technology when he noted that Chinese companies are building more of our shared future than anyone else.

These remarks carried a different kind of weight just a few days later as the news spread throughout the conference that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from his leadership post after admitting to an affair with an alleged spy.

The former CEO, after all, has been one of the strongest proponents for open source in the United States. And anyone who has followed the emergence of autonomous vehicle tech knows how central Nvidia is to that ecosystem.

Nvidia is a major supplier of AI computing technology to the industry — although the degree of reliance varies. Some companies are using Nvidia’s automotive processors to run automated driving software, while others are using Nvidia GPUs to train autonomous driving models. And then there are the full-stack partnerships, which includes Mercedes-Benz, Zoox, and Wayve.

I spoke to Leo Wang , the CFO of Chinese autonomous vehicle company Pony.ai , this week. I asked him about the challenges China’s self-driving industry faces and what he thinks will happen if the fallout from Huang’s resignation results in even stricter export controls on Nvidia chips shipped to China.

Demand is already far greater than supply, Wang said, noting that it’s one of the pain points Pony.ai struggles with. The company’s strategy is twofold. Engineers are directed to be as efficient as possible when deploying its training models. That might mean using midtier compute resources instead of high-end ones, he said.

Pony.ai is also turning more to domestically produced chips to help close the gap.

“If you look at the whole ecosystem, especially in recent years, definitely domestic chips in China also get lots of attention and development,” he said, noting that these chips provide another option for AI training. “I think that gives us some flexibility.”

When asked what he thinks will happen if export restrictions on Nvidia chips tighten, Wang said Chinese companies have already been preparing.

“If you look at the whole situation, this has been developing for already a couple of years,” he said. “Everyone, I would say, is also practicing kind of like a Plan B for a few years, so at least if you think about that, I would say there are alternatives. Although cost-effectiveness-wise, probably it’s not the best choice yet. But still, it’s an alternative way that already exists and which is more mature than a few years ago.”

May Mobility plans to use the Volkswagen all-electric ID. Buzz for its global ride-hailing platform. The company said it is targeting the deployment of more than 10,000 autonomous vehicles through 2031. This does not mean that VW’s MOIA group is ditching Mobileye, I have been told. Instead, VW told me, the company is offering an automated driving-ready base vehicle to other companies that develop their own self-driving systems. (This was just presented last month during Nvidia GTC in Berlin.)

Newmo , a Japanese robotaxi startup, raised a ¥20.8 billion (roughly $135 million) round led by KDDI.

ParkBee , a Dutch parking technology company, acquired Mobian’s city and parking operations.

Port , an urban logistics company, raised €14.5 million in a round led by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Balnord.

Lucid reported Q3 revenue of $350 million, below Wall Street expectations, and it is still losing money. Although its Q3 net loss did narrow to $830.9 million. Notably, the EV maker increased its delayed draw term loan from its largest shareholder, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, to $1.75 billion.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is investigating a Waymo software recall from a year ago that was issued after numerous reports that its robotaxis were illegally passing school buses. The agency said that a majority of these reported incidents occurred after the company deployed a software update intended to fix the problem. Sources familiar with Waymo tell me that there have not been school bus-related incidents since March. I have not been able to independently verify that with the Austin Independent School District.

The Tesla Cybertruck will live on through next summer, but production will ultimately end , according to Elon Musk, who defended the polarizing steel-clad truck.

Tesla is expanding its robotaxi service to San Antonio, Texas, as it seeks to compete with Waymo and position itself as more than just an automaker.

Uber is launching a new service that lets customers reserve and pay for parking in major U.S. cities, about nine months after the ride-hailing company acquired parking app SpotHero. Meanwhile, the company is notifying thousands of drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers.

United Airlines will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf.

We’ve been reviewing a bunch of new gadgets and hardware at TechCrunch this year: dumb phones , bird feeders , health trackers , slushy machines , AI mattress pads , you name it. Sometimes we think they’re unnecessary and expensive , but other times, we try out devices that we love so much that we go out and buy them ourselves.

If these products can impress a group of (sometimes) curmudgeonly tech reporters, then they’re sure to please whoever you’re shopping for this holiday season.

We’ve reviewed a lot of e-readers this year. What can we say? We’re nerds. We work for a tech website. But after trying devices from the usual suspects as well as some wildcards, we have recommendations. Evidently, 2026 was the year we fell in love with the pocket-sized e-reader.

It’s an e-reader so small that it can fit in your wallet, or even magnetize to the back of your phone. Do you dream of a world where instead of scrolling Instagram when you’re waiting in line for coffee, you actually opt to read books? There’s really something special about the X3, and it’s only $55 during Xteink’s Black Friday sale. Fair warning, it takes some fiddling with to set up, and it has no integration with Kindle, Libby, or any other apps, so only buy this for someone willing to do a bit of Reddit browsing and tinkering to get it up and running.

If you aren’t planning to magnetize the XTeink to your phone, you’ve got to go with the X4 Pro . It’s slightly bigger, but it has a backlight, which makes it way more versatile. After using both the X3 and the X4 Pro, I find that the backlight really is a game changer, since I do a lot of reading in bed — plus, I like my Pop Socket wallet a bit too much to displace for the X3, and I’d rather just carry an extra credit card-sized device than risk forgetting my actual credit and ID cards, which I have grown too used to having on my phone.

If I’m being honest, reading my colleague Aisha Malik’s review of the Boox Palma Pro 2 is making me want to buy one. I love using the Xteink e-readers, but they don’t connect to any outside apps. As a hardcore Libby power user (a phrase I am saying in earnest sincerity), it’s a bit frustrating that I can’t get my library books on Xteink e-readers. The same goes for apps like Kobo and Kindle, where any e-book you already own cannot be transferred out of the Amazon ecosystem unless the publisher agrees, which most do not.

If you’re looking for an e-reader with a screen that’s actually book-sized, my favorite that I’ve used is the Kobo Libra Colour , which is $259. The Amazon Paperwhite line is great, but c’mon, Amazon. Branch out!

Hey, we’ve all got to eat. And if you want, you can make that eating process overly techy. Why not?

The Ember Mug 3 is the latest iteration in Ember’s line of coffee/tea cups that actually stay warm. Our reviewer Lauren Forristal especially appreciated that you no longer need to use your phone app to change the mug’s temperature, which seems like it would be really annoying!

This mug is perfect for gifting to someone, or to put on your own wishlist — you might not want to spend $99 on a mug for yourself, but these sorts of luxury, nice-to-haves are what holidays are made for!

Ah, Ninja, the premiere company in the business of turning every appliance into a two-in-one air fryer. I jest, but at least Ninja knows it’s onto something. Despite the high price point, Lauren says that this new product made “a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one.” You can’t buy more counter space (without moving), but you can buy more versatile appliances.

Sure, there are cheaper ice makers on the market. But Aisha clarifies that this is the ice maker for “those who crave what’s called ‘the good ice.’” If you feel so passionately about the ice in your beverages that you know what she means, then maybe this is for you.

What they really want is a Mac mini or Claude subscription, but if that’s out of budget, we have some other ideas that might impress your AI-pilled, vibe-coder loved ones…

When I asked my colleague Lucas Ropek what about his favorite product he reviewed this year, he mentioned the Codex Micro . Some hard-core coders — who the product is aimed toward — have found this thing less than pleasing, but Lucas seems to have had fun figuring out this first attempt by OpenAI at hardware.

Best case, it’s a productivity game-changer for your friend who has a hardworking team of AI agents within the OpenAI ecosystem. Worst case, this will be a great piece of tech history in a few years.

As people have become more conscious about how much time they spend online, new tech has emerged that, ironically, is designed to keep you away from tech. Some of these products can really make a difference in your life.

For about six months, I’ve consistently used the Brick to prevent me from using social media as the last thing I do before bed, or the first thing in the morning. Some people use it to help them focus during the work day, but evidently, I was not the only one who needed Brick’s help with sleep. The company recently launched its second device, Brick Night, which “Bricks” your phone when you are in the same room. You can customize the times that the Brick Night is active, so it’s not as though you can never, ever use social media in your room. Both Brick and Brick Night are very customizable, so you can create the perfect set-up tailored to your needs.

It’s embarrassing how whole-heartedly I recommend the Brick, which is basically just a hunk of plastic with an NFC chip in it and a companion app. But my sleep has improved significantly — I even do 8 AM Pilates now. Who am I?

I’ve tried out far pricier smart phone alternatives, but the Dumb Phone was both the most affordable, and the most usable for me. In the humble shell of a $20 TCL flip phone , Dumb Co loads its own software so that users can access apps like WhatsApp, Spotify, Apple Music, and Uber. You can even access iMessage through a third-party app, though Apple could probably get that shut down… no one tell Apple, please!

The Dumb Phone is particularly usable because it’s not intended to be a complete replacement for your smartphone — it’s more like a companion device that you can take out with you when you want to feel more present in the world but still may need to call an Uber home.

Wearable health trackers are pretty common nowadays, but after reviewing several different rings and wristbands , Aisha has named a winner.

There are a lot of ugly health trackers. And then there’s the Oura Ring 5 , the leading smart ring maker’s first product that’s thin enough to wear without loudly broadcasting to the world that you’re monitoring your heart rate. (For what it’s worth, I tried the RingConn 3 — which is about the same size as Oura Ring 5 — but returned it, unsatisfied. Womp womp.) Aisha notes in her review that the newest Oura ring is more durable, has a better battery life, and looks more premium than its predecessors.

items.title: Bessent calls for ‘dramatic shakeup’ at Nvidia, urges outside CEO
items.summary: Bessent has criticized Howard Lutnick’s department over suspected chip diversion to China while defending President Donald Trump’s handling of the matter.

scraped.title: Bessent calls for ‘dramatic shakeup’ at Nvidia, urges outside CEO
scraped.description: Bessent has criticized Howard Lutnick’s department over suspected chip diversion to China while defending President Donald Trump’s handling of the matter.
scraped.author: Luke Fountain
scraped.h1: Bessent calls for ‘dramatic shakeup’ at Nvidia, urges outside CEO
scraped.body_text:
In this article

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation, questioning whether the chipmaker pursued illicit sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to boost earnings.

Bessent said Nvidia's board should look outside the company for its next chief executive and suggested other executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls.

"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said in an interview on Fox News.

The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the suspected diversion of advanced AI chips to China, even as the Treasury secretary continues to defend President Donald Trump's handling of the matter.

Both Bessent and Lutnick are expected to accompany Trump to China this week, Semafor reported Sunday, putting the two Cabinet secretaries alongside the president as he prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit.

A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in Lutnick, despite mounting scrutiny of the secretary’s handling of the Nvidia matter.

Huang resigned Thursday following revelations about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed , whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.

Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO.

Bessent suggested Sunday that Nvidia's problems extended well beyond Huang.

"If this were a bank and they hadn't complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed," Bessent said, referring to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

Bessent also questioned Nvidia's financial disclosures, pointing to a surge in reported Singapore revenue as its China sales fell.

Nvidia stopped separately reporting Singapore revenue in November 2025, saying a new methodology based on customers' headquarters rather than billing addresses better reflected the geographic distribution of its sales.

Bessent's remarks came two days after he told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that several federal agencies had supported adding Megaspeed to the government's export blacklist for months.

"But Commerce has the pen," Bessent said.

The public rebuke followed reporting by Axios that Bessent confronted Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over Commerce's failure to act against Megaspeed. Commerce denied that the confrontation took place.

Lutnick is also facing scrutiny over his family's financial ties to Nvidia. CNBC reported Friday that Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm formerly run by Lutnick and now led by his sons, has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners.

Cantor said Nvidia share holdings fell nearly 50% over six months as national security concerns surrounding Huang escalated. The positions were associated with client swap transactions, not proprietary investments, the investment bank said.

There is no evidence Lutnick shared sensitive information with his sons or that Cantor traded on such information.

Bessent on Sunday said Trump had drawn a firm line against sales of chips more advanced than Nvidia's H200 to China . Trump himself authorized H200 sales to approved Chinese customers in December —following months of lobbying by Huang — in an arrangement under which the U.S. government would receive a 25% cut.

Bessent's latest criticism comes two days before Nvidia is scheduled to report its first quarterly earnings since Huang's departure.

items.title: Anthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spot
items.summary: Anthropic's IPO has outsized importance in the tech industry, which is heavily invested in the AI lab and is desperate for some positive momentum.

scraped.title: Anthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spot
scraped.description: Anthropic's IPO has outsized importance in the tech industry, which is heavily invested in the AI lab and is desperate for some positive momentum.
scraped.author: Jordan Novet
scraped.h1: Anthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spot
scraped.body_text:
In this article

Between rising interest rates, a nationwide AI backlash, a major political shift in Washington, D.C., and the sudden ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , the tech industry is under mounting strain.

Now comes the most important tech IPO in years, and a defining event for the burgeoning but still young artificial intelligence market.

With Anthropic expected to debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, the stakes are sky-high for almost every major tech company. Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company are collectively investing $26 billion at the IPO price, which is currently expected at $70 to $78 a share. Some of those companies are existing investors, as is early backer Amazon , whose stake could be in the hundreds of billions of dollars.

In addition to all the cash on the line, tech giants also need Anthropic's spending for many years to come. The Claude creator and its top rival, OpenAI, are driving an outsized amount of the AI buildout, and are burning historic amounts of money in the process.

Anthropic has outstanding spending commitments of over $900 billion, according to its latest prospectus . It's on the hook to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon over the course of a decade, and another $400 billion with other companies for cloud capacity, according to filings and partner disclosures. The lab also made $300 billion in commitments with data center and chip partners. Anthropic intends to lay out $125 billion to $150 billion for AI chips from Google , though delivery won't start until 2028.

"The numbers are just staggering," Joe Fath, a partner at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager, said in an interview. "It's hard to get your head wrapped around it."

Cloud partners Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31% of contractual obligations, Anthropic said in its prospectus. Last year, Amazon built an Indiana data center just for Anthropic, using custom chips.

By going public now, Anthropic can raise a large portion of the money it needs to pay for the technology and infrastructure required for building and hosting its frontier models and expanding portfolio of services. The company recorded a net loss of $104 billion through the first nine months of 2026. The IPO could yield over $90 billion in proceeds, on top of Anthropic's $132 billion in existing cash, including short-term investments.

The length of Anthropic's contracts is also unique. Typically such contracts last five years or less, while Anthropic's agreement with Amazon extends for twice that amount of time.

"Realistically, anything past three to four years, you're basically throwing darts in the dark," said Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at spend management software vendor Duckbill. "It is almost a certainty that it will be renegotiated long before the culmination of that contract."

Meanwhile, a data center for Anthropic that starts leasing in 2027 has a 20-year term. For both space and computing, Anthropic is splurging now so it doesn't end up short on capacity long into the future.

"In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment," Anthropic said in the prospectus.

Anthropic and Amazon didn't provide a comment.

It's a tough time for Anthropic to hit the Nasdaq, with the offering coming as tech investors are desperate for some good news. The Nasdaq is down to start November after dropping 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025.

Rising interest rates pushed investors out of debt-heavy neoclouds , which have become a critical piece of the infrastructure buildout. And in the midterm elections earlier this month, Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress and in key gubernatorial races, while dozens of ballot measures were passed that will potentially limit new data center development across the country.

Then came the Nvidia crisis. Shares of the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom tumbled 13% this week to their lowest since July 2025, after Huang's multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, led to his ouster early Thursday. Huang was replaced on an interim basis with CFO Colette Cress , who faces a major test on Tuesday, two days before the Anthropic debut, as Nvidia is set to report quarterly results.

The ongoing Nvidia fallout and the Anthropic IPO create quite the split-screen moment for tech's heavyweights, which are closely tied to both companies.

Google will be paying particularly close attention.

The company is set to own about 13% of Anthropic after the IPO, and is backstopping the lab's $19 billion in lease commitments to Terawulf , which will supply data center space in Kentucky. If Anthropic goes insolvent, Google will step in and pay the remaining rent or a termination fee, Terawulf said .

"Everybody knows that Anthropic is going to be the future of Google," said Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google cloud partnerships leader who now advises companies.

Google didn't provide a comment.

One major impetus for Anthropic to enter costly and long-term guarantees is that OpenAI is being equally aggressive, and capacity is limited, particularly for graphics processing units. Going long can mean locking in rates as the industry confronts questions about whether data center development will slow.

"You will need to be in a rush to get infrastructure, and if you are not going to be there, you will be out of business," said Eli Mansoor, CEO of OskaQ Consulting, which advises companies on cloud negotiations. "It used to be that prices always go down, but this is changing, especially in the GPU world."

Big financial firms are lining up to help Anthropic get what it wants. Bank of America , Blackstone , Citigroup and Morgan Stanley have offered $63 billion to buy racks full of Broadcom AI chips that Anthropic will rent. Broadcom has provided a backstop with a maximum liability of $43 billion .

That's a lot of silicon and a massive bet for a five-year-old company that's never lived through a technology downturn.

"It's not a risk-free prospect, but I would call it smart investing," said David Tollen, founder of Sycamore Legal, where he specializes in IT contracts. "They're investing, in a sense, in themselves. They're putting money into something that if it succeeds, they get a piece of the action."
