items.title: 'We slept here': Flight delays linger but schedule is back on track for Monday
items.summary: Flight disruptions lingered two days after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours.

scraped.title: 'We slept here': Flight delays linger but schedule is back on track for Monday
scraped.description: Flight disruptions lingered two days after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours.
scraped.author: Leslie Josephs
scraped.h1: 'We slept here': Flight delays linger but schedule is back on track for Monday
scraped.body_text:
In this article

U.S. flights are set to run close to normal on Monday as airlines scramble to get back on track after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours on Friday.

Disruptions lingered on Sunday, but passengers were getting on their way.

More than 1,600 U.S. flights there were canceled as of noon ET and more than 4,000 were delayed, according to FlightAware data. That was far fewer than the almost 6,700 cancellations on Saturday and more than 9,200 on Sunday when the FAA halted all departures into U.S. airports.

"We slept here," said Beth Martin, who was trying to travel home to Birmingham, Alabama, from New York's LaGuardia Airport on Sunday at the end of her daughter's birthday trip. They were booked for Saturday night, and when delay announcements started rolling in from Delta Air Lines , they decided to make good use of the extra time: after strolling through Central Park, they went window shopping on Fifth Avenue.

But when the flight was canceled, the standby list on a backup flight looked grim, and their original midtown hotel was charging about $700 for an additional night, the two of them slept at LaGuardia on Saturday. She said they found wheelchairs to sleep in outside security.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday tied the issue to a router and work to update from copper wires, a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies , to a fiber-optic system. FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over to fiber optic.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," L3Harris said in a statement Saturday afternoon.

Airlines waived change fees and fare differences and offered pilots and flight attendants extra pay to ease the delays.

Customers told CNBC they were booked on several flights before getting on board.

Justine Fritz, who works in sales for a consumer goods company, was in New York for a business event on Friday. She tried five different flights before getting on a flight to Houston, then flew four hours out of her way to get back to Minneapolis after her Saturday flight was canceled. Fritz said she had so many boarding passes that TSA wouldn't let her through security at first.

"It's been bananas," she told CNBC at the gate. Fritz said she made the best of it by shopping and getting a haircut, but she's still disappointed.

"I'm missing the first hour of the Vikings game," she said.

Martin said her trip home with her daughter will take even longer. Delta booked them to Memphis, and her husband will drive the four hours from Birmingham to pick them up.

Shortly after the groundstop, the longest since 9/11, Duffy pushed Congress for as much as $50 billion for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system. A day later, Democratic lawmakers pushed back, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress's approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

"Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again," said Reps. Rick Larsen (D.-Wash.), ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and Rep. Andre Carson (D.-Ind.), ranking member of the aviation subcommittee, said in a joint statement.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has wrapped up a brief visit to the Philippines and is heading to Cambodia, as the government pushes for more trade access in the region.

On his one-night visit to Manila, Carney attended a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, announced the conclusion of free-trade negotiations with the Philippines and unveiled funding for protecting tropical rainforests.

“What Canada presents is certainty to the world,” Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu told reporters in Manila on Sunday, which was late Saturday in Canada.

Carney was among foreign leaders including U.S. President Donald Trump who were invited to the summit by the Philippine chair, who is holding the rotating presidency of ASEAN, a bloc of 11 countries.

Ottawa is continuing talks for a trade deal with ASEAN, which Sidhu said would give Canada access to smaller countries, while Canada also has deeper agreements with Indonesia and the Philippines.

“You can get more into the weeds. You can upgrade later on, when you’re dealing with (one deal that is) bilateral, as opposed to an agreement with 11 partners,” he said in Manila on Sunday, which was late Saturday in Canada.

“It’s the fastest growing region in the world, 700 million consumers, an economy valued at $6 trillion.”

Sidhu also expressed confidence for Canadian pork producers, as the Philippines moves toward restricting pork imports from a wide array of countries, including Canada.

“They’ve got a global safeguards investigation … for 60 days. Canada is not the culprit, and you’ll find out once the investigation is done,” he said.

Carney also met meet with Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on the sidelines of the summit, where he announced $540 million for an initiative to protect rainforests, as part of a project co-led by Brazil and Norway.

The money is part of a $6 billion fund promised by Ottawa this spring in support for international climate finance. It is meant to attract public and private investment for preserving biodiversity and supporting communities that rely on these ecosystems.

Through an interpreter, Lula described the money as investments that will yield a profit and not “donations, money for free.”

Carney suggested he would have further talks with Brazil, which is part of the Mercosur trade bloc with whom Canada is negotiating a trade deal. Lula’s office has previously said Carney would visit the country.

“By May, we will also have an opportunity to discuss our economic co-operation, our largest training partner in Latin America by far, (with) $15 billion dollars in trade,” Carney said.

Carney is now en route to Cambodia for a summit of the Francophonie, including a side event on technology trade in Phnom Penh.

While there, Carney will meet with Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon who is pushing for more autonomy in Quebec’s international relations, though Sidhu says Ottawa is working constructively with the province.

“Quebec has many of their own trade officers in our embassies around the world, and we’ll continue working collaboratively,” Sidhu said, noting that Quebec’s aerospace sector has recently achieved large sales in Asia.

Later this week, Carney will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit in China, months after Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to have a limited number of Chinese electrical vehicles sold in Canada.

Sidhu also said Chinese automaker Chery is among those seeking Transport Canada certification to sell lower-cost vehicles into Canada. He said some Chinese manufacturers will likely clear that process by the end of the year.

He said he is also hopeful Chinese companies will create automotive jobs for Canadians.

“There is an interest from Chinese manufacturers to utilize our workforce in Canada, but before you invest billions of dollars you need to understand the market,” he said.

“Every time I sit down with them I look at what they’re doing in Europe and I ask them how they can replicate that in Canada with Canadian supply chains, with Canadian workers.”

The minister said Canada is still navigating trade issues with China, despite some recent progress on extending access to beef, canola meal, crab and peas.

“We’re still continuing to engage on pork, on pet food and others. We’re not relenting,” he said.

Sidhu also said Canada is working with Beijing to have more opportunities for Canadian small and medium businesses to sell consumer goods to China on online platforms like Alibaba.

scraped.title: Taiwan farmers revive climate-resilient millet which disappeared 60 years ago
scraped.description: Once grown by Indigenous farmers in Taiwan in case their staple crops died, oil millet largely disappeared from fields more than 60 years ago as rice became more available.
scraped.author: AFP
scraped.h1: Taiwan Indigenous farmer revives climate-resilient millet
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Indigenous farmer Banu Ismahasan walks through a golden field of tall stalks in southeastern Taiwan , harvesting by hand the grain heads of an ancient crop resistant to extreme weather.

Once grown by Indigenous farmers in Taiwan in case their staple crops died, oil millet largely disappeared from fields more than 60 years ago as rice became more available.

Over the past decade, Ismahasan and his elderly parents have worked to revive the nearly forgotten crop in the Bunun community in Buklavu, a village surrounded by lush green mountains in Taitung county.

“We just hope to bring back many traditional Bunun crops and grow them on this land again,” Ismahasan, 48, told AFP in his oil millet field under a clear blue sky.

Oil millet, or “dill” in the Bunun language, is endemic to Taiwan and can be found growing wild in the mountains.

Ismahasan first read about the plant online and then embarked on his own research, combing through historical documents and speaking to tribal elders, including a woman who recalled last eating it half a century ago.

He discovered that Bunun farmers used to grow oil millet alongside their staple crop foxtail millet as a “back-up” when harvests failed or disasters hit.

After years of growing oil millet himself, Ismahasan came to understand why his ancestors relied on the crop.

A single oil millet seed can grow 15 to 20 panicles, or branching seed clusters, and the stems regenerate on their own, while foxtail millet typically grows one panicle per seed and must be sown again after being cut.

It has also proven hardier than foxtail millet when extreme weather or disease outbreaks have ravaged his 2.2-hectare (5.4-acre) farm.

During a drought several years ago that lasted more than 200 days, the oil millet “stayed bright green” while other crops withered, Ismahasan said.

Typhoons, floods and even a rust disease outbreak have not affected it either.

Hsing Yue-ie, a retired professor from Taiwan’s Academia Sinica and an expert in plant genetics, first heard of oil millet 15 years ago at an international forum.

Unbeknownst to Hsing, specimens of Taiwan oil millet collected in the 1890s were sitting in Britain’s Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew.

Hsing led a research team to find oil millet in the mountains of southeastern Taiwan and began studying the little-known cereal.

She found that the seed’s protective wax coating enabled it to grow without irrigation, fertilisers or pesticides, even on poor-quality land.

Rich in oil, protein and minerals, it can be used for human and animal consumption, as well as for fuel.

“It’s naturally very efficient at using sunlight and water,” said Hsing.

“As for soil conditions, even in mountainous areas where the ground is full of large rocks, it can still grow very well.”

Ismahasan started his crop with one panicle of oil millet. The family now harvests oil millet twice a year on a section of their property where they grow other traditional Bunun cereal crops.

Tiny and tasteless, oil millet can be used in porridge, steamed buns, bread and even popcorn.

But the family has struggled to convince other farmers to grow it because it is not yet commercially viable.

Oil millet is not only labour intensive but also significantly more expensive for consumers than rice, by far Taiwan’s most popular staple.

While the current market for oil millet is limited, Taiwan’s National Crop Germplasm Center sees value in preserving its seeds for the future, when climate change might force more farmers to consider growing the crop.

Oil millet seeds are “very precious” because of their genetic diversity and ability to adapt to the environment, Lin Yen-yu, an assistant researcher at the centre, told AFP.

Seeds are kept in aluminium foil packets and stored at -18C under low-moisture conditions where they can last for decades, Lin said.

“In the future, when cultivation methods or climate change undergo certain shifts, their value may start to be recognised and discovered,” he said.

“It preserves many possibilities.”

Ismahasan said his priority for now was to get more people in his community growing and eating oil millet, bringing “it back into our everyday lives, just as it was for our elders”.

“If we don’t even eat it ourselves anymore, how can we expect to turn it into a viable business?” he said.

scraped.title: How a housing safety disaster was averted, four decades before the Tai Po fire tragedy | Hong Kong Free Press HKFP
scraped.description: Public complaints, an enterprising NGO and investigative journalists helped avert a potential disaster at an estate in Kwai Fong, Tim Hamlett recalls.
scraped.author: Tim Hamlett
scraped.h1: How a housing safety disaster was averted, four decades before the Tai Po fire tragedy
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

According to the Wang Fuk Court fire inquiry , residents of the doomed estate made no fewer than 180 efforts to ward off the danger presented by careless building work. They sent complaints or inquiries to at least five government departments.

This was not a success. We must note in particular the Labour Department’s achievement. During 15 site visits, their inspectors concluded that there was no evidence of workers smoking and complaints were “not justified.” Whoops.

See also: Takeaways from the independent probe into the Tai Po fire

There is an interesting contrast here with a rather similar story from long ago. The present Kwai Fong Estate is a perfectly satisfactory piece of work constructed between 1987 and 2002. But there was a previous Kwai Fong Estate.

This was built between 1972 and 1975 at a time when the supervision of building work was marred by rampant corruption in the relevant department. By 1982, it became clear that, as a result, the estate featured a lot of questionable concrete.

In the ensuing three years, residents became increasingly concerned, particularly about Block 5, and there were petitions, pleas to the district board and legislators, and press conferences. The housing authorities, meanwhile, maintained that there was nothing to worry about, an assurance somewhat diluted when they decided to evacuate the top two floors of Block 5.

Eventually, one of the more enterprising local NGOs colluded with a local newspaper to organise a clandestine inspection of Block 5 by an engineer, armed with a gadget for testing the quality of concrete. This produced some readings at the fried tofu end of the scale, which a newspaper gleefully splashed.

The Housing Authority then collapsed in a heap, which was embarrassing, but not as bad as having one of its buildings collapse in a heap. It announced an immediate evacuation of Block 5, and plans to demolish the whole estate. It also published the results of safety assessments of its entire stock, and plans to replace all the older buildings in it.

This left everyone feeling good about themselves and is perhaps a good example of how public pressure can goad government departments into doing things they know they ought to do but have been putting off.

The enterprising NGO, the Society for Community Organisation, is still with us, as is the newspaper, the Standard, though the investigative team which did this sort of story was disbanded in 1987.

But of course this kind of thing could not be repeated now. Nous avons , as Molière put it, changé tout cela . Nowadays, raising a petition or holding a press conference could prompt a knock at the door. Meanwhile, your district councillor and lawmaker have been carefully selected for their willingness to admire the government, while investigative journalism is discouraged and public records are increasingly put off limits to protect the privacy of miscreants

This is a pity. Let us look at it this way. One of the great unsung improvements to aviation safety was the abandonment of the system in which the captain was the undisputed sovereign of his cockpit and the co-pilot was just expected to push buttons and pull levers as instructed.

The replacement arrangement is that the two pilots decide among themselves who will be the “pilot flying” and the “pilot monitoring,” with the clear understanding that – regardless of who is most senior – the pilot monitoring is expected to watch for and object to questionable moves.

In moments of crisis, the senior pilot may decide to take over the “pilot flying” role, or they may not, because the pilot monitoring has the time to deal with other matters, like diagnosing the problem and contacting the ground.

The Hong Kong government has now switched back to the “captain in charge” system and input from the underlings is no longer encouraged, or even tolerated. This system may have many advantages but it has a cost, which might be payable in blood.

The National Commission for Women (NCW) has written to the Tamil Nadu Director-General of Police seeking a fair and impartial enquiry into the allegations that “C. Arul Vignesh, MLA from Kallakurichi, Tamil Nadu, sent obscene WhatsApp messages to J.E. Padmaja, District Collector, Kallakurichi.”

The NCW in a social media post said its chairperson Vijaya Rahatkar has written to the DGP, Tamil Nadu, seeking a “fair and impartial enquiry into the allegations, including examination of the representations reportedly made by the District Collector to senior officials and the action taken thereon.”

The Commission, which took suo motu cognisance of a media report, has called for the preservation and examination of relevant digital evidence and emphasised that the matter must be investigated without any political or external influence, irrespective of the position held by the person concerned, according to its social media post.

“The Commission has sought a detailed Action Taken Report (ATR) within seven days. The dignity, safety and security of women public officials must be upheld without exception. No position or influence can place anyone above accountability for alleged harassment or misconduct,” it said.

Cochin International Airport Limited (CIAL) has set up a dedicated pilgrim facilitation centre at the airport for Sabarimala pilgrims. Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan will inaugurate the centre on November 17.

scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: US Airmen Arrested in Okinawa for Public Indecency and Drunk Driving
scraped.body_text:
NAHA - Two members of the US Air Force stationed at Kadena Air Base in Okinawa were arrested on November 14 in separate incidents involving public indecency and drunk driving, raising fresh concerns about discipline among American military personnel following a robbery-murder case involving a US Marine last month.

Hunter Edrington, an airman assigned to Kadena Air Base, was arrested at the scene shortly after 11 p.m. on November 14 on suspicion of public indecency after allegedly exposing his lower body in a plaza at a commercial facility in Okinawa City. Police said Edrington appeared to be heavily intoxicated at the time of his arrest. Earlier that day, in the early hours of November 14, a US Air Force captain stationed at the same base was arrested in Okinawa City on suspicion of driving under the influence of alcohol. The two arrests come as the US military is working to tighten discipline among its personnel following the arrest of a Marine in connection with a robbery-murder case in October. Despite these efforts to improve conduct and prevent further incidents, the latest arrests have renewed concerns over the behavior of US military personnel stationed in Okinawa.

items.title: Are You a Dopamine Addict?
items.summary: A new Japanese slang term describing children and young people addicted to the instant stimulation of social media has been nominated for Japan's 2026 Buzzword of the Year, drawing attention to growing concerns that endless short videos are undermining concentration, disrupting sleep, and creating addictive behavior among adults as well as children. (News On Japan)

scraped.title: Are You a Dopamine Addict?
scraped.description: A new Japanese slang term describing children and young people addicted to the instant stimulation of social media has been nominated for Japan
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Are You a Dopamine Addict?
scraped.body_text:
TOKYO - A new Japanese slang term describing children and young people addicted to the instant stimulation of social media has been nominated for Japan's 2026 Buzzword of the Year, drawing attention to growing concerns that endless short videos are undermining concentration, disrupting sleep, and creating addictive behavior among adults as well as children.

The term "dopagaki," shortened from the Japanese expression meaning "dopamine-addicted brat," refers to young people who become hooked on the rapid stimulation provided by short videos and other social media content, leaving them increasingly unable to maintain concentration for extended periods. Although the expression initially gained popularity as internet slang describing children and teenagers, researchers warn that the psychological mechanisms behind compulsive smartphone use affect people of all ages. Dopamine is an important neurotransmitter involved in motivation, concentration, and feelings of achievement. Research by Yasue Mitsukura, a professor at Keio University, has examined how the brain responds when people repeatedly scroll through short videos on smartphones. According to Mitsukura's research, measurements of brain activity suggest that dopamine levels, which gradually decline while watching content, rise again each time a user scrolls to another video. Crucially, the increase is not necessarily caused by enjoyment of the video itself. Instead, dopamine is released in anticipation of what interesting or entertaining content might appear next. This expectation encourages users to continue scrolling, creating a cycle of stimulation that can gradually develop into compulsive behavior without the individual realizing it. When dependence becomes severe, it can interfere with everyday life and learning, contributing to sleep disorders, disturbances in autonomic nervous system function, and difficulty concentrating. Digital addiction has become an increasingly serious international concern, prompting governments to consider restrictions on children's social media use. Australia became the first country to introduce a nationwide legal ban on social media use by children under 16 in 2025, requiring platforms to take measures to prevent underage users from creating accounts. Companies that fail to comply could face fines equivalent to approximately 11.8 billion yen. The European Union also announced a proposed children's protection law in September 2026 that included restrictions on social media use by children under 15. Measures under consideration include limiting recommendation algorithms that continuously deliver videos tailored to individual preferences, restricting viewing time to one hour per day, and introducing stricter age verification requirements. Such recommendation systems have attracted particular scrutiny because they continually present content designed to keep users engaged, potentially reinforcing patterns of excessive consumption. However, Australia's experience has illustrated the difficulties of enforcing age restrictions. Some children under 16 have reportedly circumvented the rules by using other people's identification documents, while others have drawn mustaches on their faces to fool facial recognition systems intended to verify users' ages. These attempts to evade restrictions demonstrate how difficult it can be to make social media regulations effective, even when governments impose substantial penalties on platform operators. Japan is also considering how to protect children from excessive internet use. The Children and Families Agency has presented its first draft guidelines outlining how parents and guardians should be involved in children's use of the internet. The government is also expected to reach a conclusion on possible age restrictions for social media by the end of 2026. While much of the international debate has focused on protecting children, experts emphasize that smartphone dependence is not confined to younger generations. A growing number of adults are also showing signs of potentially addictive behavior. Mitsukura has developed a simple four-question checklist designed to help people assess their level of smartphone dependence. The first warning sign is thinking about a smartphone even when not using it, or automatically reaching for it whenever there is nothing else to do. The second is feeling restless or irritated when the smartphone is not nearby. The third is attempting to reduce smartphone use but repeatedly failing to do so. The fourth is losing sleep or becoming unable to complete necessary tasks because of time spent using the device. According to Mitsukura, people who recognize three or more of these four behaviors may have a high level of smartphone dependence. As for preventing addiction, Mitsukura recommends taking regular breaks rather than allowing stimulation to continue uninterrupted. "When dopamine levels remain continuously elevated, it can lead to addiction, so it is important to take breaks and reset," Mitsukura explained. Even when total smartphone use amounts to one hour, dividing that time into shorter sessions, such as 15-minute intervals separated by breaks, may reduce the risk of developing dependence compared with watching continuously for an entire hour. The difficulty, however, lies in putting that advice into practice. For people who find themselves unable to stop scrolling despite intending to take a break, the popular expression "dopagaki" may describe more than just the behavior of children.

scraped.title: Keisei Skyliner Reservation System Hacked, Up to 3.37 Million Records at Risk
scraped.description: Keisei Electric Railway has suspended online seat reservations for its Skyliner express service connecting central Tokyo with Narita Airport after a cyberattack potentially exposed up to 3.37 million personal information records, with no indication of when the booking system will resume operations.
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Keisei Skyliner Reservation System Hacked, Up to 3.37 Million Records at Risk
scraped.body_text:
TOKYO - Keisei Electric Railway has suspended online seat reservations for its Skyliner express service connecting central Tokyo with Narita Airport after a cyberattack potentially exposed up to 3.37 million personal information records, with no indication of when the booking system will resume operations.

The railway operator announced that its Skyliner seat reservation system was accessed without authorization by an external party late at night on November 11. According to the company, up to approximately 3.37 million records containing personal information, including names, telephone numbers and email addresses, may have been compromised. In response to the incident, Keisei Electric Railway has completely suspended its online reservation system for the Skyliner, which operates between Ueno Station in Tokyo and Narita Airport. The company has not established a timetable for restoring the service, leaving passengers unable to reserve seats online. Until the system is restored, travelers wishing to use the Skyliner must purchase tickets directly from ticket vending machines or staffed counters at railway stations.

A woman was seriously injured in a wild boar attack in Nishinomiya, Hyogo Prefecture, as sightings of unusually large boars increase across the Kansai region, with some weighing nearly 150 kilograms and capable of running at speeds of 45 kilometers per hour.

Arriving in Japan after a long-haul flight is so exciting. But dragging a 25kg suitcase through a busy train station is less so.

scraped.title: A Cop Was Charged With Causing His Wife’s Miscarriage. Alabama’s Laws Came Down Harder on Pregnant Women Who Used Drugs.
scraped.description: In Alabama, politicians and prosecutors have long proclaimed their mission to defend the unborn. But it’s easier to punish women who take drugs while pregnant than abusers who endanger the unborn.
scraped.author: Amy Yurkanin
scraped.h1: A Cop Was Charged With Causing His Wife’s Miscarriage. Alabama’s Laws Came Down Harder on Pregnant Women Who Used Drugs.
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

This story includes descriptions of pregnancy loss and domestic violence.

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up for Dispatches , a newsletter that spotlights wrongdoing around the country, to receive our stories in your inbox every week.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

On the night of Feb. 15, 2022, Robert Maddox Jr., a rookie cop in a small Alabama town, called his colleague in a panic. His wife was about three months pregnant and bleeding heavily. They needed someone to watch their two sleeping children while they went to the hospital.

Headland police Officer James “Bo” Knight arrived with his wife. He had been serving as a mentor of sorts to Robert, who had just recently joined the department, and had urged him to reach out if he ever needed help.

The situation Knight encountered was a heavy one. Robert had something in a plastic bag that looked to Knight like fetal remains. His wife stood by silently. Robert said he’d be back as soon as possible, that he was taking both his wife and the bag to the hospital.

When the couple returned three hours later, Robert was holding a white container.

“They put my fucking baby in a box,” he said.

Investigators soon began building a case that it was Robert who caused the miscarriage. About six weeks after she lost the pregnancy, Brittany Maddox reported her husband for assaulting her before and after she went to the hospital. She first went to an abuse-prevention organization, which connected her to the police and helped her get a protective order from the court. She provided the Houston County judge with a description of how Robert choked and beat her in front of their 1- and 2-year-old children just before the miscarriage, as well as pictures taken starting the following week of marks on her neck. She handed over text messages from Robert in which he promised not to hurt her again and begged her to consider how his imprisonment would hurt their family.

“Being honest is going to get us both screwed,” he wrote. “The truth is going to give me locked up.”

Then, the Headland Police Department colleague who had offered to help Robert stepped forward. Knight gave a sworn statement to investigators in Dothan, the nearby city where the young couple rented an apartment. He recounted how, weeks after the incident, Robert confided in him that he had hit Brittany in the stomach, choked her and pushed her to the ground.

“I asked him how many times he has done this,” Knight said in his statement. “He stated many.”

According to the statement, Knight asked when he had last hurt her — and Robert responded “the night before you kept my kids.”

In Alabama, the legal implications of causing a miscarriage are severe. Politicians and prosecutors have long proclaimed their mission to defend the unborn. The state has gone further than almost every other to embrace “fetal personhood” — the legal concept that embryos and fetuses deserve the same rights and protections as children. The result is that people charged in Alabama with harming a fetus face especially lengthy prison sentences.

The authorities came down hard on Robert, at least at first. He was charged with murder.

But in the years that followed, Houston County’s criminal justice system would prove lenient for him. Robert was released on bond about five weeks after his arrest and never again saw the inside of a jail or prison cell.

His case stands in stark contrast to dozens of other fetal personhood prosecutions in Houston County, which sits in the corner of the state near the borders of Florida and Georgia. Those defendants were pregnant women. They were charged not for actually harming their unborn babies but for potentially endangering them — not by violence but by using drugs.

In all but one of those cases, which date back nearly two decades, their babies survived. Some of the women spent months in jail and even went to prison.

A former nurse, who had been battling a meth addiction for years, was arrested in 2018 after she tested positive for drug use while in labor and wound up spending nearly 10 months in prison. Another woman, who also tested positive at the hospital where she gave birth, ended up in jail for four months in 2024 — and said many fellow inmates were women who’d been arrested for using drugs while pregnant.

Houston County District Attorney Russ Goodman, who took office in January 2023, said in an email that his office has made efforts to help the women by recommending addiction treatment as part of their sentences. He also said some were rearrested and imprisoned for violating probation — or never completed the treatment offered by the court.

“During my term it is rare that we would sentence a defendant in these types of cases to a straight prison sentence,” Goodman said, “unless of course there were other extenuating circumstances, such as prior criminal history.”

As for Robert Maddox, Goodman said that the evidence against him was inconclusive, and he questioned the prior district attorney’s decision to seek an indictment. “It pained me as a prosecutor that I was not to be able to seek justice in this case,” he said.

Robert declined an interview but said in an email, “I was made out to be someone I wasn’t.” He did not respond when pressed to elaborate. ProPublica later sent him a detailed list of the allegations against him. He replied, “That is not what happened.” In response to a follow-up email, he said his wife had no bruising or marks at the hospital.

“If I was abusive and abused her then took her to the hospital they would have saw the marks and not let me leave with her,” he wrote in an email.

Lourdes Rivera, president of the advocacy group Pregnancy Justice, said her organization has identified 2,298 cases of women arrested since 2006 on charges related to their pregnancy. Most of those were for drug use and are concentrated in Oklahoma, South Carolina and Alabama. Rivera said the numbers of women prosecuted for pregnancy loss appear to be on the rise compared with the years before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the right to an abortion.

“Law enforcement is using laws that were never intended to apply to pregnancy to investigate, arrest and punish women,” Rivera said. “And it’s only getting worse.”

Robert’s promise not to hurt Brittany again after the miscarriage lasted about a week, she said. She would later tell a judge that he began hitting and choking her again, and photos from that time show bruising on her neck and eye. In that time, something shifted.

“I started hating him when I saw my baby dead,” she wrote in response to ProPublica’s questions.

She said it took her several weeks to come forward because she had to work through complicated feelings about the loss of both her pregnancy and a husband she still loved despite the hatred that was building. She also wasn’t sure if she and her daughters could safely leave him.

About a week before she went to the authorities, she got a text from her husband asking if she’d give him one more chance. “I can’t give you your baby back,” he wrote. “That’s something I’m always going to live with knowing I did that.”

For help in English or Spanish , call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233 or text “start” to 88788.

Asked about the text, Robert wrote to ProPublica, “I was referring to having to pull my kid out a toilet I couldn’t believe I had to do that. It was painful emotionally.”

Robert had started working as an officer at the Headland Police Department about four months earlier. Brittany worried the other officers would side with her husband, but she quashed her fears and reached out on social media to several of them anyway. She said Robert went into her account and deleted the messages she’d sent. But it was too late.

Knight, one of the officers she messaged, confronted Robert, who admitted that he had hit Brittany in the stomach before the miscarriage, the officer later told the Dothan police. Robert furiously messaged Brittany.

“If you want me to go to jail keep accusing me of it,” he wrote. “Just know I love you and it will never happen again but I think I’m getting fired.”

Domestic abuse is a leading killer of pregnant women. And for every fatal case, there are an estimated 70 nonfatal ones. Researchers have found that almost 13% of women surveyed experienced domestic violence during pregnancy.

Nonfatal cases usually go unreported, according to Maeve Wallace, an expert on domestic violence at the University of Arizona. The same goes for miscarriages, which often happen at home and may leave no medical record. That can make it difficult to determine how often abuse causes miscarriage, she said.

Brittany said her relationship with Robert had been turbulent from the start. She was still in high school when they started dating, and she uprooted her life to relocate to his hometown of Dothan. She said he started physically hurting her months into the relationship and that it escalated after the move. Brittany found herself isolated in Alabama, where life revolved almost entirely around her husband, two young children and the couple’s car-detailing business.

“Robert would also hurt me if things weren’t done perfectly or if any issues happened,” Brittany wrote.

Unlike many other victims of domestic violence, she hounded the police and prosecutors to take her case seriously after the miscarriage.

Cases against abusers accused of causing pregnancy loss can be tricky to prove, often requiring evidence that the abuser intentionally struck the victim in the stomach and testimony from a forensic pathologist linking the violence to the pregnancy loss. In one strange turn, a grand jury in a city outside of Birmingham indicted a woman for starting a fight that led to her being shot in the stomach and suffering a miscarriage.

It’s easier and more common to pursue charges against defendants when they are accused of killing both a pregnant woman and her fetus.

Laws don’t provide an easy path for punishing abusers of pregnant women, especially when the baby survives, according to law professor Mary Ziegler, who teaches at the University of California, Davis. But laws do make prosecution of pregnant women who use drugs astonishingly easy. Those cases come to light almost automatically — and there is little opportunity to challenge them. Hospitals frequently administer drug tests to pregnant women and notify child protective services of positive results. Those agencies often turn over that information to police in Alabama, where drug use is not grounds just for a child welfare investigation but for a felony charge.

The women are prosecuted under Alabama’s chemical endangerment law, which makes it illegal to expose children to drugs. Although the 2006 law initially was designed to address the dangers of home-based meth labs, prosecutors almost immediately began using it against pregnant women.

ProPublica identified more than 40 pregnant women arrested in Houston County since 2009 on chemical endangerment charges after testing positive for drugs. An analysis of court data also found that the county prosecuted women for chemical endangerment at one of the highest rates in the state, though the data doesn’t specify whether the cases involved pregnancies.

In one case, a 24-year-old whose newborn tested positive for methadone and marijuana received a five-year prison sentence in 2009. Another woman, who’d been convicted for exposing her fetus to THC in 2013, had her probation revoked for possessing synthetic marijuana and spent about nine months in prison.

Pat Jones, who was Houston County’s district attorney at the time of these cases, did not respond to a request for comment.

According to Ziegler, there is a pronounced unevenness in who gets punished under statutes that protect fetuses.

“The versions of personhood that are enshrined in our laws have tended to focus on the conduct of women,” she said.

Courtney Haney grew up in Dothan but left at age 18 to join a high-pressure sales crew that traveled across the country, selling boxes of frozen meat door-to-door. The work was stressful, and it attracted misfits and risk-takers. Several of her colleagues used drugs, but Haney became pregnant unexpectedly and stayed clean.

Her daughter was born healthy, arriving exactly on her due date. But soon, cracks appeared in her relationship with the father, and he split, taking the baby with him. When her colleagues moved on to other cities, Haney remained in Denver to look for her child. She had no family there and no friends. Her despair became overwhelming. She turned to drugs and became homeless, eventually losing custody.

Almost a year later, Haney found out she was pregnant again and returned to Dothan in 2020 with a full-blown addiction to heroin. She went to the hospital with contractions the week before she gave birth and knew she would test positive for drugs. She also said no one offered her options for drug treatment, even after she asked for help. Instead, hospital staff stabilized and discharged her. She kept using until she returned to give birth, when she was drug-tested again.

“I was holding my daughter in my hands and the police walked in,” Haney said.

They asked her questions, and she hoped they might show mercy and allow her to go home with her child. After they told her she might be charged with a felony for exposing her fetus to drugs, she burst into tears.

“I answered honestly, thinking that if I’ve answered honestly they wouldn’t press charges,” she said. “And that was pointless.”

She was arrested for chemical endangerment three months later.

For women struggling with addiction during pregnancy, a chemical endangerment arrest can initiate a cycle of devastating court fees, imprisonment on probation violations and even additional charges. And the separation from their newborns and other children can drive them deeper into addiction. Unlike in many other counties, Houston County does not offer a drug court program, which allows defendants to get substance-abuse treatment instead of prison time and avoid a felony on their record.

A woman who was about seven months’ pregnant was arrested in Houston County the very same day as Robert Maddox, in 2022. She was briefly jailed for violating probation stemming from a past chemical endangerment conviction. She then faced additional felony charges when, weeks later, she tested positive for cocaine at the hospital where she gave birth. She later received a five-year sentence and wound up at Tutwiler Prison for Women.

Her release date is right before Christmas in 2028.

Haney had no felony convictions, but a sentencing report recommended against straight probation due to charges in other states that had been dismissed. Ultimately, the Houston County district attorney’s office offered a plea deal for a lesser charge and just over a year of probation.

Haney struggled to abide by the conditions of her sentence. She did not complete court-ordered drug treatment and failed to report to her probation officer several times. As a result, she was jailed for a total of four months.

Many of the other women jailed with her also had been arrested on charges of chemical endangerment as a result of failing drug tests during childbirth.

“Whenever I went to jail, that’s where I met most of them,” Haney said. “There’s a whole lot of them in Houston County.”

Haney became pregnant two more times while she was addicted. For her third child, she traveled to nearby Georgia to give birth, and then to Florida for her fourth. Neither state arrests women for prenatal drug use at the same high rate as Alabama.

Xaviera Smith, a former nurse and mother of three from Tennessee, said she knew she would be arrested before she even gave birth in Houston County to her youngest son in 2018. Smith couldn’t deny the results of the drug test that had been administered while she was in labor. She had been battling a meth addiction for years.

She said that, fortunately, her baby was born healthy and did not need to go to the neonatal intensive care unit for drug withdrawal.

Smith had a court-appointed attorney who negotiated a deal on her chemical endangerment charge. She was sentenced to 10 years but could avoid prison by serving time through the local work-release program.

“I just went to court and took what they gave me,” Smith said. ”There’s nothing I really could do.”

After violating the terms of work release, she ended up in prison for nearly a year.

Brittany Maddox believed the case against her husband was a straightforward one. She felt there was solid evidence that the abuse caused her miscarriage. But the effort proved to be harder than she anticipated.

A few months after his arrest, the grand jury declined to indict him for murder, opting instead for a lesser charge of manslaughter.

The indictment alleged that Robert had “recklessly” caused the death of his wife’s fetus by “punching her in the stomach with a closed fist.” The maximum punishment would be 20 years in prison.

As Robert waited for his day in court, he asked the judge to relax some of the conditions of his bond. He had lost his job with the Headland police because of his wife’s claims of abuse and had started washing cars again. He wanted the court to remove the ankle monitor so he could more easily travel to work in Florida, which is near Dothan.

From her home out of state, Brittany had been calling the district attorney’s office once or twice a month to ensure authorities kept an eye on her estranged husband’s whereabouts. She was shocked to learn of his out-of-state travel request — not from prosecutors but from a news story. For the first time since his arrest, she felt unsafe.

A judge denied his motion to remove the ankle monitor but granted his request to commute to north Florida.

Brittany stayed in touch with prosecutors and began to mentally prepare for trial. She said that as months stretched into years, the conversations with them began to shift. They asked her how she felt about a plea deal, and she said she would be open to it, as long as the charge related to her miscarriage wasn’t dropped completely.

“I told them I could push through a trial emotionally,” Brittany wrote.

Finally, almost four years after Robert was arrested, his attorney brokered a plea deal with prosecutors. He would plead guilty to domestic violence, and the prosecution would recommend the manslaughter charge be dismissed.

Goodman, the district attorney, told ProPublica that he would not have been able to prove at trial that Robert committed manslaughter. “There was never any evidence that tied the actions of the defendant to the death of the baby,” he said, adding that “no expert could tie a causal connection.”

He also said he explained to Brittany that “we would not have moved forward on the manslaughter case” had he been in office when his predecessor chose to seek an indictment against Robert.

Brittany said if Goodman believed the charge should be dropped, he should have done it sooner, instead of having her spend years preparing for trial.

“The charge being dropped four years after he was arrested as part of a plea deal makes no sense to me,” she said. “That wrecked me in a lot of ways, more than the times I laid in bed for days after he hurt me.”

On May 18, 2026, Robert appeared before a judge in a Houston County courtroom. Brittany attended the hearing as well. She had traveled to Alabama for all of the hearings, even though she still feared being in the same room with Robert.

After all that waiting, the sentencing felt surprisingly short to her. When the judge moved to dismiss the most serious charge, he didn’t say the word manslaughter or mention the miscarriage. Brittany said she tried to ask questions about the deal, but she wasn’t sworn in, and the judge quickly moved on.

“The victim and the defendant were in a verbal dispute whereas the defendant was alleged to throw the victim down and choke her,” the judge said. “The state alleges that this occurred in front of their minor children as well.”

The judge went on to say that the presence of the children might have increased Robert’s punishment to a minimum six months’ imprisonment. But because he was a first-time offender, that minimum didn’t apply.

The judge sentenced him to five years’ probation and fined him about $3,000, which he could pay off at $50 a month. Then the judge added one more thing: anger management classes, to be completed through the court referral office.

I cover criminal justice and reproductive health in the South.

scraped.title: Prostate cancer testing now urged for men in their 50s and 60s – a lead author of the new screening guidelines explains why
scraped.description: The American Cancer Society has found that the benefits of the PSA blood test outweigh its harms. Black men and those with a family history of prostate cancer may especially benefit from screening.
scraped.author: Andrew Wolf
scraped.h1: Prostate cancer testing now urged for men in their 50s and 60s – a lead author of the new screening guidelines explains why
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

The American Cancer Society announced on Nov. 12, 2026, that it has released major changes to its prostate cancer screening guidelines to improve detection and treatment of the disease.

The Conversation asked Dr. Andrew Wolf , a physician at the University of Virginia who was one of the lead authors of the new guidelines , to walk readers through the changes and why they were made.

The biggest change is that we are making a proactive recommendation to screen for prostate cancer . Previously, we recommended that people talk with their healthcare provider to decide whether or not screening is right for them.

Our new recommendations vary by age and by a person’s risk of developing prostate cancer.

For people at average risk of developing prostate cancer, we recommend they be screened with the prostate-specific antigen, or PSA, blood test every two years from age 50 through 69. PSA is a protein that prostate cells make. Cancer and other conditions can cause PSA levels to rise.

People at higher risk, including Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer, should be screened annually from age 45 to 69. A strong family history means having a family member who was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or multiple family members diagnosed at any age. People with a single family member diagnosed at age 65 or older should be screened every two years from age 45 years to age 69 years.

For people ages 70 to 74, we recommend they talk with their healthcare provider about whether or not to continue screening. Because there is uncertainty about the benefit of screening for people in this age group, decision-making around screening depends on their personal preferences, overall health status and life expectancy.

For those over age 74, we recommend against prostate cancer screening. The potential harms of screening, such as more invasive follow-up tests and treatment, are likely to exceed the benefits for people in this age group.

Finally, we recommend against using a digital rectal exam to screen for prostate cancer, as it is less effective than the PSA test . The digital rectal exam may still be helpful when further evaluating elevated PSA levels or symptoms related to the prostate gland.

The past decade has seen mounting evidence supporting the benefits of using the PSA blood test to screen for prostate cancer.

The ability of the PSA test to reduce the risk of death from prostate cancer or of being diagnosed with metastatic disease are actually greater than researchers previously thought.

At the same time, there have been significant developments to reduce the potential harms associated with prostate cancer screening, including false positive PSA test results and diagnosis and treatment of prostate tumors that are unlikely to harm patients in the long-term.

Black men have an approximately two-thirds higher risk of developing prostate cancer compared with white men. They are also at greater risk for having more advanced disease at the time of diagnosis. These disparities are likely due to a combination of genetic, environmental, social and healthcare access factors .

Men with a family history of prostate cancer in a close relative – such as a parent, sibling or child – are also at elevated risk.

There are also a number of genetic mutations, such as BRCA2 , that confer significantly elevated risk of prostate cancer. Though screening recommendations for these cases are beyond the scope of our guideline, several professional medical organizations, including the National Comprehensive Cancer Network and the American Urological Association , have issued recommendations for screening people with these high-risk mutations.

For years, clinicians believed that the benefits of PSA screening were uncertain and didn’t necessarily outweigh the potential harms. This stance was in part because of the results of two large prostate cancer screening trials that were published in 2009. One, a U.S. study , found no benefit to screening; the other, a European study , found only a relatively small benefit.

However, it later became clear that the U.S. study was seriously flawed in such a way that it couldn’t have shown a benefit: Almost 90% of the men in the control group – that is, the group that wasn’t supposed to get screened – actually did get screened, and many of the men with abnormal PSA levels didn’t follow-up.

Conversely, most of the men in the European study who were randomized to standard care – no testing – instead of screening did not, in fact, get a PSA test, so it was more of a true comparison of the effect of screening versus not screening.

After researchers followed patients for over two decades in the European study, the effects of screening became clear: Screening reduced the risk of dying from prostate cancer by 13%. And about 500 men needed to be screened to avert one death from prostate cancer.

This may not sound very impressive, but it’s comparable to other routinely offered cancer screening tests, such as mammography for breast cancer . And the proportion of people needing to be screened to save a life would be significantly lower if extrapolated to a lifetime of screening starting at age 45 or 50, rather than the average number of two screenings that men received in the study.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force also has its own prostate cancer screening guidelines. The task force’s guidelines currently recommend that clinicians not screen for prostate cancer unless the patient indicates a preference to proceed. At the time of the task force’s last update in 2018 , it determined that the potential benefits and harms of screening were too closely balanced to recommend screening.

The task force has been in the process of updating those guidelines over the past several years. It is possible that their update will more closely align with that of the American Cancer Society.

I do think we have both sufficient evidence of benefit and sufficient reduction of the risks to now proactively recommend screening. Where the two guidelines do align is that both recommend that patients be informed of the benefits, risks and limitations of prostate cancer screening so they know what they’re getting into.

It is likely that our new screening recommendations will be covered by most insurers. However, patients may have out-of-pocket costs for further testing their doctor orders as a result of an abnormal PSA level.

Even though the benefits far outweigh the risks, there may be legitimate reasons why some people may not wish to undergo screening.

Some people might want to avoid the possibility of needing to get a prostate biopsy , which is how clinicians diagnose prostate cancer if a patient has an elevated PSA and an abnormal follow-up MRI scan or biomarker test. Prostate biopsies are uncomfortable, and they may cause some bleeding or occasionally an infection.

Some people may want to avoid the possibility of needing to undergo active surveillance if they discover they have a tumor that isn’t growing aggressively . Active surveillance involves periodic biopsies, MRI scans or both, which can be inconvenient and anxiety-provoking.

Some people may want to avoid the potential side effects of treating early-stage prostate cancer with surgery or radiation, which can cause sexual, urinary and bowel problems.

Forgoing screening, however, also means forgoing the opportunity to find cancer at its earliest stages, when the chance for a cure is very high.

Professor Emeritus of Medicine, University of Virginia

scraped.description: A crisis communications expert looks at how the Trump administration handled the massive disruption to the nation’s air travel when all planes were grounded on Nov. 13, 2026.
scraped.author: Shannon A. Bowen
scraped.h1: National ground stop response highlights critical errors in public reassurance – saying ‘nothing nefarious’ did the opposite of quelling public concern
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

Thousands of travelers were stranded on Nov. 13, 2026, when the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all domestic flights in the U.S. because of what they said were failures in decades-old air traffic communications systems . Crisis communications expert Shannon A. Bowen , a scholar at the University of South Carolina’s College of Information and Communications, spoke with The Conversation’s Politics and Legal Affairs Editor, Naomi Schalit, about how the Trump administration handled the first day of the crisis.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Is there a first principle in crisis communications?

The first principle would be to react quickly and react with accuracy, react with everything you know at the moment, truthfully, but always react quickly. Because if you delay until you gather information, a vacuum will ensue. Information fills that vacuum that may not be accurate. And so that’s the enemy of accurate crisis communication, but you want to always speak quickly and be the most authoritative and definitive source, even if very little information is known.

What did we see on the day of the ground stop?

A crisis unfolded and to the administration’s credit, they did react very quickly , in a way that offered the information that was known at the time, even though not a lot was known about why the ground stop was issued until later.

You’re speaking about the short press conference that afternoon with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin?

He did keep saying that nothing nefarious was at hand . And for a crisis communication scholar, you would not want to introduce the idea that something nefarious was at hand, unless, indeed, something nefarious was at hand. So by the very act of introducing this concept and this idea, I think the talking point, “Nothing nefarious,” then went across multiple networks, and it became the center of a controversy rather than quelling a controversy.

By saying nothing nefarious is at hand, that indeed confirmed something nefarious was at hand, even if the nefariousness was only the mismanagement of the air traffic control systems routers that they claimed caused the problem. By introducing this idea, I believe it did bring to mind that there may be other state actors behind whatever happened, that it could be a cyber attack. It would have been better to say, “We have evidence that this was not a cyber attack but a hardware failure.”

How did the later press conference with Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy go from your perspective as an expert on crisis communications?

They handled the questions that they received correctly. They told us as much information as they knew.

However, they did seem to downplay the extent of this crisis, because we have to remember the traveling public is not just people trying to get to business meetings.

We had football teams stranded. Now football Saturday , all over the SEC, has been disrupted. And there’s probably disruption in other areas of the country, but to us in the South, SEC football is almost a religious experience on Saturday . Luckily, the University of South Carolina football team had already flown out . But our marching band was stuck in this crisis, and so we have a lot of ripple effects from something like this happening, and it definitely says to me that this was an emergency situation. It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale.

If it were simply routers being overloaded, as we’ve been told, why wouldn’t they already know this situation and restart those routers the night before or over Friday night after most of the traveling public is out of the air?

What was Mullin’s and Duffy’s job when they got out there? What did they need to do?

To inform the public about the danger, why this happened, the extent of the problem, and what they’re doing to remediate the problem. We keep hearing that they’re asking for US$30 billion and more to repair the whole infrastructure for the air traffic control system, which is great, but what are they doing right now?

How do we know that flights in the air, right this minute, are any safer than the ones yesterday, a minute before the ground stop? Do we have that information? I don’t feel confident that they addressed that question appropriately. I don’t think that the traveling public entirely feels safe at this point or adequately informed that they will arrive at their destination.

They introduced politics into the press conference as well, didn’t they?

It’s something that they have the prerogative to do. They are both political appointees and members of the cabinet . So I understand that aspect, but I really wish they had addressed the traveling public’s concerns more overtly before making it political, that they need more money to fix this. We know they need more money to fix it, and I’m sure the American taxpayers are aware of the problem and willing to fund those corrections. But the more expedient issues would be, what about all these people who were stuck in airports ?

Were there warning signs for this crisis?

I believe there were. We had another ground stop about three years ago , due to air traffic control problems, and that is what we call in crisis communications a “prodrome ,” a warning sign of larger impending problems. When you see these types of warning signs, it really gives us a reason to think it’s going to get worse.

Duffy did say on Nov. 13 that, because of the condition of the air traffic infrastructure, “ you will have more ” ground stoppages. If you had a piece of advice for the administration regarding their future communications, what would you tell them?

I would say to communicate in advance as much as possible, so if you’re even considering a ground stop, it may be a good idea to put out a public notice so that people don’t go to the airport on a vacation flight, maybe they delay that for a week or two. It might also be a good idea to speak with the airline industry representatives and say, “Here’s what we’re thinking. Can you work with us? How can we make this better for the traveling public?” Also, if 17 of 22 routers were malfunctioning, could we have had a partial ground stop at only the affected airports, rather than a nationwide stop?

My silly last question: Do crisis communications experts have any theories about Friday the 13th?

We consider it more of a superstition, but I have noticed that there does tend to be a lot of activity on Friday the 13th. It might be placebo effect, it might be because we expect something bad to happen and we’re looking for it. But that day does seem to always have some type of activity. This is also when organizations release bad news, oftentimes, they say, “Let’s hold it until Friday the 13th, because bad news is expected.” People will assume, on Friday the 13th, that negative things are going to come out, so the shock value won’t be as much.

Professor of Journalism and Mass Communications, University of South Carolina

scraped.title: How Wildfire Litigation Became Big Business in America - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: Wildfire litigation against utilities has become a fallback strategy to deal with rising losses in a warmer world. But as payouts reach into the billions of dollars, is it sustainable—or just?
scraped.author: By Gloria Dickie
scraped.h1: How Wildfire Litigation Became Big Business in America
scraped.body_text:
Trial by Fire: First in a series about the impacts of wildfire litigation.

On a November morning in 2018, the foothills of the Sierra Nevada were primed to burn. Northern California had received little rainfall, and the grasses and shrubs above the town of Paradise were bone dry. Humidity levels were dangerously low as winds up to 40 miles per hour gusted downslope toward the 26,000-person community.

When a live wire broke free from a 99-year-old transmission tower owned by Pacific Gas and Electric Co., Paradise stood little chance.

The arcing wire ignited the brush below to start the Camp Fire, which claimed the lives of 85 people and destroyed more than 18,000 structures in a matter of hours, charring whole neighbourhoods to displace tens of thousands of people. It was the deadliest wildfire in California’s history.

But another metric would later come to define the fire that destroyed Paradise.

We deliver climate news to your inbox like nobody else. Every day or once a week, our original stories and digest of the web’s top headlines deliver the full story, for free.

Our #1 newsletter delivers the week’s climate and energy news – our original stories and top headlines from around the web.

Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.

A once-a-week digest of the most pressing climate-related news, written by Kate Waxman and released every Tuesday.

Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.

An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

Thousands of victims sued PG&E. The utility eventually agreed to settle their claims for $13.5 billion in compensation for the Camp Fire, as well as other blazes ignited by its equipment in Northern California in 2017 and 2018. It was one of the largest civil settlements for an environmental disaster in U.S. history, driving the company to bankruptcy and demonstrating that utilities could be held liable for huge sums when faulty equipment ignites conflagrations.

The settlement sparked a wave of lawsuits against utilities implicated in wildfire ignitions across the country. Today, wildfire litigation is a multibillion-dollar business in the U.S., with more than $18 billion awarded or agreed to in civil settlements for victims in California, Hawaiʻi, Colorado and Oregon since 2017. Utility companies PG&E, PacifiCorp, Xcel Energy and Southern California Edison have so far borne the brunt of such claims.

This year is shaping up to be among the worst on record for U.S. wildfires. Following a mild winter in which precipitation often fell as rain, mountain ranges including the Rockies and California’s Sierra Nevada were left with one of the lightest snowpacks in recent history. As of October, more than 9 million acres have burned in wildfires across the U.S.—about 1.5 times the average in the past decade for the year to date, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

Lawsuits have followed in lockstep. Already, some Colorado residents have sued San Isabel Electric Association, a not-for-profit rural electric cooperative, for allegedly sparking the Aspen Acres Fire, which ranks as the seventh-largest wildfire in state history and destroyed more than 320 homes. An investigation into the fire by state officials found that an aspen tree had fallen onto energized powerlines, starting the blaze.

As the wildfire crisis confronting America accelerates and intensifies, some question whether a litigious approach to address mounting losses is sustainable—or just—in a world reshaped by climate change. Especially so because the actual number of wildfire ignitions hasn’t changed much over the decades.

“California hasn’t seen a big increase in the number of fires,” said Chris Field, a climate scientist at Stanford University. “What’s really changed is the probability that a little fire grows into a gigantic, devastating one.”

As the planet has warmed, landscapes have grown more flammable. At the same time, millions of houses have been built in wildfire-prone areas, risking greater property losses.

Yet utility lawsuits have emerged as a seemingly state-sanctioned climate resilience strategy to help homeowners deal with losses as the insurance industry backs out of areas with high fire danger. With such an approach, if your house burns down in a wildfire, you had better hope a large utility with deep pockets was responsible for the ignition, rather than lightning or a private individual.

“The people in the Palisades Fire, they’re just out of luck,” said Richard Bridgford, a California trial attorney who has represented close to 12,000 wildfire victims in cases against utilities in California and Hawaiʻi.

Authorities arrested a 29-year-old former Uber driver in connection with that blaze, one of the two large fires that tore through Los Angeles County in January 2025, causing tens of billions of dollars in damage. (A federal judge declared a mistrial of the alleged arsonist in June, with jurors deadlocked 10-2 in favor of his acquittal in the criminal case.) With no legally definitive source of ignition, thousands of victims are now suing the city of Los Angeles, the L.A. Department of Water and Power and the state of California for $10 billion for alleged contributions to the fire’s damage, including gross negligence in failing to fully extinguish hot spots from a previous fire and failing to provide sufficient water to fight the blaze.

Left to market forces alone, wildfire litigation shows little sign of slowing down. But the U.S. appears to be heading toward a reckoning over ever-rising payouts, as policymakers grapple with whether—and how much—the power sector should be made to bear the costs of a warming world.

America’s reliance on wildfire litigation has sent shockwaves through the country’s social and economic systems, raising electricity rates, contributing to power shutoffs and draining public funds when governments are found liable. And it is jeopardizing interventions, such as prescribed burns, that can meaningfully reduce the destructive potential of wildfires.

“It’s not just the spark that starts the fire that is really solely responsible for the damage.”

But even beyond such consequences lies a more foundational question of justice. Climate scientists and legal analysts have challenged the idea of singular liability versus collective responsibility: Is it appropriate, or fair, to hold one person or entity responsible for a massive wildfire enabled by the burning of fossil fuels alongside decades of federal fire suppression and development policies? Judgments against oil majors for their climate impacts have so far proved nearly impossible to win in U.S. courtrooms, leaving utility companies holding the bag for worsening wildfires that other corporations helped fuel.

While governments consider who to hold accountable and how, a new legal industry is growing almost as fast as the wildfires ravaging the country.

Gerald Singleton, a managing partner with Singleton Schreiber law firm in San Diego, has specialized in wildfire litigation since the mid-2000s and has been behind some of the largest wildfire lawsuits against utilities. Currently, he is serving as the court-appointed liaison counsel in the 2025 Eaton Fire in Los Angeles, which involves more than 50 law firms representing plaintiffs, and the 2021 Dixie Fire in Northern California, which devastated large parts of the Sierra Nevada.

The firm, he said, now has a couple dozen lawyers and 200 or so staff members working exclusively on wildfire cases. Over the past two decades, he and his team have represented over 30,000 fire victims and recovered $3 billion on their behalf. “My practice is pretty much 90 percent fires,” he said.

For a long time, Singleton said, just a few firms in the state did this work. But since the 2017 fires in both Northern and Southern California, “there are just more and more firms that are getting involved.”

California has a strict liability standard for investor-owned utilities, which means a utility can be held financially liable for a wildfire even if it was not negligent in igniting the fire. This rule, known as inverse condemnation, has historically allowed claims in California to soar far beyond those in other Western states. (The U.S. precedent for assigning wildfire culpability to ignition alone dates back to the late 19th century, when railroad companies were often subject to such rulings.)

But in the past six years, California firms have begun trying their luck at litigating multibillion-dollar claims against energy companies implicated in wildfire ignitions in other states, including Oregon, Colorado and Hawaiʻi.

“California is not Vegas. What happens in California does not stay in California,” said Marek Smith, North America fire director at The Nature Conservancy, an environmental nonprofit. “It is significantly influential. The 2017-18 fires started to have this ripple effect, and then it just went exponential last year with the Southern California and LA wildfires.”
