Attorneys have flocked to the booming niche. Dozens of law firms now advertise themselves online as wildfire litigation experts in the American West.

Bridgford said that at least 95 percent of his practice’s focus over the last decade has been wildfires. The firm’s primary form of advertising, he added, is through town hall meetings held in communities from Pasadena to Maui that have been devastated by wildfires, encouraging victims to sign up to large lawsuits.

Wildfire claims are often handled as mass torts—a large pool of plaintiffs pursuing claims against one or more defendants over the same event. The scale of the cases, and the billions of dollars at stake, has made wildfire litigation a lucrative specialization. Mass tort lawyers are generally paid through contingency fees, receiving a percentage of any settlement or jury judgment rather than charging clients upfront. These fees generally fall between 30 percent and 40 percent of the total compensation recovered, although some states may dictate how much lawyers are able to receive.

The 2023 Maui wildfires in Lahaina, for example, ultimately led to a $4 billion settlement—including $1.99 billion from the utility Hawaiian Electric Industries and its subsidiary, and $800 million from the state of Hawaiʻi. A Hawaiian state statute notes that attorney fees must be “limited to a reasonable amount as approved by the court having jurisdiction of the action,” while another statute caps reasonable fees to a total of 25 percent.

The plaintiff’s lawyers in the Maui wildfires were hoping for a $1 billion payday, local media reported , before a judge in June capped attorneys’ fees at $222 million.

Eric Macomber, a wildfire legal fellow at Stanford University, said that as cases expand beyond the Golden State, he expects utilities will prefer to settle, as Xcel Energy did with the 2021 Marshall Fire in Colorado, rather than go to court for a public jury judgment. The lawsuits for that wildfire outside of Boulder were brought, in part, by law firms headquartered in California.

“Utilities don’t want to generate bad precedent in states that haven’t really litigated a lot of these cases yet,” Macomber explained.

Although most of the large wildfire payouts to date have been the result of a settlement, some have been awarded by jury verdicts, including more than $1 billion against PacifiCorp in litigation over Oregon’s 2020 Labor Day fires. (That ruling has since been reversed by the Oregon Court of Appeals.)

More recently, Wall Street has taken notice of lucrative settlements. Hedge funds and investment banks made a move last year to back California law firms in hopes of making a profit off fire litigation. Jefferies Financial Group Inc. and Oppenheimer Holdings Inc. were among the companies trying to broker arrangements to finance residents’ lawsuits against utilities for the Eaton Fire, Bloomberg reported last year.

These third-party funders help law firms shoulder the costs of suing a utility, providing loans that cover their caseloads. Such litigation finance often comes with interest rates above 20 percent on an annualized basis. Jefferies and Oppenheimer did not respond to requests for comment.

Many lawyers have bristled at Wall Street’s interest and the resulting optics that could lead to greater government intervention. “I think it’s awful,” Singleton said, adding he would support a ban on the Wall Street arrangements.

“Hedge funds don’t come out and say, ‘We care about the community. We’re trying to make the world a better place.’ There’s none of that. It’s, ‘We are here to make a profit.’”

Intervention may be coming either way. More and more Western states—California included—are considering legislation that would afford greater protections to utilities, perhaps putting an end to ever-growing litigation. And the utility companies themselves are pushing back.

“There are many things that contribute to the spread and the severity of a wildfire,” said Douglas Dixon, a lawyer with Hueston Hennigan who has also worked with roughly a dozen utilities or defendants accused of igniting wildfires across the Western U.S. since 2018. “It’s not just the spark that starts the fire that is really solely responsible for the damage.”

Coming on Monday: Wildfire lawsuits fuel a debate over who should pay.

scraped.title: As Texas embraces carbon storage, a Black community questions the risks
scraped.description: Texas now issues permits for companies to store carbon dioxide underground. East Texas residents fear safety risks, and skeptics doubt the climate benefits.
scraped.author: Emily Foxhall, The Texas Tribune
scraped.h1: As Texas embraces carbon storage, a Black community questions the risks
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

On a rural road outside Beaumont, a Texas energy giant is preparing to pump carbon dioxide underground to permanently store it and keep the gas from contributing to global warming. The project could be the first of its kind to start operating in the state .

It’s a long-awaited milestone for the oil and gas industry, which has touted carbon capture and storage as an important tool for cleaning up industry emissions. Texas lawmakers threw their support behind the technology , while state regulators spent years seeking permitting authority from the federal government to try to clear projects faster.

The Texas Railroad Commission , which oversees the oil and gas industry, won that authority late last year and approved this Exxon Mobil project in September. But the nearby community of Cheek has asked commissioners to reconsider the permit decision.

The area close to the project is predominantly Black, and many residents are working-class or elderly. People there don’t trust the company’s assurances that it will keep residents and their groundwater safe.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Only a small number of carbon storage wells have been permitted so far across the United States, and some CO2-related accidents have already happened. Experts and community advocates have warned of the risk for pipeline accidents and potential underground leaks. Leaders in Cheek are concerned the injected carbon dioxide could contaminate groundwater or get into the air and suffocate them. They worry emergency responders won’t be equipped to rescue them.

“We’re just shocked that they would want to do this so close to homes,” said Douglas Cormier, the 67-year-old president of the Cheek Texas Community Association, who grew up in the rural town and lives there with his wife near his daughters and grandkids.

Residents explained they don’t want to be the test subjects for the technology, and some experts argue it’s more distracting than effective in fighting climate change. Harvard University History of Science Professor Naomi Oreskes, who studies disinformation and climate change, has called carbon capture and storage “ mostly a dangerous distraction .”

A recent investigation by Drilled and ProPublica showed it would take more resources than feasible for carbon capture and storage to reduce emissions enough to avoid extreme warming. Companies have canceled or paused nearly a third of 19 proposed carbon storage projects in Texas so far.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

But carbon capture supporters argue that storing emissions is an important part of an “all of the above” approach to fighting climate change. Federal tax credits support carbon capture projects. Locally, East Texas remains attractive because of its existing carbon dioxide pipeline network (owned by Exxon Mobil), its geology, and nearby industrial facilities that might pay for their carbon to be stored.

Exxon Mobil has seven agreements with companies to store the greenhouse gas. The volume of carbon dioxide injected underground through those agreements will equal emissions from 2 million cars.

“The community’s concerns around safety of any sort of an injection project are valid and real and need to be taken seriously,” said Nichole Saunders, senior director and lead counsel for energy transition with the Environmental Defense Fund. “At the same time, the need for more carbon management infrastructure to get to where we want to go on climate is also real.”

So far, the case has raised questions about whether companies and the Railroad Commission are doing enough to address community concerns as a backlog of projects awaits approval.

Agency watchdogs say the commission has a history of failing to keep communities safe from industry risks. It’s also facing pressure from state Representative Drew Darby , leader of the House’s energy resources committee, who told the agency at a September hearing that carbon-capture projects needed to be moving at “utmost pace while protecting the public.”

In a statement to the Tribune, Railroad Commission spokesperson Bryce Dubee said the organization has a record of protecting drinking water while regulating injection wells. Winning the authority to regulate carbon storage “speaks volumes to this expertise,” Dubee said.

Exxon Mobil held early meetings with community members in Cheek. The company’s permit requires it to install automatic shut-off systems for the injection wells, monitor the underground carbon dioxide plume, and post a phone number where the operators can be reached around the clock.

The permitting program requires coordination with local emergency officials, according to the commission. Exxon Mobil sponsors emergency training programs through the Texas A&M Engineering Extension Service in College Station.

“We want community members to know they can count on us to operate responsibly, communicate openly, and put safety first every day,” Senior Vice President Dominic Genetti wrote in a blog post.

But the day following Darby’s comments, after hearing Exxon Mobil hadn’t talked with the community since the residents hired lawyers, Railroad Commission Chair Christi Craddick scolded Exxon Mobil for not supporting residents enough. Some people from Cheek had taken a bus to be there to voice their concern.

“Give them information,” she said. “Be there for their safety. Give ’em a fire truck if that’s what they want.”

Then Craddick voted for the permit.

Photos and posters about the area’s decades-long history hosting local rodeos hang in 81-year-old Preston Frank’s self-made museum in Cheek. Like many who live here, Frank, an upholsterer, inherited the land from his family. He considers it an important way to build generational wealth.

“That’s the reason why we’ve been fighting Exxon Mobil,” he said. “We don’t want them coming in here and diminishing the value of the land.”

Just west of Beaumont off Interstate 10, the unincorporated community of Cheek is split by the highway and railroad, with many homes sitting on large tracts of land dotted with cattle and horses. People wave to each other. On the north side, there’s a Catholic and a Baptist church. Once a year, residents gather for a community picnic at the park.

Exxon Mobil plans to compress carbon dioxide into an “ almost liquid state ,” pump it thousands of feet deep into the Earth and let it flow into little spaces in the rock, where scientists expect some to dissolve into salty water in those spaces or get stuck like a drink spilled in sand. Residents from the start had concerns.

How does Exxon Mobil know where the molecules will go? What if they don’t behave as expected? What if the project gets abandoned?

Carbon dioxide leaking into water could increase its acidity and cause metals to contaminate it, according to advocacy groups and experts. If it leaks back into the air or a pipeline ruptures and people are caught in a big enough plume, they won’t be able to breathe or run gas-powered cars to escape.

“Contamination of drinking water with CO2, or with metals or chemicals leaching out of rock due to CO2 acidification of the water, could be very costly if the affected aquifer is used by a lot of people,” Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory researchers wrote in a 2007 paper . “[O]nce any aquifer is contaminated, it will remain so.”

The Cheek Texas Community Association signed on in July 2025 with attorneys at the nonprofit Earthjustice, which charges no cost. They fought the permit approval all the way to a state administrative hearing in March this year where they argued Exxon Mobil hadn’t done enough to adequately ensure water and public safety would be protected and wasn’t monitoring a large enough area underground.

“It’s the first one in an area so close to a community, and that’s why the water issues and the safety issues are so paramount here,” said Jen Powis, who leads Earthjustice’s Gulf regional office.

The project also raised familiar concerns over environmental justice, a term used by researchers who have shown communities of color suffer a greater proportion of environmental harm than whiter, wealthier areas. Residents feared Exxon Mobil saw in their homes a place where the company could more easily and cheaply push a project through.

The company already built three unassuming injection wells at the edge of the community. Only some residents in Cheek signed so-called pore space agreements with Exxon Mobil for use of the small pockets in underground rock where the carbon dioxide will be stored and that property owners control under current case law .

“I’m just thinking they found an area where they can do it and not expect a lot of resistance,” said James Strambler, 70, a former IBM technician who moved there around 2017.

After the March hearing, a technical examiner and administrative law judge recommended moving the permit forward to the commission for a vote.

Texas’ work to win the authority to permit carbon storage wells dates back more than a decade.

In 2009, Texas lawmakers passed a law authorizing the railroad commission to design a framework for how the state would regulate these projects in a way that upheld federal law. In 2022, the state formally applied to the Environmental Protection Agency for that authority.

At a virtual July 2025 hearing held by the EPA, the Texas Oil and Gas Association, a trade group representing 90 percent of the state’s fossil fuel production, said approving carbon capture and injection would be an economic boom for the state.

Gaining permitting power for carbon storage wells was “essential for our state’s economic future and energy leadership,” said Todd Staples, the group’s president, following the hearing.

Supporters of the technology are quick to point out that carbon dioxide makes sodas fizzy and creates the tunnels of fog that Texas football teams run through. They cite a study done by Texas A&M researchers that found the danger of leaks presents “a low probability of occurrence” — a risk that can be monitored and managed.

Advocates also point to the state’s decades-long history of injecting carbon dioxide into wells under a different type of permit as a way to draw more oil out of the ground and also store some of the greenhouse gas, a process known as enhanced oil recovery, which Exxon Mobil has pursued for decades.

“This has been put in place now for over 50 years,” said Scott Castleman, a spokesperson for the Gulf Coast Carbon Capture and Storage Alliance, which represents Calpine, Chevron, and Exxon Mobil. “Certainly, there is more discussion and opportunity for this industry to scale, and so that’s where you’re starting to see projects and interest in areas that may not have seen this before.”

Establishing community trust will “make or break” projects as the industry grows, said Sophia Cunningham, executive director of the Houston Energy Transition Initiative at the Greater Houston Partnership. Best practices include engaging the community early and providing different, meaningful ways for people to give input and discuss possible benefits.

“It’s a technology that can reduce emissions associated with our industrial activities, and so that is a good pursuit and it’s important to support that,” Cunningham said.“But it’s also reasonable to expect that not everybody in a community is going to want that.”

Residents near projects should be asking whether there would be a helpline to call for any issues, or whether truck drivers would observe weight limits for roads and bridges, said Susan Hovorka, a research professor at the University of Texas at Austin’s Bureau of Economic Geology. In Hovorka’s mind, research and experience have already proven the technology to be safe.

“It’s not utterly without peril, and so people are not foolish to ask,” Hovorka said,“But … their anxiety is sometimes maybe higher than is practical and realistic.”

But there have been serious incidents in other parts of the U.S.

In Mississippi, a carbon dioxide pipeline ruptured in 2020 after heavy rain caused a landslide, releasing a vapor cloud of CO2. A government investigation found that first responders had not been notified about the safety risks and “had to guess” what they were. Dozens of people went to the hospital.

Injected fluid at another facility in Illinois leaked into “unauthorized zones” underground, which most residents learned about in a news article.

Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry paused the state’s review of new applications to ensure any permit issued would be in compliance with state regulations, citing a need for a review process that considers “the safety of our citizens and environment and that streamlines the process for greater efficiency.” Louisiana has permitted three carbon dioxide wells to be constructed so far but not to begin operating.

In other states with permitting authority as of mid-October, Arizona hasn’t permitted any carbon injection wells. North Dakota has approved eight active injection wells across three projects, and Wyoming has approved five wells in one project.

“The benefit isn’t there,” said Naomi Yoder, an environmental researcher who opposed Texas’ bid to regulate the technology and raised concerns about potential harm to the environment and communities. “So it doesn’t make any risk worth it, and there is risk involved. You can’t possibly sequester enough carbon dioxide to make it worth it.”

In the Texas state hearing in September, the day before Exxon Mobil’s Cheek permit won initial approval, Darby reiterated the importance of supporting the industry. Virginia Palacios, executive director of the agency watchdog group Commission Shift, told him they should also ensure companies pay for equipment and training for emergency responders.

Meanwhile, Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian has vehemently opposed these projects. Christian has argued carbon dioxide is good for plants, rather than acknowledging the robust science that shows burning fossil fuels has caused carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere to rise, driving up global temperatures.

He voted against Exxon Mobil’s permit, saying he didn’t think it was safe.

Newly elected Railroad Commissioner Jon Rosenthal , who will join Craddick and Christian on the three-person commission, told Inside Climate News he supported the state taking over regulation of the wells.

Some projects have meanwhile stalled. Oxy said in its latest earnings call in August that its carbon storage project — the first and only other one approved in the state so far — was coming online “as we look forward.”

Other projects are moving forward, including Exxon Mobil’s second project near a community not far from Cheek, called Nome. The commission is collecting public comment on that project this week at hearings on Monday and Tuesday. Exxon Mobil named this one “Sunflower,” fitting with the Cheek project called “Rose.”

In late October, environmental and community advocates knocked on residents’ doors to invite them to a meeting about how to advocate for themselves. Only one person from the project’s area attended. Several arrived from Cheek, lending advice on what they’d learned while attendees ate pasta and salad.

The meeting hosts characterized the technology as a financial boon to industry and the Railroad Commission while putting drinking water at risk. The colorless, odorless gas can also cause suffocation, presenter Alexis Iwasiw warned the group.

“At high concentrations … it can lead to serious injury or death,” she said.

The next night, Exxon Mobil held an open house in the small Nome City Hall. They served boudin balls and shrimp and offered colorful pamphlets about the company’s safety record, how to respond in an emergency and how drinking water would be protected. They displayed a poster of other pipelines in the area.

As the sun went down, the group of several dozen made its way outside, where the Exxon Mobil presenters enthusiastically launched into explaining how CO2 is safe at certain levels. With a call of “let it rip, tater chip,” they released the gas from a demonstration pipeline, where it puffed out visibly like white smoke.

Mike Doguet, a 72-year-old rice and turf farmer-turned real estate developer, looked on. He believed the company did a much better job communicating with residents in advance here than in Cheek. The company is paying for new firefighting equipment, he said, among other community support. (Cheek community leaders have a list of wants, too, including improved roads, a community center, and an emergency warning system.)

One of the Sunflower project’s injection wells sits across the street from Doguet’s home in Nome, making neighbors wonder if there was oil. Doguet’s daughter lives next door and his son isn’t far. He wasn’t worried about safety.

“In my mind, it’s going to encourage new industry. It’s going to be good for the environment. It’s all positive to me,” Doguet said. “I don’t see the negatives.”

As the presentation went on, a resident from Cheek peppered the Exxon Mobil employees with questions. One of the Exxon Mobil presenters snapped back, telling her they were in the business of keeping substances in pipelines and would always err on the side of safety.

A former Exxon Mobil employee and Nome resident in the crowd, 77-year-old Lawrence Riley, piped up to say that in his decades of experience, he’d never had a pipeline emergency: “They are very, very safe, I am telling you,” he said.

Wearing an Exxon Mobil hat, 71-year-old Mayor Kerry Abney at one point walked through the CO2 cloud. He thought the project was great: Workers were shopping at Big D’s in town, contributing to sales tax, he said. People had a chance to make money in a place where agriculture is tough.

As Abney put it in an interview: “Santa Claus came.”

The Cheek resident watching the plume crossed her arms, looking skeptical.

Carlos Nogueras Ramos and Zach Leggio contributed reporting.

The Food and Drug Administration rejected a treatment for a type of lung cancer developed by the U.S.-based biotech Summit Therapeutics and the Chinese drugmaker Akeso, Summit said on Sunday.

In a letter sent to the companies, FDA regulators said the drug, called ivonescimab, could not be approved because it didn’t help patients live longer. While the drug was found to slow lung cancer worsening in patients, the absence of a survival benefit “does not support the positive benefit-risk profile in support of approval,” FDA reviewers concluded.

The FDA’s rejection of ivonescimab is a regulatory setback for Summit, which oversees development of the drug outside of China, although one that was not entirely unforeseen.

scraped.title: The Ceaseless Ceasefire
scraped.description: For the Palestinians, the ceasefire in Israel’s war on Gaza might not be all-out war — but it’s certainly not peace, and no end is in sight.
scraped.author: Safia Southey
scraped.h1: The Ceaseless Ceasefire
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

Gaza, “peace,” and surviving a zombie conflict.

All across the world, people are trapped by forces far beyond their control. Handcuffed by situations which they are powerless to change.

I spent countless hours talking to people like this from Southeast Asia to North Africa. Their immediate circumstances couldn’t have been more different. They hailed from radically dissimilar backgrounds; they were of different races, ethnicities, and religions. But they were bound together by one unifying force: organized, armed violence. Or, rather, the imposition of it upon them. These people were just living their lives when war arrived on their doorsteps.

When most people think of war, they think of armed soldiers. But I think of grandmothers and toddlers. Modern war zones are much more the province of civilians than combatants, even if the traditional “battlefield” has made a significant reappearance this century. Soldiers die. Civilians die in droves. Soldiers deploy here and there. Civilians are put to flight, en masse, often again and again. When memories of war invade my thoughts, I remember the tween whose hand was cut off, the farmer who dug his own grave and survived his execution, the paralyzed man who had to be left behind as troops attacked the village, the 2-year-old who survived a machete attack. Since World War II, such innocents have overwhelmingly been the main victims of armed conflict.

Being a war reporter taught me that ordinary people have extraordinary capabilities. I found that people the world over had the capacity to endure the unbearable and the survive the unthinkable. What they often cannot do, however, is push back on the source of their oppression and suffering. People can run from soldiers, but they cannot outrun war. The “safety” of a refugee camp is still an extension of the war zone. You can flee violence but still remain trapped by conflict.

Today, in her inaugural article for TomDispatch, Safia Southey — an international lawyer and expert on how societies reckon with wartime abuses — examines the plight of Palestinians in Gaza imprisoned by a conflict that refuses to die, the truce ostensively meant to save them, and the outside authorities that have trapped them in this “zombie conflict.” In this singular piece, Southey offers a window into the perverse mechanics of this ceaseless ceasefire cycle and what it would take to break it.

—Nick Turse, editor of TomDispatch

If you haven’t yet, sign up to receive TomDispatch in your inbox here.

If you haven’t yet, sign up to receive TomDispatch in your inbox here.

Safia Southey is an international lawyer and writer who focuses on how societies reckon with wartime abuses.

Abdullah Abu Zubaida’s family spent the first anniversary of the Gaza ceasefire last month in a shelter they built from the debris of their own home. Ne’man Abu Jarad and his five daughters spent it in tents, still displaced and with no clear way back. These families and millions of other Palestinians find themselves in a twilight state between war and peace: a zombie conflict in which a ceasefire has been announced while Israeli military control and attacks continue. The agreement risks making that condition permanent by leaving Palestinian governance and Israeli withdrawal dependent on decisions made largely by outside powers.

For these families, whose circumstances were reported by the Associated Press , and others in their position, the ceasefire that was supposed to end the war has brought little control over what happens next. Whether they can return home, rebuild, or resume anything resembling ordinary life remains subject to decisions made by outside authorities, whose hold on Gaza’s future may be further entrenched by the agreement itself.

While violations of the ceasefire warrant the attention they receive (and more), the agreement’s own terms demand scrutiny too, since arrangements negotiated to end wars also decide who holds power once the fighting stops. Christine Bell , a legal scholar specializing in peace accords, has shown how such agreements can perform constitutional functions. They determine who governs, over what territory, and subject to whose approval.

In Gaza, the conditions for Israeli withdrawal and Palestinian self-government give outside actors considerable power to determine when, and whether, the transition ends. The framework therefore threatens to turn the temporary administration of a devastated territory into a durable system of external control with no enforceable end, legitimized by the very agreement meant to bring peace.

Gaza’s current predicament has a long history of displacement and outside control. In 1947, the United Nations General Assembly adopted a plan to partition Palestine (then under British rule) into Arab and Jewish states. While Jewish leadership accepted the plan, Arab leadership rejected it. During the war surrounding Israel’s establishment in 1948, approximately 750,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes. Many sought refuge in Gaza. The mass displacement and dispossession of the Nakba — Arabic for “catastrophe” — never ended.

Israel occupied Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, in 1967 . In 2005, it removed its settlements and withdrew its army from inside Gaza while retaining control over its airspace and maritime access and substantial authority over its borders and the movement of people and goods. In 2024, the International Court of Justice concluded that because Israel continued to exercise authority over Gaza’s borders and the movement of people and goods, the withdrawal had not entirely released it from its obligations under the law of occupation.

The current institution of Palestinian self-governance also began as a temporary arrangement intended to last no more than five years. The Oslo process of the 1990s provided for an interim Palestinian government in Gaza and the West Bank until a permanent settlement could be reached. That institution, the Palestinian Authority, remains central to proposals for Gaza’s future.

Hamas won the 2006 Palestinian legislative elections and took control of Gaza in 2007 after armed conflict with Fatah, the rival Palestinian faction. Israel, citing security concerns, tightened its border restrictions into a blockade by land, sea, and air, restricting the movement of people into and out of Gaza and the entry of food, construction materials, and other necessities. Egypt restricted passage through its own border crossing. Years before the current war, the U.N.’s humanitarian office documented the effects: restrictions on movement and trade had undermined Gaza’s economy, increased its dependence on aid, and obstructed access to healthcare and education.

On Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led groups attacked Israel, deliberately killing civilians and taking hostages; Human Rights Watch has documented these acts as crimes against humanity and war crimes. Israel’s subsequent military response devastated Gaza. By Oct. 21 of this year, Gaza’s Health Ministry reported 74,494 Palestinians killed and 175,604 injured. In an October 2026 report , the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israeli authorities and forces continued committing genocidal acts against Palestinians in Gaza after the ceasefire, with the intent to destroy the group in whole or in part. By September of this year, Israeli military control had expanded beyond the approximately 53 percent of Gaza envisioned under the ceasefire agreement to at least 60 percent .

By the ceasefire’s first anniversary, nearly two-thirds of housing units had been destroyed, many of the remaining buildings were unsafe, and large-scale reconstruction had yet to begin. With winter approaching, displaced families need immediate decisions about shelter. The Israeli authorities who control access to their homes and to building materials can postpone those decisions. Such delays favor whoever controls access, and waiting itself becomes a source of political leverage.

In June 2024, the U.N. Security Council endorsed a three-phase framework in Resolution 2735 . An initial ceasefire and exchanges of hostages and prisoners were to lead, upon agreement, to a permanent end to hostilities and full Israeli withdrawal, followed by major reconstruction. The initial ceasefire was to continue for as long as negotiations over the second phase went on.

In November 2025, the Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, endorsing U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan to end the Gaza conflict and authorizing international arrangements for its implementation. The framework retains the language of transition while placing Gaza’s administration and redevelopment under the oversight of a Board of Peace chaired by Trump. Palestinian Authority control would depend on completing a reform program and demonstrating the capacity to govern securely and effectively. The resolution refers to earlier proposals , including a Saudi and French initiative calling for reforms to governance, transparency, public finances, and service provision. Israeli withdrawal is tied to demilitarization milestones to be agreed among the Israeli military, an International Stabilization Force, the guarantor states, and the United States. The force’s mandate includes demilitarization and civilian protection. An Israeli military presence along Gaza’s perimeter could remain until the territory is judged secure against a renewed terrorist threat.

The plan endorsed by the resolution states that Israel will not occupy or annex Gaza, that no one will be forced to leave, and that full humanitarian aid will enter immediately. Continued attacks and restrictions on assistance must therefore be assessed against those obligations, but compliance with these provisions would still not resolve the deeper problem. The framework grants outside institutions concrete powers over Gaza while making the restoration of Palestinian political authority dependent on future conditions. It establishes who governs during the transition far more clearly than it establishes how the transition ends.

The resolution authorizes the international arrangements until Dec. 31, 2027, subject to further Security Council action, but it sets no deadline for full Israeli military withdrawal or the transfer of political authority to Palestinians.

Israeli withdrawal depends on milestones agreed with Israel and other actors, but the criteria for determining when those milestones have been satisfied, and the consequences of disagreement, remain ill defined. Whoever can set the benchmarks, withhold agreement, or dispute compliance has considerable power over how long Gaza remains under outside supervision. This effectively means that the decision will be made in large part by Israel and institutions overseeing the transition, including Trump’s Board of Peace, which counts Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as a member.

No security arrangement can eliminate every future threat; clear benchmarks and a truly independent arbiter are essential if the ceasefire is to ever become a lasting peace.

The demand for protection against another attack is understandable. Hamas’s weapons, and its coercive power over Palestinians, are serious problems. But if the security conditions for withdrawal can be revised indefinitely, Palestinians cannot know when the promised transfer of authority will occur. The obligations of one armed faction should not determine whether an entire population has a political future.

Israel Policy Forum , a U.S. policy organization supporting a two-state solution, analyzed and supported the basic approach of the July 2026 road map . The proposal linked phased Hamas disarmament to incremental Israeli withdrawal and the creation of a new Palestinian civilian administration. The organization’s analysis described Israel’s refusal to accept that bargain, conflicting explanations of when withdrawal could proceed, and unresolved definitions and verification arrangements.

No security arrangement can eliminate every future threat; clear benchmarks and a truly independent arbiter are essential if the ceasefire is to ever become a lasting peace. Otherwise, the conditions for withdrawal could be extended indefinitely. If Hamas disarms and the promised withdrawal never comes, the disarmament stands while Israel’s commitment remains open to renegotiation. A single attack by a faction opposed to the agreement could then be invoked to suspend the political future of an entire population, allowing armed spoilers to trigger further delays in Palestinian self-government and giving Israel and the United States grounds to prolong those delays.

Palestinians have seen an interim arrangement outlast its deadline before. The 1993 Oslo agreement between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization established a framework for interim Palestinian self-government and negotiations toward a permanent settlement. It envisioned a transitional period of no more than five years, with negotiations on permanent status to address the sovereignty and governance of Jerusalem, the fate of Palestinian refugees since 1948, Israeli settlements, and state borders. More than three decades later, there is still no comprehensive settlement. The new plan follows the same design: concrete authority now, political rights later.

In an Oct. 2 report , the UN’s humanitarian office identified 217 displacement sites at medium to high risk of flooding, hosting approximately 235,000 people. Nearly 44,000 people were sheltering in unsafe buildings that required full or partial demolition, the report said. Restrictions on land access and on the entry of supplies continued to hamper preparations for winter.

Read Our Complete Coverage

No later breakthrough can give back a lost winter, a child’s interrupted schooling, or a patient’s postponed treatment. The longer a household has to survive elsewhere, the harder it may become to rebuild the life it was forced to leave, and an agreement can keep promising recovery while the conditions for recovery disappear.

Palestinians are also asked to prove they can govern before they are allowed to do so, and governing requires revenue . In the October report , the U.N. described how Israel’s withholding of approximately $6 billion in tax revenues it collected on the Palestinian Authority’s behalf was undermining that government body’s ability to provide services and pay salaries. The crisis extends beyond Gaza and exposes a circular test of readiness. An administration deprived of its own revenue struggles to deliver services, and those failures can then be invoked to justify continued outside supervision.

Blame works the same way: If a Palestinian administration is responsible for public services while other actors control access, security, and funding, residents may blame its officials for failures it could not prevent. The resulting loss of public trust would make representative government harder to build, and that weakness could in turn be cited as a reason for continued outside supervision.

Nathan J. Brown, a scholar of Palestinian politics, has argued that Gaza diplomacy is separating administrative functions from national political representation. A committee of technocrats can run clinics and restore water service, but deciding the political future of the people it serves requires authority grounded in their consent. An administration accountable primarily to a foreign board chaired by Trump lacks that democratic mandate.

The United States helped broker the Gaza ceasefire, holds a central position in the system meant to implement it, and underwrites Israeli military power. According to the Congressional Research Service , the 2016 memorandum covering fiscal years 2019 through 2028 pledged $38 billion in military assistance, subject to congressional appropriation. Without credible American consequences for obstructing withdrawal, the material advantages of continued control may outweigh any incentive to implement the agreement.

Donors providing humanitarian aid may end up paying to keep civilians alive while decisive political control remains elsewhere . Each emergency would then produce another funding appeal, while the authority to lift the restrictions causing the emergency would remain in place. Humanitarian funding could consequently help sustain that arrangement. The proposed International Stabilization Force , tasked with demilitarization and civilian protection, would need the authority and backing to restrain abuses by all parties, including Israel.

Lebanon offers a warning. After the April truce in the Iran war, Pakistan’s prime minister said the ceasefire included Lebanon. U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Washington had agreed to no such thing. Israeli attacks in Lebanon continued while the parties disputed what the agreement covered. Lebanese civilians were exposed to violence while governments argued over whether their country was protected at all. Whoever defines a ceasefire’s scope decides whose security it guarantees.

Gaza already displays the features of a zombie conflict, with an announced ceasefire, recurring military operations, and unresolved struggles over territory and power. The danger is that this condition becomes entrenched. Diplomats go on describing a transition, while people live under a system of control that survives one round of negotiations after another.

Read our complete coverage

These conditions, though, are sustained by identifiable governments and institutions, through decisions they could make differently.

In a July 2024 advisory opinion , the International Court of Justice stated that the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination could not be made conditional by the occupying power, and it concluded that Israel must end its unlawful presence in the occupied Palestinian territory as rapidly as possible. The Security Council’s Resolution 2803 places Palestinian statehood after reform and redevelopment, saying that the conditions for a credible pathway “may finally be in place” at that time. The political framework thus makes progress toward exercising an existing right dependent on conditions assessed by outside actors, while establishing their immediate authority much more clearly.

Every grant of outside authority under the ceasefire needs an expiration date: thresholds that can actually be met, independent assessors to judge them, and consequences for any party that blocks the next step. Without them, Israeli withdrawal and Palestinian self-government in Gaza will remain promises that outside actors renew indefinitely and never keep. For the families still displaced, another anniversary will mean another year in a tent or a ruined home, waiting for decisions they cannot make. Their ability to return, rebuild, and determine their own future remains subject to a political framework in which authority rests largely elsewhere. The Gaza ceasefire risks giving the structures of control that preceded the war a new institutional form, backed by the U.N. Security Council and administered indefinitely in the name of peace.

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

scraped.title: South Africa’s ANC Is Collapsing. The Far Right Is Rising.
scraped.description: The African National Congress is losing its working-class base. The beneficiaries: parties of the Right. South Africa’s local elections expose the fallout of three decades of economic failure — and the need to rebuild working-class power.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

The African National Congress is losing its working-class base. The beneficiaries: parties of the Right. South Africa’s local elections expose the fallout of three decades of economic failure — and the need to rebuild working-class power.

South Africa’s transition to democracy from apartheid was a victory for popular movements globally. That its political future could now be shaped by authoritarian forces should concern everyone committed to democracy and international solidarity. (OJ Koloti / Gallo Images via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

W hile the global left celebrates the recent successes of the Workers’ Party in Brazil and the Democratic Socialists of America in the United States, the African National Congress (ANC) has suffered a historic collapse in South Africa’s November 4 local government elections. After three decades of mass unemployment, deepening inequality, corruption, and economic policies that have failed the working class, the former liberation movement is losing its political authority. The principal beneficiaries of the ANC’s electoral rout are parties of the Right, including an increasingly powerful far right that has built its project around aggressive and often violent xenophobia.

With more than 70 percent of votes counted, the ANC’s national share of the vote fell to around 32 percent. The ANC is not expected to retain an outright majority in any major city, and the center-right Democratic Alliance (DA), historically the principal party of the white liberal establishment, is making substantial gains and is projected to become the largest party in most of South Africa’s big cities. Former President Jacob Zuma’s Zulu nationalist uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) is on track to be the largest party in Durban. The far-right ActionSA has made a strong showing in Johannesburg and Pretoria and is likely to be the second-largest party in Pretoria, with the ANC in third place.

The central question is not only why the ANC has lost so much support. It is why the suffering and anger of the working class have failed to produce a powerful democratic socialist alternative, and why the Right has been so successful in presenting itself as the answer to a crisis created by the existing economic and political order.

T he defeat of apartheid was an extraordinary achievement. We won universal suffrage, democratic institutions, constitutional rights, and legal protections for workers. Those victories were won through generations of sacrifice and collective struggle, and they must be defended. But political apartheid was defeated while the economic structures inherited from apartheid remained largely intact.

The liberation movement historically brought together different classes and social groups united against racial oppression. That unity was indispensable to apartheid’s defeat. But national identity does not abolish class contradictions. Instead of using democracy to transform the ownership and control of the economy in the interests of the majority, the ANC increasingly became an instrument through which a new elite could enter and benefit from the existing economic order.

The ownership and control of the commanding heights of the economy were never fundamentally transformed. Land ownership remained extraordinarily unequal. The former Bantustans, created as reservoirs of cheap African labor, were never provided with the productive economic foundations needed to overcome their inherited poverty.

Over time, the ANC came to treat the advancement of an emerging black capitalist class as evidence of economic transformation. A narrow layer of businesspeople accumulated wealth, in some cases extraordinary wealth, through access to political power, state contracts, and opportunities created by the Black Economic Empowerment policy, while the overwhelming majority remained excluded from meaningful economic power.

The ANC’s adoption of neoliberal economic policies in the 1990s deepened this problem. The language of economic liberation gave way to investor confidence, competitiveness, and market reform. Brutal austerity, liberalization, and dependence on private investment displaced the redistributive ambitions of the liberation struggle.

We were repeatedly told that economic growth would eventually deliver employment and redistribution. We were also told that redistribution must wait for economic growth and the development of the productive forces. But if redistribution had to wait while productive capacity developed, why did South Africa simultaneously deindustrialize?

We have become what I have described as a “warehouse economy.” We export raw materials and insufficiently processed mineral wealth, allow other countries to manufacture finished products, then import those products for domestic consumption. We export jobs embedded in raw materials and import unemployment embedded in finished goods.

Factories have closed while warehouses have remained open. South Africa continues to extract enormous mineral wealth without developing the productive industries capable of turning that wealth into decent employment on the scale required.

It is a very painful fact that, after decades of mass unemployment and deindustrialization, the poor are now poorer and more numerous than under apartheid. In the second quarter of 2026, South Africa’s official unemployment rate stood at 33.6 percent. Including people who want work but have stopped actively searching, the rate was 43.8 percent. Among young people age fifteen to twenty-four who were in the labor force, unemployment reached 62.8 percent.

This crisis has meant the destruction of hope for millions of people. It has also been accompanied by the weakening of the organized working class. Mass unemployment undermines bargaining power, makes workers afraid to exercise their rights, and encourages casualization and precarious employment. A worker who knows that thousands of unemployed people are desperate for a job is in a much weaker position to resist exploitation.

The crisis has also fragmented the working class itself. Millions of people are unemployed, casually employed, working in the informal economy, or moving between different forms of insecure work. Traditional trade unions organize only a section of this wider class.

The working class cannot be reduced to people fortunate enough to receive a regular pay slip. The unemployed, precarious workers, labor-broker workers, informal workers, women carrying the burden of unpaid care, and young people who have never had secure employment must all be part of the social movement capable of transforming South Africa.

At the same time, the combination of austerity and extreme corruption has resulted in the decay of the state and the collapse of public services. Municipalities have become centers of patronage, political competition over tenders, and the accumulation of private wealth. Water systems collapse, roads deteriorate, sewage flows through communities, and public transport becomes increasingly unreliable. It has become normal for even middle-class areas to go for weeks or even months without water, while the poor live among stinking piles of uncollected refuse.

The crisis is also visible in the ANC’s conception of the state. A developmental state cannot simply outsource development and then claim the credit. It requires public institutions with the capacity to plan, build, maintain infrastructure, and provide services directly.

South Africa has developed a system in which government contracts out essential functions while state capacity deteriorates. The result is an expanding network of contractors, consultants, and intermediaries whose accumulation depends on public expenditure, while the institutions responsible for serving the people become weaker.

The tragic reality is that the ANC’s neoliberal policies have not simply failed to resolve the economic crisis. They have also undermined the credibility of the very idea of democratic transformation, opening the door to right-wing demagoguery.

E conomic failure has been compounded by the degeneration of political leadership. The ANC once insisted that leadership required exceptional qualities: political understanding, integrity, discipline, courage, humility, service, and sacrifice. Its own document, “Through the Eye of the Needle,” expressed the idea that leadership should be earned through commitment to the people rather than acquired through personal ambition.

Today the competition for leadership largely revolves around factions, access to resources, control of organizational structures, and the distribution of positions. Political office has become a route to private accumulation.

This cannot be understood merely as a series of individual moral failures. It is connected to a political culture in which access to the state and public wealth becomes a route to private economic advancement. Where the public sector is treated as a source of tenders and contracts rather than an instrument for meeting social needs, the distinction between political leadership and business accumulation becomes blurred. The result is a profound loss of moral authority.

When working people see leaders acquiring enormous wealth while unemployment rises, schools deteriorate, hospitals struggle, and the water supply fails, they inevitably begin to lose confidence in the institutions that claim to represent them. The ANC’s electoral collapse is therefore not mysterious. It is the political expression of a much deeper social, economic, and organizational failure.

At the same time, trade unions have been divided, and some have become very corrupt, as corrupt as the ANC. The capacity of unions and community organizations to develop working-class leaders has weakened. Organizations have often concentrated on internal contests or debates between established political figures instead of building the democratic power of ordinary people. Political education, once central to the union movement, has declined. With the exception of Abahlali baseMjondolo, the two-hundred-thousand-strong movement of the urban poor, community organizations have lost much of their former strength, with many collapsing completely.

A rapidly growing Right has been very successful in redirecting legitimate popular anger away from those responsible for generalized social suffering and toward African and Asian migrants. Fascist organisations such as Operation Dudula and March and March have built movements around violent hostility toward African migrants. In communities devastated by unemployment, crime, and failing services, they offer a simple explanation: foreigners are responsible for the crisis. Political parties have increasingly adopted the same language. Like many centrist parties elsewhere in the world, the ANC made a profound error of political judgment in indulging organized xenophobia rather than opposing it.

The two parties that have surged forward in these elections, ActionSA and the MKP, have both actively supported the xenophobic street thuggery that forced up to 150,000 migrants, including refugees and other documented migrants, from the country in a matter of months.

This right-wing mobilization, which includes fascist elements, does not only target migrants. It increasingly argues that South Africa has too many rights, that the Constitution should be changed to do away with some of these rights, and that strong leaders should be freed from democratic constraints.

The result is a political paradox. South Africa faces one of the most severe crises of unemployment and inequality anywhere in the world, yet the electoral beneficiaries of popular anger are largely forces advocating policies that will deepen inequality as they redirect anger toward vulnerable minorities.

T he Left is also in crisis. For decades, the South African Communist Party (SACP) presented itself as the socialist component of the ANC-led alliance. Yet it remained politically committed to governments that implemented austerity, privatization, and other neoliberal policies. Its leaders participated in those governments while continuing to speak in the language of socialism and working-class liberation. The contradiction between revolutionary language and participation in the administration of neoliberal capitalism became increasingly difficult to ignore.

This contradiction has never been satisfactorily resolved. Earlier this year, the SACP proposed convening a “Conference of the Left,” inviting organizations including the ANC and Zuma’s MKP, which had been on the streets with the xenophobic mobs. How could a conference claim to unite the Left while including a governing party responsible for decades of neoliberal economic policy and a political formation associated with state capture, ethnic chauvinism, and xenophobia? The independent South African Federation of Trade Unions (SAFTU) considered the invitation carefully and decided not to participate. Other progressive organizations, such as Abahlali baseMjondolo, took similar positions.

Working-class unity is indispensable, but it must be based on principles and a shared program. A Left that abandons its defining commitments in pursuit of alliances with corrupt or reactionary organizations will not resolve the present crisis. It will only deepen it.

T he answer cannot be to demand that workers and the poor continue supporting political organizations that have repeatedly failed them. Nor can we respond to the advance of the Right with moral denunciations while leaving the underlying conditions of life unchanged.

South Africa needs a new working-class political project rooted in a credible program of economic transformation. But no program, however coherent, will succeed without organized social power. A genuine working-class political alternative must emerge from renewed organization, political education, democratic debate, and collective struggle.

The principles of such a movement cannot be negotiable. It must be independent of employers and the capitalist state, committed to socialism and worker democracy, and resolutely opposed to racism, xenophobia, sexism, patriarchy, and ethnic chauvinism. It must be internationalist in its outlook and rooted in the everyday struggles of workers and poor communities.

Rebuilding working-class power also requires reconnecting workplace struggles with those of communities. Water is a workers’ issue. Electricity is a workers’ issue. Public transport, housing, health care, education, gender-based violence, and the climate crisis are all workers’ issues.

The struggles of an employed factory worker cannot be separated from those of an unemployed young person, a mother trying to feed her children, a shack dweller fighting for water, or a community resisting the destruction of its environment.

The organizations capable of creating a new political alternative will have to emerge from these connected struggles.

South Africa’s democratic transition was a great victory for popular movements across the world. The possibility that its political future could now be shaped increasingly by xenophobic and authoritarian forces should concern everyone committed to democracy, equality, and international solidarity.

Zwelinzima Vavi is the general secretary of the South African Federation of Trade Unions.

scraped.title: A Childlike Devotion Runs Through Godzilla Minus Zero
scraped.description: It’s heartwarming the way Takeshi Yamazaki has been able to channel his childhood commitment to that ultimate destructive monster, Godzilla, into Godzilla Minus Zero.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

It’s heartwarming the way Takeshi Yamazaki has been able to channel his childhood commitment to that ultimate destructive monster, Godzilla, into Godzilla Minus Zero .

Set in 1949, Godzilla Minus Zero is a somber film entirely preoccupied with the relentless calamities besetting Japan — from the US nuclear bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki to the past destruction wrought by Godzilla. (Toho Studios / Robot Communications)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

T here’s a familiar but always thrilling moment in Godzilla Minus Zero when Godzilla is fighting the newer, faster, entirely more visually glamorous monster King Ghidorah — an immense three-headed, golden-ray-shooting dragon that seems set on destroying the human race — and Godzilla is losing. In fact, it seems Godzilla is beaten and dying.

But then Godzilla goes deep and dredges up the last of his prehistoric mojo and comes back to win the brutal kaiju battle. Godzilla the destroyer from the sea becomes Godzilla the hero and savior of the Japanese protagonists watching in wide-eyed terror. All the viewer’s childhood love of Godzilla, who lumbers around on big, squat feet like a crude, clumsy dinosaur based on some devoted but impractical kid’s drawing, surges to the fore.

Writer-director-CGI effects master Takeshi Yamazaki seems highly motivated by such lingering childhood feelings. He cautions us in interviews, in a caringly paternal sort of way, to remember that though Godzilla fights King Ghidorah, it’s not because he sides with human beings: “He can’t become humanity’s friend.”

Oh, we know . But many small children aren’t entirely on the side of humans either. Personally, I was all for the animals as a kid and relentlessly pretended to be an animal for years before the US educational system crushed it out of me. And most little children are united, at least for a few years, in a love of dinosaurs that borders on obsession. Though I’ve known a few kids who loved and identified with cars and trucks and industrial vehicles more than adult people.

Yamazaki seems to understand all that. He says he opted to revive King Ghidorah and have him wreak havoc on Yamazaki’s own hometown of Matsumoto in the first scene of destruction in Godzilla Minus Zero , then fight the climactic epic battle with Godzilla because, fifty-five years ago, he was a seven-year-old kid in Matsumoto eagerly awaiting a revival screening of the Godzilla movie sequel Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster from 1964. The promotional flyer specifically promised, “King Ghidorah attacks Matsumoto!”

But he was terribly disappointed when “the monster finally appeared [and] all he did was clip the roof tiles of the city’s castle before flying off.”

Yamazaki said, “I was so frustrated, so heartbroken. . . . I held a grudge for years.”

But ultimately, it’s heartwarming the way Yamazaki has been able to channel his childhood commitment and frustration into making the gorgeous and emotionally compelling Godzilla Minus One , released in 2023 and Godzilla Minus Zero , currently playing in theaters. It goes a long way toward explaining the immense critical and popular appeal of both.

Yamazaki was stunned by the global success of the first film, which he claimed he never expected to get such a warm reception beyond Japan. Its embrace by mass audiences in the United States was especially surprising, since we’re notorious for refusing to see “foreign films” requiring us to read subtitles. But a grand exception is made in the case of Yamazaki’s Godzilla films.

And Yamazaki isn’t conciliating American feelings either. Given the subject matter, it wouldn’t make any sense.

In Godzilla Minus Zero , the characters representing the US military brass in post–World War II Japan are all sinister, arrogant conquerors clearly up to no good, always plotting ways to harness additional power and further subjugate the Japanese. Even the lowly GIs stationed in Tokyo are portrayed as a disturbing alien presence — jittery, full of directionless aggressivity, vaguely looking for trouble. One American soldier chews gum with a manic ferocity.

The satirical portrayal of this platoon looks a lot like British filmmakers Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger’s 1946 take on American GIs in A Matter of Life and Death , and Powell and Pressburger were being conciliatory to the United States in a “hands-across-the-pond” manner. Their GI Joes, killed near the end of World War II, arrive in heaven all hopped up on a similarly strange, angsty energy and immediately scramble over to a suddenly revealed vending machine stocked with Coca-Cola.

Set in 1949, Godzilla Minus Zero has no humor of that kind. It’s a somber film entirely preoccupied with the relentless calamities besetting Japan: World War II, the US nuclear bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, living in postwar poverty and wreckage, the Godzilla attacks in Godzilla Minus One , and the King Ghidorah attacks in Godzilla Minus Zero . The character of Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), the elderly biologist who found the charred bodies of his family in the aftermath of the bombing of Hiroshima, miraculously comes through all the mayhem, exclaiming bitterly, “And again, I survive!”

He joins forces to face the King Ghidorah threat with Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), director of the government’s Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau, who has to put together the reluctant team that will fight this new monster. Former kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who flew the mission that apparently destroyed Godzilla in the previous film, is hoping — in vain — to avoid having to go up against King Ghidorah. Kōichi has married Noriko Ōishi (Minami Hamabe), a survivor of a previous Godzilla attacks, and together they’ve adopted war orphan Akiko (Sae Nagatani). The investment in their new family gives them a great stake in escaping any further life-threatening calamities.

Director Yamazaki particularly wanted a woman represented among the experts on the disaster team, so he created the character of Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a meteorologist with a useful theory about King Ghidorah’s attraction to lightning storms.

Godzilla Minus Zero has that typical sequel effect of moving away from a streamlined narrative toward a complicated one involving more monsters, more characters, more plotlines, more everything. There are promising story developments that aren’t fully explored and are presumably there as starter plotlines for sequels, such as the way living “Godzilla cells” are affecting humans, with a handful of scientific subjects who’ve survived contact with Godzilla but are now manifesting mutations. Noriko wears an eyepatch to cover her one reptilian yellow eye, and she also has Godzilla scales and spikes beginning to grow on one shoulder-blade, hidden by her clothing.

Still, the film maintains that basic rhythm also remembered from childhood when watching old Godzilla films: big action scenes full of exciting destruction and terror interspersed with far duller but somehow reassuring meeting scenes when characters representing science, government, the military, and the model family unit regroup to try Plan B, Plan C, and so on. Yamazaki hasn’t come to challenge the genre conventions but to fulfill them and render them more beautiful.

He makes vast CGI action sequences as sensational as it’s possible to make them, and it seems churlish to complain that, though generally magnificent, it’s still so much goddamn wearying CGI. It’s a generational viewership problem, really. I don’t think young people miss the sense of imprinting off of physical reality that once defined the film medium.

But the figure of Godzilla has such lasting, surefire appeal, it’s hard to quell the basic moviegoer longing to see him again. As Yamazaki put it about his own lifelong obsession,

As a kid, it was just: monster, cool, scary, amazing. Making these films now, I understand how much anxiety Japanese audiences were carrying when the first film came out in 1954, and how the monster’s shape matched that fear exactly. . . . Godzilla was never just a cool monster that wrecks things; he’s always carried the weight of the nuclear question, of war. The more I make these films, the more I feel that weight, and I think it’s exactly why people are still drawn to him.

Godzilla brings his fear-shaped silhouette into contemporary times as we’re “drifting toward conflict” on a global scale, in Yamazaki’s view. He meant the sequel to be weightier and more complex: “It’s entertainment, but I wanted it to leave something heavy behind, too.”

Yamazaki’s ability to unite fond nostalgia for Godzilla movies past, reaching back to childhood, with intensified modern angst forged in twentieth-century horrors that only grow over time, creates a riveting emotional combination. The third sequel is guaranteed, but it’s easy to imagine Yamazaki’s Godzilla movies maintaining their global appeal for as long as we’ve got a habitable globe to stand on.

Eileen Jones is a film critic at Jacobin , host of the Filmsuck podcast, and author of Filmsuck, USA .

scraped.description: Capitalism turns children’s play into preparation for work, but it cannot fully contain what play makes possible. In her new book, Susan Ferguson explores how the openness and pleasure of play can help us imagine other ways of being together.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

Capitalism turns children’s play into preparation for work, but it cannot fully contain what play makes possible. In her new book, Susan Ferguson explores how the openness and pleasure of play can help us imagine other ways of being together.

The modern ideal of childhood as a sacred time apart from work emerged under capitalism, but that ideal is under pressure. Schools and developmental norms increasingly shape children for the labor market, undermining the freedom the ideal promises. (Eileen T. Meslar / Chicago Tribune / Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

Review of Child’s Play: Childhood in and Against Capitalism by Susan Ferguson (Pluto Press, 2026)

A central concern of feminist Marxist theory and practice has been how to understand the relationship between paid and unpaid labor. Marxist feminists have drawn on Karl Marx’s observation that capital leaves workers to ensure their own reproduction, a process that depends on their instinct for self-preservation. They have shown how capitalist accumulation depends on reproductive labor, work that has fallen primarily to women. But what, exactly, is being reproduced? Workers must replenish their strength so that they can work again the next day; importantly, reproduction also encompasses bearing children and creating future labor power.

But it does not stop there of course: children must then be shaped into capable workers, a process that does not happen by itself and in which social reproduction is by no means simply left to the workers themselves. For anyone who has attended school, and perhaps even more so for those of us — myself included — who are now experiencing school all over again through our children’s education, it is more than apparent that school is, in many ways, an institution designed to socialize children into their future roles as wage workers.

As E. P. Thompson writes in Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism , schooling can be understood as an acclimatization to the factory’s temporal discipline. Today, however, this involves more than the straightforward discipline Thompson identified. It also entails producing flexible, self-directed learners who can seamlessly retrain and acquire new skills in an ever-changing and volatile labor market.

D espite this recognition of the importance of shaping working-class children in particular ways, children, and their role and position within capitalism, have remained marginal concerns within Marxist theory, as well as within feminist social reproduction theory. Perhaps this is precisely because children are not regarded as workers: neither productive nor reproductive. In her new book , Child’s Play: Childhood in and Against Capitalism , Susan Ferguson turns her attention to children, challenging the idea that they do not participate in reproductive activities. Ferguson argues that children are constantly involved in processes of creating and sustaining life, but primarily through play rather than through reproductive labor in any conventional sense.

While Marxism has shown limited interest in children’s creative and life-sustaining activities, Ferguson argues that capitalism has a contradictory relationship with children, and particularly with children’s play. On one hand, the ideal of childhood as a sacred time for play, exploration, and curiosity emerged under capitalism and has since become firmly established. On the other, the regulation of children’s play, along with models from developmental psychology for determining whether play is age-appropriate, has become increasingly pronounced. Under capitalism, not only schooling but play itself becomes a preparation for the future. In this way, play acquires a kind of constructive dimension, with a clearly defined purpose, rather than being something free and open-ended, with no explicit goal beyond the sheer satisfaction that play itself provides. Learning to play properly becomes part of learning to work. In this sense, we are dealing with a form of alienated play.

Beyond learning to play properly, it is also important to learn how to stop playing: to make the transition from being a “player” to being a “worker.” Children who deviate from the expected developmental trajectory, or who fail to acquire certain abilities according to an imagined timeline, quickly become targets of intervention. It is partly against this backdrop that we can understand the dramatic increase in ADHD diagnoses and other neurodevelopmental diagnoses that we are witnessing around the world. Children who cannot seamlessly adapt to the routines of school, whose minds wander during lessons, who are too lively or struggle to sit still, children who want to play rather than work, become problems to be solved, sooner rather than later.

B ut what problem is solved by these interventions? Rates of depression and burnout are particularly high among women aged forty to fifty who work in health and social care. Women experiencing these problems are often medicated them rather than offered changes to their working conditions — changes that would require a redistribution of economic resources.

Following a similar logic, instead of creating a school system that does not systematically produce failure, children are increasingly medicated so that they can cope with school. More than one in ten boys aged ten to seventeen in Sweden has an ADHD diagnosis . Surely this should prompt us to reconsider what counts as normal, and to place the school system that sustains this state of affairs under scrutiny, rather than focusing on how individual children can be helped to integrate into this abnormal normality?

But Ferguson’s book is not only about how play has become subject to capitalist control; it is also about how children’s play can be understood as a site of resistance to capitalist logic. Although children’s games can, of course, be cruel, exclusionary, and governed by clear norms, Ferguson nevertheless sees the possibility of something transformative in children’s play. She describes this as “the embodied capacities of imagining and acting on and in the world in ways that fulfill our needs while nurturing human connections to the self, others and our environments.” Just as play can be utopian in its creation of new worlds, political organizing can also adopt a playful — that is, open-ended — attitude toward what might become possible. This does not mean that we can play capitalism to pieces, but that we can resist capitalism’s attempts to instrumentalize our creative impulses.

Despite attempts to curb children’s play, whether through direct intervention or by restricting it to specific times, the games children play cannot be understood as exclusively capitalist or alienated activities. Rather, they can be seen as practices grounded in the sheer pleasure of playing, in the possibility of exploring, imagining and creating together without the activity necessarily having to lead to anything beyond itself. In this sense, play holds the potential to elude the capitalist logic that seeks to make every activity productive, measurable, and purposeful. Perhaps it is precisely in this openness, in the unpredictability of play and its capacity to imagine other ways of being together, that its political potential lies. Remember that you were once a child.

Evelina Johansson Wilén is an associate professor of gender studies at Örebro University in Sweden. She serves on the editorial board of the Marxist theoretical journal Röda Rummet and is the author of a forthcoming book on family abolition.
