Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Wrapping up the NLC and trying to get home after a groundstop.

Josh Blackman | 11.15.2026 11:21 AM

The 2026 Federalist Society Convention is a wrap. I have attended every NLC since I was a 1L in 2006 (except for the cancelled COVID year). At each convention, the focus is a bit different but the overall takeaway is similar. There is a healthy a mix of timeless topics and topical topics, with an infusion of the political landscape of the day. It is very hard to capture the essence of a convention by watching some or even all of the panels, as so much business transpires in the hallways and at the bars.

I think much of the press coverage failed in attempt to to consolidate a very broad movement into a few paragraphs. For example, CNN blared "After blue wave, Federalist Society is ready to move on from Trump." Really? Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered the Olson Lecture, White House Counsel Will Scharf had a fireside chat, White House Advisor May Mailman discussed over-regulation, and Gene Hamilton favored restrictive immigration policy on behalf of America First Legal Foundation. Plus there were other members of the administration from the EPA and OLP.

I think there are a range of opinions about how the conservative legal movement should respond to the current political situation. I don't think anyone actually knows exactly what to do. The midterm election, of course, was the elephant in the room. I offered my take here . A lot can happen over the next two years.

I'm flummoxed by the uproar about the commemorative coins celebrating Calais , Slaughter , and other decision. These were in fact generational wins at the Supreme Court. Justice Scalia established overruling Humphrey's Executor as a founding principle of FedSoc. Since the 1980s, conservatives--including John Roberts--have seen the Voting Rights Act as violating the Constitution. And West Virginia v. B.P.J. was such an obvious outcome--except perhaps at CNN. Plus, this was the swaggiest NLC I've ever been to. There was an entire room to pick up FedSoc swag. The coins were a nice touch.

Perhaps the biggest disruption at the convention was the groundstop. My flight home Saturday evening was cancelled, as were many others. I was able to get a room at the Mayflower for another day. Fortunately, one of the few remaining perks of United status is priority rebooking during "irregular operations." I was originally scheduled to fly home Sunday evening around 7:30 p.m. The United App has a new feature that lets you be on standby for up to three flights at once without losing your confirmed seat. United will send you a text notifying you that a seat opened up on an earlier flight, and you have twenty minutes to accept it. I was able to jump from the 7:30 p.m. flight to the 12:50 p.m. flight. A few hours later, I was given a chance to jump from the 12:50 p.m. flight to the 10:58 a.m. flight. For both of these flights, I was number one on the standby list. Around 5:00 a.m., I was offered the chance to move to the 8:20 a.m. flight, but I was sleeping and missed the window. The system worked very well. And without my status, I doubt I would have been able to get the earlier flight. As things turned out, the 12:50 p.m. flight was cancelled. I will get home today.

scraped.title: The legal battle over who gets to show their genitals at a nude spa takes an unexpected turn
scraped.description: Olympus Spa found itself in hot water with Washington state because it turned away a customer with male genitalia.
scraped.author: Billy Binion
scraped.h1: The Legal Battle Over Who Gets To Show Their Genitals at a Nude Spa Takes an Unexpected Turn
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

First Amendment

Billy Binion | 11.15.2026 7:00 AM

The Washington State Human Rights Commission (WSHRC) voted last month to permit businesses to set entry requirements based on genitalia when nudity is a core part of the operation—thus allowing, say, an all-female nude establishment to reject customers with male genitals without having to fear anti-discrimination enforcement from the state.

This is not a sentence you necessarily see every day. But it is the latest plot twist related to the legal odyssey that is Olympus Spa v. Armstrong , a case concerning a nude spa that has been embroiled in a yearslong, ever-crescendoing fight with the state after it declined to admit a preoperative transgender woman to its location in Lynnwood, Washington.

The legal question at issue: Did it have the right to do that? It's one that Olympus Spa has asked the Supreme Court to answer .

Haven Wilvich, who has identified as a "nonbinary trans woman," filed a complaint with the WSHRC in 2020, alleging Olympus Spa—a traditional Korean establishment that requires nudity in its pool area and thus caters to a single-sex clientele—had violated the Washington State Law Against Discrimination (WLAD). That statute bars discrimination on the basis of several characteristics, including sexual orientation, which is defined under the law to encompass "heterosexuality, homosexuality, bisexuality, and gender expression or identity."

That last part has proven thorny for the spa. When the business sued on First Amendment grounds, it fared poorly . "We are not unmindful of the concerns and beliefs raised by the Spa," wrote Judge M. Margaret McKeown for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit last year. But the First Amendment, the court said, did not provide an avenue to address those concerns. The government's "objection to the entrance policy was not based on 'disagreement with the message it conveys' but rather with the practice it described—a practice that was unlawful under WLAD," said McKeown. The WSHRC, in other words, did not compel the business to change its beliefs; it was instead enforcing a law as written. Olympus Spa "simply did not challenge the statute itself," McKeown noted, "and it is not our role to rewrite the statute."

As unsatisfying as this was to many onlookers, it was also likely correct under current law. "Generally speaking, the [Supreme] Court has been reluctant to allow businesses to say, 'We get to associate with whomever we please,'" Eugene Volokh, a law professor emeritus at UCLA who specializes in First Amendment issues, told me in September. "That would spell, at least, if not the end of anti-discrimination law, at least very broad challenges to anti-discrimination law….As a libertarian matter, one could argue that there should be such a right, but the Supreme Court has repeatedly rejected any such claim."

In an appeal to the Supreme Court, Olympus Spa renews its First Amendment claim. Yet it also leans heavily into another argument emphasizing religious exemptions. The spa's owners are devout Christians and, according to their petition , "hold the religious conviction that men and women should not be unclothed together unless married to each other." Consequently, they maintain the spa should be exempt from public accommodations laws insofar as they apply to its single-sex admissions policy.

That is still not a slam dunk. The case law around religious exemptions is somewhat Wild West–esque. That it's so unsettled, though, may encourage the Supreme Court to take a look.

Washington state appears to want to avoid that, if its vote to update the law is any indication. "In the limited circumstance where a business requires nudity as a central purpose of the business," the addition reads, "such business may maintain a rule that entry to spaces where nudity is required be based on genital characteristics." After the vote, the executive director was to work with the Office of the Attorney General to officially file the rule.

That victory may be more superficial than it looks. Nor does it seem likely to deter the business from pushing forward with its appeal. "The Spa is still weighing the legal effect of the Commission's actions," says a source familiar with the litigation. "To begin, the Commission does not have the power to change state law, so it's unclear how much protection—if any—this rule change will give the Spa if a male sues under the Washington Law Against Discrimination for access to areas where the Spa's nude, female patrons congregate. In addition, the Spa's complaint sought nominal damages and is entitled to have its case reinstated to pursue that relief."

The story, while niche, has elicited some strong reactions. "This is a case about swinging dicks," wrote Judge Lawrence VanDyke of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit in March. "You may think that swinging dicks shouldn't appear in a judicial opinion. You're not wrong. But as much as you might understandably be shocked and displeased to merely encounter that phrase in this opinion, I hope we all can agree that it is far more jarring for the unsuspecting and exposed women at Olympus Spa—some as young as thirteen—to be visually assaulted by the real thing."

However crass the phrasing, the fact that Olympus Spa's request—that it not be forced to admit customers with penises to its all-female nude space—has led to such a prolonged battle in the courts understandably strikes many as, well, odd at best. It epitomizes how our legal architecture is sometimes ill-equipped to address commonsense, good-faith objections, even if this example is an edge case.

Yet it also serves as a memorable reminder that resolutions to such disputes often emerge not from the courts but from the people who make the rules. The commission's alteration is a start, though how much protection it really offers remains to be seen. But a more lasting change could come from the Legislature. After Olympus Spa's loss at the 9th Circuit last year, Volokh told me that the most apt remedy would be to go to the source: Amend WLAD. It should be possible, he said, to allow "places of public accommodation to segregate facilities by gender however the places define it," like by anatomy. Sometimes, alas, the threat of a lawsuit is what it takes to get things moving.

scraped.title: Iran War Day 261: Iran Attacks U.S. Radar in Bahrain for Second Time in Two Days
scraped.description: State of the Union: The U.S. intelligence community believes Iran has between 1,500 and 2,500 missiles, per a report.
scraped.author: Jude Russo
scraped.body_text:
Iran targeted an American air defense radar installation in Bahrain with drones early Sunday, the second such incident in two days.

The IRGC claimed to have successfully launched six drones against the radar at an air base in Riffa. Bahrain’s military claimed to have intercepted the attack. CENTCOM, which denied that Saturday’s attack was successful, has yet to release a statement.

The island kingdom of Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Fifth Fleet, was subject to heavy bombardment in earlier phases of the war.

The strikes demonstrate the ongoing threat posed by Iran’s drone and missile stockpiles. The Wall Street Journal reported Sunday that American intelligence organs estimate that Iran still has between 1,500 and 2,500 ballistic missiles, suggesting that the Islamic Republic’s military capacities are largely intact after eight months of fighting.

Other Iran-aligned actors in the region also appear to retain significant drone and missile capabilities. Yemen’s Houthi rebels claimed Saturday to have targeted the airport and the financial district of Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh.

AAA reported national average prices per gallon of $3.82 for regular gas and $6.02 for diesel.

Jude Russo is the managing editor of The American Conservative and a contributing editor of The New York Sun . He is a 2024–25 James Madison Fellow at Hillsdale College and was named one of the ISI Top 20 Under 30 for 2024.

items.title: What Trump Can Get Out of the Trilateral Shenzhen Summit
items.summary: There are several files on which three great powers can make tangible progress at the upcoming meeting. The post What Trump Can Get Out of the Trilateral Shenzhen Summit appeared first on The American Conservative. Foreign Affairs What Trump Can Get Out of the Trilateral Shenzhen Summit There are several files on which three great powers can make tangible progress at the upcoming meeting. (Win McNamee/Getty Images) In an era of global conflict and turbulence, the prospect of a trilateral summ...

scraped.title: What Trump Can Get Out of the Trilateral Shenzhen Summit
scraped.description: There are several files on which three great powers can make tangible progress at the upcoming meeting.
scraped.author: Jude Russo
scraped.body_text:
There are several files on which three great powers can make tangible progress at the upcoming meeting.

In an era of global conflict and turbulence, the prospect of a trilateral summit bringing together the leaders of China, Russia, and the U.S. is a hopeful sign. But whether the aspiration for a more peaceful and stable global order can be met during the Shenzhen meeting expected this month is open to question.

Doubts are visible in all corners. Still, it would be a mistake to pass up such an extraordinary opportunity. I have written in a recent book that this brand of trilateralism is necessary to knit a dysfunctional global order back together. In particular, this three-way meeting has the possibility to make progress on both nuclear stability and regional conflict, issues that are haunting our world at present with the specter of uncontrolled, violent escalation to even more tragic levels.

Trilateral diplomacy presents unique challenges, but such a summit contains the potential of breaking free from the assumptions that too often stall bilateral or multilateral agreements. Moreover, the China–Russia–U.S. triangle brings together the three most powerful military forces on earth, so difficult but necessary discussion about security issues naturally comes to the fore.

This is likely one reason why the Chinese hosts seem somewhat reluctant to support the trilateral meeting. Beijing has demonstrated a willingness to help mediate various conflicts, but it knows well that U.S.–Russian relations are still fraught and does not wish to be caught in the crossfire.

Russia, perhaps, wants the meeting most of the three powers, if for no other reason than to promote its status as a near-superpower.

President Donald Trump also seems relatively eager. Fresh off his major domestic setback in the midterm elections earlier this month, perhaps he is inclined to seek out positive optics on the world stage. Yet Trump is likely to be disappointed if he thinks that the meeting would yield major movement on either of the two tragic wars that are vexing his foreign policy.

First and foremost, the three leaders should focus on looming nuclear dangers. All three states are sinking enormous resources into nuclear forces modernization. This presents the possibility of more weapons on a higher level of alert, but also the no longer far-fetched possibility of exotic nuclear weapons , such as those deployed in space or working in combination with drones and artificial intelligence.

At a minimum, Putin, Trump, and Xi should agree that such exotic nuclear weapons undermine global stability.

The Trump administration has shown great interest in a broader trilateral arms control agreement, especially after the expiration of Washington and Moscow’s arms control measures. However, insisting on China’s involvement in a three-way arms control accord risks serving up a poison pill which could prevent meaningful progress on other critical issues. It would be prudent to save discussion of a more comprehensive trilateral arms control accord for future meetings once the U.S. has found the format productive.

Strategists know well that nuclear conflict, if that terrible day ever comes, would likely arise out of uncontrolled escalation of a regional conflict. That is why the three leaders should also focus on the two most dangerous situations: Ukraine and Taiwan. In the case of the former, Washington and Beijing can help by pointing out tangible gains for the Kremlin if Putin agrees to end the war in the short term. Such carrots could include trilateral activation of the Arctic transit corridor that has been a long-time goal of the Russian leader and/or legal recognition of Russian sovereignty over Crimea and Donbas.

With respect to Taiwan, the three leaders could helpfully reaffirm Beijing’s cherished principle of “ one China ” and could go further to jointly recognize that the Taiwan situation should not evolve in the direction of Ukraine, namely as a proxy war impinging on one of the great powers’ core interests. If Washington were to exercise restraint with respect to those two ultra-sensitive situations for Beijing and Moscow, it might receive additional help in ending the U.S.–Iran War.

Beijing, in particular, has strong incentives to help Washington end this unfortunate conflict that endangers the global economy. China’s influence in Tehran should not be underestimated and Moscow could help rein in Iran and its proxies. These three global conflicts top the agenda, of course, but the trilateral summit could also usefully address the deteriorating situation in the Horn of Africa, wherein a thicket of brewing conflicts threatens to grow into a full-blown region-wide catastrophe.

This trilateral summit has the potential for significant progress in easing global tensions and returning to overall strategic stability. But this meeting should also set the stage for other small groupings, for example a China–Japan–U.S. trilateral, as well as a Europe–Russia–U.S. working group. Likewise a regular P5 summit gathering the leaders of the permanent members of the UN Security Council is long overdue. Regularizing small groupings of powerful leaders can play a role in arresting and reversing the current slide into global chaos and war.

items.title: The War Must End Before It’s Too Late for Ukraine
items.summary: Kiev should cede the Donbas and accept non-membership in NATO to remain a viable, sovereign state. The post The War Must End Before It’s Too Late for Ukraine appeared first on The American Conservative. Ukraine The War Must End Before It’s Too Late for Ukraine Kiev should cede the Donbas and accept non-membership in NATO to remain a viable, sovereign state. (Photo by Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images) After more than eight months without direct negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, ...

scraped.title: The War Must End Before It’s Too Late for Ukraine
scraped.description: Kiev should cede the Donbas and accept non-membership in NATO to remain a viable, sovereign state.
scraped.author: The American Conservative
scraped.body_text:
Kiev should cede the Donbas and accept non-membership in NATO to remain a viable, sovereign state.

After more than eight months without direct negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, talks between them, mediated by the U.S., resumed in Abu Dhabi last week. Much in the war has changed since the February negotiations. Russia’s terms have not changed, but the certainty of its achieving them has.

Three things are certain. The first two: Ukraine will not become a member of NATO, and Russia will obtain most or all of the Donbas. These things are certain because of the third reality: Russia has won the war.

Ukraine is dying, and the clock is ticking. The only uncertainty is how long Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders will hold out before terminating the life support.

Not only are Ukrainian soldiers being killed or maimed at a staggering rate—perhaps as high as 30,000 a month —but the population of Ukraine has been vanishing. Millions of Ukrainians have fled, and many do not plan to return. Almost a quarter million left in the first half of this year, and many more are on the verge of leaving this winter as life in Kiev becomes unbearable. Among those who stayed, deaths outnumber births. Life expectancy is the lowest in Europe . There are not enough people to man the labor force or pay taxes for social services.

Ukraine can no longer defend itself. Kiev has run out of air defense interceptors and of nations willing and able to supply them. The U.S. supply of Patriot interceptors has slowed to worse than a trickle and may take several years to deliver, and Germany has told Ukraine it has no more to send. As a result, Russian missiles and drones are hitting their targets practically at will. Ukraine’s ports are constricted, and its grain cannot be exported at necessary scale. Its steel mills are closing , its mining operations are shutting down, and its digital infrastructure is coming under attack. Transportation is at a standstill as key bridges are damaged and hundreds of locomotives destroyed. In Kiev, the capital, blackouts occur semiregularly.

And all the while, the Russian armed forces are slowly, but inexorably, advancing across Donbas. Ukraine must acknowledge that inevitability now and save lives. Lost fortress cities can be built further west, but lost lives cannot be recovered.

Russia’s war on Ukraine was never primarily about territory. The key reasons for the invasion were keeping Ukraine out of NATO and, as the Kremlin sees it, protecting the ethnic Russian citizens of Donbas. The previous Minsk agreements had been meant to solve the latter problem. It was only when Ukraine failed to implement them, the U.S. failed to pressure Ukraine to implement them, and Europe used them as a delaying tactic to arm Ukraine for war on Russia that Moscow saw annexing Donbas as a necessary solution.

So, though the war was never fundamentally about territory, the negotiated end to the war is to a large extent about territory. Russia will not end its assault until Donbas is Russian.

Washington may be prepared to recognize that reality as essential for ending the war diplomatically. President Donald Trump recently said that a negotiated peace is going to happen but that “they’re gonna end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine.”

U.S. officials reportedly believed that privately Kiev has shown flexibility on the issue. Kiev’s willingness to countenance relinquishing territory, however, is understood to be linked to its demand for strong security guarantees.

Nevertheless, following the Abu Dhabi talks, a Ukrainian source told the Telegraph that Ukraine “will never recognize” Russia’s control of Ukrainian territory, “neither de facto nor de jure .” Moscow may not demand de jure recognition of its control of Donbas, but a rejection of de facto recognition means the war goes on.

On the first day of talks in Abu Dhabi, Zelensky posted on X that “ceding Ukrainian land for peace” is not “about reality” but just “abstract words.” He complained that the Americans ask, “Can you exchange Donbas for security?” but then define security as “Not NATO, but similar to NATO.”

He has a point. But that is as good as he is going to get. Putin will not end a war to keep Ukraine out of NATO (and NATO out of Ukraine) by agreeing to NATO Article 5 security guarantees for Ukraine. But the U.S. has made it clear that it won’t agree to that either. Republican and Democratic administrations have made clear they would not fight a direct war with Russia over the Donbas. And Europe has made it clear by their actions that they will not, and cannot, guarantee Ukraine’s security without significant U.S. backing. They lack the troops, the technological capabilities, and the finances to do so.

The best security guarantees Ukraine is likely to get are commitments that fall short of NATO: some weaker, “similar to NATO” form of Article 5 coupled with security assurances that come with European Union membership. Ironically, the strongest security guarantee Ukraine could get would involve NATO’s closing its door to Ukraine, thereby easing Russia’s own security concerns and beginning the process of establishing the wider European security architecture now apparently on the table.

For Ukraine to survive, the war must be ended now, so, fair or unfair, Russian control of Donbas must be conceded and NATO membership must be taken off the table. Once freed from war, Ukraine would remain a sovereign nation on most of its territory, and it could turn westward, taking a path that leads to the European Union. It won’t have Donbas, and it won’t have NATO. But it won’t border a threatened Russia.

Ted Snider is a contributing editor for The American Conservative . He is also a frequent contributor to Responsible Statecraft and other outlets.

scraped.title: A Wife’s Revenge from Beyond the Grave
scraped.description: Our blockbuster 2024 piece—about the world’s worst divorce—has been turned into a documentary!
scraped.author: Frannie Block
scraped.body_text:
If the headline above has given you déjà vu, that’s because we’ve shared this piece with you before, back in July of 2024. The reason we’re resending it today is that, in the years since, it has been turned into a documentary on Paramount+ —called “He Said, She Said: Till Death Do Us Part”—which will be available to stream starting Tuesday, November 17. I’ve seen the first episode—and it’s haunting.

If I had to describe this story in three words, it’d be “world’s worst divorce.” Allan Kassenoff and Catherine Youssef were high-flying New York City litigators, living in a dark-wood-paneled house in Westchester with their three daughters—until their relationship unraveled into screaming matches, abuse allegations, and a bitter custody battle that remains infamous in the county’s family court.

The divorce was still ongoing when, in the spring of 2023, Allan received a horrifying email: Catherine had traveled to Switzerland, where she would die by assisted suicide.

And that’s when the campaign to destroy his life began in earnest.

When Frannie started digging into the story of the Kassenoffs, she found that nothing was as it seemed. To get to the truth, she spent more than eight months speaking to dozens of people and reading hundreds of documents—and soon realized that this isn’t only the story of one family’s domestic dispute. It’s a story about how social media can distort our perceptions, and courtrooms can flatten our judgement, both of them boiling even the most complicated human beings down into stock characters in simple tales of good and evil.

“More than any story I’ve ever worked on, this one kept me up at night,” Frannie told the audience last week at a screening of the first episode of the docuseries. I think you’ll see why. —Freya Sanders

This is a story that ends with my own assisted death in Switzerland.

That is how the suicide note began.

Allan Kassenoff was standing in the driveway of his Westchester home on Saturday, May 27, 2023, when he read it. His wife, Catherine, had emailed it to dozens of people—including judges, attorneys, journalists, police, friends, and even staff at Allan’s law firm, Greenberg Traurig—but she hadn’t sent it to her husband. A colleague had forwarded it to him.

Allan and Catherine had spent the previous four years fighting in court over the custody of their three young daughters. After millions of dollars, and over 3,000 court filings, the divorce still hadn’t been finalized.

In four single-spaced pages, the email detailed how Allan had been an abusive husband who had manipulated the corrupt court system into cutting off Catherine’s parental rights. She accused him of “ruining the lives of my children, me,” and so many other “parents (mostly mothers) who have tried to stand up against abuse.”

“Perhaps if I had not been re-diagnosed with cancer I could have lasted in this fight longer,” she wrote, disclosing a recurrence not even her closest friends had known about, and which Allan told me he doesn’t believe was real. “But I do not have the strength to go forward,” she concluded.

Catherine also embedded a Dropbox link that included hundreds of court documents, police reports, her children’s therapy records, and videos of her husband yelling—evidence that showed, she wrote, “exactly how abusive Allan Kassenoff is.”

While reading Catherine’s suicide note, Allan started to cry, he told me. “I felt bad for her,” he said. But he also admits he felt relieved. According to him, his wife was the abusive one, and had “made my life a living hell for so long.”

But while Catherine’s story may have ended that day, Allan’s torment had only just begun. In her suicide note, Catherine told readers, “Don’t let my death be in vain.” And whether she knew it or not, there were plenty of people willing to avenge her.

To keep reading this terrifying story—which is all about pride, vengeance, and the disturbing truth about what goes viral—click below:

In October of last year, Free Press reporter Francesca Block came across a fascinating tip in her inbox. It told the story of Allan Kassenoff and Catherine Youssef, a couple of New York City litigators who married in 2006. It was a tempestuous union, which resulted in three daughters, and ended with a series of terrible abuse allegations. Allan finally …

Remember that advice column last week about guy whose wife didn't give him sex for seven years?

It could always be worse.

Those poor kids.

scraped.title: A Dark Storm Is Gathering Over The Housing Market
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: A Dark Storm Is Gathering Over The Housing Market
scraped.body_text:
Submitted by QTR's Fringe Finance

I’ve been warning about the continued risks surrounding AI steadily since August , and I continue to believe we’re going to see more bad news from the sector that has driven the bull market of the last few years.

I also think more bad news is coming for Nvidia and I’ve also warned about crypto , and the shaky price action we saw this weekend reinforces my view that more volatility and downside could be ahead.

I know, it’s a downer for a Sunday morning. And spoiler alert: today’s column isn’t going to be bright and cheery, either. Hey…if I have to suffer on Sundays as an Eagles fan this year, I’m insisting you must suffer, too.

But in all seriousness, today I’m going to focus on a concern I’ve had dating back for the last year or so in an area that isn’t talked about much, but where a deluge of newly released data is giving cause for some nascent concern: housing.

Financial stress doesn’t necessarily remain confined to one asset class. It’s the reason I’ve been barking about commercial real estate, subprime auto paper, regional banks, equities, crypto and bonds for the last year. Today I’m going to bark about housing.

Weakness in speculative investments can coincide with a broader pullback in risk-taking, tighter credit conditions, and more cautious consumer behavior. That doesn’t mean declining crypto prices automatically translate into falling home prices, but it’s worth considering how financial pressure moves through household balance sheets, particularly when housing affordability is already stretched.

There’s a general sequence that often develops when people need cash. They typically begin with their most liquid assets…first stocks, crypto, and other investments that can be sold quickly. Cashing out CDs, savings accounts and the likes. Then, when cash is scarce, they sell the dung heap of crap they’ve been amassing…their collection of Jordans or Pokemon cards or Steve Wilkos show official memorabilia (or whatever the hell ‘collector’ shit is in in the year 2026) …then their new consumer electronics they just bought for themselves on credit that they don’t need.

“Get the hell off my stage! You don’t deserve a chair!”

As financial pressure builds, some households increasingly rely on credit cards, followed by unsecured personal loans when additional borrowing is available. Eventually, larger assets such as cars, boats, or other possessions may be sold to generate cash or reduce monthly expenses.

Housing often comes way later in that process. Selling a home takes time, involves substantial transaction costs, and may require finding somewhere else to live. Homeowners generally have strong incentives to avoid selling unless circumstances require it. But prolonged financial stress can eventually lead to more listings, increased borrowing against home equity, missed HELOC or mortgage payments, and forced sales.

Housing has historically experienced long boom-and-bust cycles, sometimes spanning 15 to 20 years or more, although there is no fixed timetable. We’re now approaching 20 years since the 2007–2008 housing crisis, making it worth considering where we stand in the current cycle. Not every household follows the same financial progression, but housing often responds to economic deterioration with a significant lag, which is precisely why the emerging weakness in today’s data deserves attention.

I’ll say up front these are not “outright panic” numbers. But they are a collection of multiple newly released data points all heading in the very wrong direction at the same time peoples’ retirement accounts and stock portfolios are starting to come under pressure . And the point of this “fringe” blog that I write is to be early…very early…in pointing out trends.

So think of this data not as definitive proof we’re going to see a housing crash , but maybe a damn important ingredient in a potential recipe for a perfect storm at some point that may start a housing correction in 2027.

The latest debt data suggests some of that financial pressure is already building, according to Bloomberg . Per the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s third-quarter Household Debt and Credit report, released November 10, the share of overdue consumer loans increased to 5% from 4.7% in the previous quarter, while total household debt rose 1.8% to $19.1 trillion.

Separately, Urban Institute research found that 5.8% of Americans had at least some delinquent credit card debt, compared with 4.3% in August 2019. Approximately 5.5% had delinquent auto or retail loans, up from 3.9% before the pandemic. These figures suggest that financial pressure is extending beyond housing and affecting multiple categories of household borrowing.

More concerning for housing, the share of mortgage balances more than 90 days overdue reached 1.13%, its highest level since the first quarter of 2018.

Meanwhile, outstanding home equity line of credit balances increased by $23 billion during the quarter, the largest quarterly increase since 2005 and the 18th consecutive quarter of growth.

Rising HELOC balances don’t necessarily indicate financial distress, since homeowners also borrow against equity for renovations and other expenses. And New York Fed researchers emphasized that overall mortgage credit quality remains strong. Nevertheless, the combination of rising household debt, elevated consumer delinquencies, and increasing mortgage distress deserves attention, particularly given how weak housing demand has already become.

Again….not “panic” numbers, but not pretty, either. We’re not at the point where widespread mortgage defaults or forced selling are driving the national housing market. However, the latest data suggests the market is weakening, and several indicators are moving in the wrong direction.

According to Redfin’s November 10, 2026 report , the median U.S. home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year in October, reaching approximately $388,634. This marked the first annual decline in more than three years.

Just two months earlier, home prices were still increasing approximately 2.5% annually. A 0.4% decline isn’t particularly large on its own, and median prices can be affected by the mix of homes being sold, but the change in direction is worth noting.

The bigger concern is transaction activity.

Redfin reported that pending home sales declined 15.1% year over year and 3.6% from September. Pending sales reached their lowest level since 2013, excluding April 2020 during the initial pandemic shutdowns. Because pending sales represent homes under contract, they provide an indication of future completed transactions. Sustained weakness suggests that buyers are having difficulty absorbing available inventory at current prices and financing costs.

The National Association of Realtors reported similarly weak conditions in its November 12 release. Existing-home sales declined 5.5% month over month and 8.8% year over year in October, falling to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million homes.

That was the lowest level since August 2010. The comparison doesn’t mean today’s market has the same underlying problems as the post-financial-crisis housing market, but it does demonstrate how severely transaction activity has slowed.

Inventory is also increasing relative to demand. The National Association of Realtors reported 1.59 million existing homes available for sale in October, an increase of 4.6% from the previous year. Months of supply rose to 5.1, compared with 4.4 a year earlier. Redfin separately reported that active inventory reached its highest level since early 2020. These measures aren’t identical, but both point toward a market in which homes are taking longer to sell and available supply is increasing relative to the number of buyers.

One particularly notable detail is that inventory has been rising even as new listings have softened. That suggests some of the increase is coming from homes remaining on the market longer rather than a sudden surge of homeowners deciding to sell. If economic conditions weaken and more households need to list their properties, that could add supply to a market already struggling with demand.

Sellers are also making more concessions. Redfin reported that approximately 61% of homes sold in October closed below their original asking prices, while 36% of sold homes had experienced at least one price reduction. Nearly 15% of pending transactions fell out of contract. Selling below an asking price doesn’t necessarily indicate a decline in a property’s underlying value, but the frequency of reductions and canceled contracts provides additional evidence that buyers have gained negotiating power.

People aren’t getting “desperate to sell”…it’s just a “record buyer’s market”, right?

Regional data shows that some markets are already experiencing considerably larger price declines than the national average. Redfin reported year-over-year median sale-price decreases of 6.5% in Austin, 5.1% in Seattle, and 4.9% in Nashville. Pending sales also fell sharply in several large metropolitan areas, including Seattle, San Diego, and Denver. These differences matter because a national correction doesn’t have to occur uniformly. Markets with weaker employment, greater inventory growth, or particularly stretched affordability can experience substantially larger declines than the country as a whole.

Mortgage rates remain another major obstacle. According to the National Association of Realtors’ October report, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was approximately 7.33%, compared with 6.25% a year earlier. On a $400,000 mortgage amortized over 30 years, that difference raises the monthly principal and interest payment from approximately $2,463 to $2,750. That’s roughly $287 more per month, excluding property taxes, insurance, and maintenance.

Higher borrowing costs reduce purchasing power and limit the number of qualified buyers. At the same time, homeowners with mortgages originated or refinanced at much lower rates have little incentive to move.

That lock-in effect has restricted supply and helped support prices, but it also contributes to low transaction volumes. If homeowners eventually need to sell because of unemployment, debt, relocation, or other financial pressures, those properties would enter a market where affordability remains difficult.

The mortgage delinquency data is worth examining because it helps distinguish a weak housing market from a potentially more serious correction. According to Intercontinental Exchange’s September 2026 mortgage report, the national mortgage delinquency rate was 3.66%. Serious delinquencies were approximately 1.04%, close to their 2017–2019 September average.

These figures remain relatively contained and don’t suggest a nationwide mortgage crisis. However, the direction of several distress indicators is less encouraging. Serious delinquencies increased approximately 21% year over year, while active foreclosure inventory rose 37%, reaching its highest level since early 2019. Completed foreclosure sales also increased 15%. Mortgages originated in 2022 or later accounted for 43% of foreclosure starts and 49% of completed foreclosure sales during September.

Those increases are coming from relatively low levels, which is an important qualification. Distressed transactions still represented only about 2% of existing-home sales in October, according to the National Association of Realtors. Nevertheless, the foreclosure figures suggest that financial pressure is increasing among a portion of mortgage borrowers, particularly some who purchased or refinanced more recently.

The key question for 2027 and 2028 is whether these conditions stabilize or deteriorate further. Major housing forecasters have generally projected modest national price growth rather than a crash. Fannie Mae’s third-quarter 2026 expert survey anticipated home-price increases of approximately 2.2% in 2027 and 2.7% in 2028. Goldman Sachs has also projected very limited price appreciation in 2027, with growth below 1%. These forecasts suggest a market that remains relatively stagnant, rather than one experiencing a broad collapse.

I think the downside risks to those forecasts are increasing. Housing demand is already weak, inventory is building, and mortgage distress is moving higher. A further deterioration in employment would make that combination more concerning.

Homeowners who can comfortably afford their mortgage payments have little reason to sell into a weak market, but job losses and prolonged income disruption can change that decision. More forced selling would increase inventory at precisely the time buyers are already constrained by affordability.

This is where my concerns about AI and other speculative markets become relevant. Weakness in those markets doesn’t establish that a housing correction is coming, and there isn’t sufficient evidence to conclude that this weekend’s crypto volatility is directly affecting housing.

However, a broader decline in asset values, combined with layoffs, tighter lending standards, and weaker consumer confidence, could eventually affect housing demand and household finances. Technology-heavy housing markets may be particularly sensitive to changes in employment and compensation.

There are still important reasons not to expect a repeat of 2008. Mortgage underwriting standards have generally been stronger, many homeowners have substantial equity, and a large share of existing borrowers have fixed-rate mortgages with relatively low payments. The current delinquency rate is also far below the levels associated with the worst period of the financial crisis. Those factors provide meaningful protection against widespread forced selling.

85% OFF FOREVER IF YOU SUBSCRIBE TODAY: I am again offering an 85% discount to anyone that wants to become a Fringe Finance annual subscriber today. It’s a discount you can keep and stays applied for as long as you wish to remain a subscriber: Get 85% off forever

But a housing correction doesn’t require another 2008. Prices can decline because buyers can no longer afford prevailing valuations, sellers become more willing to negotiate, and available inventory exceeds demand at current prices. A national decline of 5% to 10% over the next couple of years is increasingly plausible in my view, particularly if sales remain depressed and inventory continues growing.

A 10% to 15% decline would likely require more significant economic deterioration, while a nationwide decline exceeding 20% would probably require a much larger employment or credit shock.

What makes the latest data concerning to me is the combination of weakening indicators rather than any single statistic. National median prices have turned slightly negative in Redfin’s data, pending sales are down double digits, existing-home transactions have fallen to levels last seen in 2010, inventory is increasing, and sellers are reducing prices more frequently. Meanwhile, serious delinquencies and foreclosure activity are rising even though overall mortgage distress remains relatively low.

I’ve warned about AI, and I continue to expect more difficult developments there. I’ve warned about crypto, and this weekend’s price action hasn’t changed my outlook. Housing is now another area where I believe the risks deserve closer attention. We haven’t reached the stage of widespread mortgage defaults or a national wave of forced selling, but several of the conditions that can precede a correction are already present.

The next phase will depend heavily on employment, household credit conditions, mortgage rates, and whether inventory continues to outpace buyer demand. If those indicators worsen together, a more substantial housing correction becomes increasingly likely. The data doesn’t yet establish that a nationwide crash is coming, but it does suggest that the housing market is more vulnerable than it was a year ago.

scraped.title: Iran Hits Bahrain Again As Guards Declare Hormuz "Closed"
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Iran Hits Bahrain Again As Guards Declare Hormuz "Closed"
scraped.body_text:
Iran fired drones at Bahrain early Sunday, its second attack in three days on the Gulf kingdom that hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet , after a lull that had held since September, as months of diplomacy to end the war have produced no breakthrough.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said six drones targeted "the US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain," calling the strike the second phase of its response to hostile US actions. "Any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response," the Guards said in a statement carried by Iranian state television, according to AFP. The IRGC released footage of the launches:

IRGC releases footage of launches toward Riffa Air Base in Bahrain IRNA: 'A radar at a U.S. air defense site at the Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones' pic.twitter.com/MmH38uaPJa

— RT (@RT_com) November 15, 2026

The general command of the Bahrain Defence Force said "Iran continues its systematic hostile approach through its sinful attacks targeting the Kingdom of Bahrain" (translated), and that its air defenses intercepted the drones before they reached their targets . There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage.

تعلن القيادة العامة لقوة دفاع البحرين أن إيران تواصل نهجها العدائي الممنهج عبر اعتداءاتها الآثمة التي تستهدف مملكة البحرين. https://t.co/XJbdf7MMVp pic.twitter.com/HbU0hzAZNs

— قوة دفاع البحرين (@BDF_Bahrain) November 15, 2026

Explosions were heard over the island around 4 a.m. local time, with residents reporting a second series of blasts around 6:30 a.m., AFP reported . The Interior Ministry put out two nationwide alerts, Bahrain's first since September , telling citizens and residents to "remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location":

An alert of potential threat. The Ministry of Interior urged citizens and residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels for the protection of public safety. #Bahrain #MOI

— وزارة الداخلية - Ministry of Interior (@moi_bahrain) November 15, 2026

Bahrain's Foreign Ministry said the kingdom "rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible" for the attacks on Friday and Sunday and their consequences, RFE/RL reported .

On Friday, the Guards claimed they had destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for American strikes on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, in southern Iran, as we reported . Central Command disputed that, saying both drones the IRGC launched toward Bahrain were shot down by US forces, with "no injuries or damage" :

🚫 CLAIM: Today, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it attacked a "U.S. early-warning radar" in Bahrain. ✅ FACT: The IRGC launched two one-way attack drones toward Bahrain and both were shot down by U.S. forces. There were no injuries or damage. pic.twitter.com/mGvAJJGM6x

— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) November 13, 2026

After the US and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, Tehran fired thousands of missiles and drones at the Gulf states that host American forces, Bahrain among the most heavily hit. Those attacks had largely died down until Friday.

The Guards also had a warning for shipping on Sunday: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed." The IRGC Navy separately claimed two oil tankers had struck naval mines south of the strait, a claim maritime authorities had not verified, The National reported. It is the latest in a run of mine claims: the Guards said three more tankers were hit in the strait on Nov. 10 , and Iran said a day later that it had struck Oman's Didamar Island , whose lighthouse and radar guide tankers through Hormuz's southern lane.

Saudi Arabia condemned the attacks on Bahrain as a violation of international law. Its own air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles that Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis fired at Riyadh, along with drones over the Eastern Province. On Friday, Gulf states demanded that Iran pay full compensation for every attack since February.

In Washington, Trump has held off on new strikes but is keeping the naval blockade of Iran's ports in place, and declared on Thursday: "We don't need a deal with Iran" , as we noted . He is set to raise the war with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin at their three-way summit in Shenzhen on Thursday.

Tehran has been widening the map: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, warned this week that if American aircraft use bases in Europe to attack Iran, "we may even target some US military bases in European countries."

scraped.title: Schumer, Jeffries Pledge To Ban Stock Trading By Members Of Congress
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Schumer, Jeffries Pledge To Ban Stock Trading By Members Of Congress
scraped.body_text:
Authored by Chase Smith via The Epoch Times ,

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said on Nov. 12 that Senate Democrats will ban stock trading for members of Congress and White House officials once they take the majority in January .

Responding to a post from President Donald Trump, Schumer wrote on X, "Senate Democrats will ban stock trading for all Members of Congress and White House officials, and hold you and your administration accountable for all the ways your rampant corruption has made life more expensive for families."

Trump had written on Truth Social that Schumer "just stated that he wants to end corruption in the United States." Trump said he assumed Schumer meant Democratic-run states, naming California, Minnesota, Illinois, Maine, and New York, where he said "Billions of Dollars are being stolen on an hourly basis."

"Hopefully his words will ring true! It will be an honor to work with him on this very big Democrat problem," Trump wrote.

Schumer replied that he was referring to the president's own stock trades, which he said were more than those of all members of Congress combined at nearly 30,000 . He also cited what he called Trump's cryptocurrency "scam," a "Qatari-gifted luxury jet," a "billionaire-funded ballroom," and "pardons for big donors."

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is expected to become speaker in January, has also made a stock trading ban part of the new majority's plans.

"In cleaning up the mess here in Congress, one of the most decisive things that we can do is to ban members of the House and Senate from trading stock. It is our intention to do just that," Jeffries said at a press conference on Nov. 9.

On Nov. 12, Jeffries said again that Democrats need to "get big money out of politics and end Citizens United," and "that should begin by prohibiting members of Congress from trading stock."

He also mentioned ending the war in Iran, reversing Medicaid cuts, and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits.

In both remarks, Jeffries named only members of Congress in regard to stock trading. In July, he said House Democrats would only support a ban that also covers the president, the vice president, and the Cabinet .

That question was at the center of the last fight over a ban. On July 22, the House passed the Stop Insider Trading Act from Rep. Bryan Steil (R-Wis.) 232-198, with more than a dozen Democrats voting for it. The bill would have barred members, their spouses, and their dependent children from buying stocks. It would not have required them to sell stocks they already own.

The Senate blocked the bill on Sept. 30 in a 53-47 procedural vote, short of the 60 votes it needed , as Senate Democrats voted against it. The bill also included a requirement that voters show photo identification. Democrats objected that the bill did not cover the president, and Schumer called the voter ID provision a "poison pill."

"If Senate Republicans cared about reining in stock trading, they would advance a bill that prohibits the president from trading stocks," Schumer said on the Senate floor on Sept. 29.

In a floor speech before the vote, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said the bill's rules "are enforced with real penalties." He said "the American people overwhelmingly support a photo ID requirement," and that Democrats were treating it as a problem.

The White House backed the bill. "President Trump has called for a stock trading ban to be passed without delay," it said in a July 22 statement of administration policy.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement to The Epoch Times that Trump "has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government" and that congressional Democrats "have refused to do anything to stop waste, fraud, and abuse in our government."

"The Democrats unanimously voted against the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would have ensured that Members of Congress cannot profit from insider information. They have no credibility on this issue," Bis said.

The Epoch Times reached out to Thune and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), who will lead House Republicans in the minority, for comment.

scraped.title: How the CCP Hides Its Debt: Beijing Says Hidden Local Debt Is Shrinking, IMF Says LGFV Debt Hit $10.5 Trillion * The Gateway Pundit * by Antonio Graceffo
scraped.description: Beijing says its narrower measure of hidden local debt fell, while the IMF estimates that debt owed by the companies Chinese cities use to borrow rose about 14…
scraped.author: https://www.thegatewaypundit.com/author/antoniog/
scraped.h1: How the CCP Hides Its Debt: Beijing Says Hidden Local Debt Is Shrinking, IMF Says LGFV Debt Hit $10.5 Trillion
scraped.body_text:
Beijing says its narrower measure of hidden local debt fell, while the IMF estimates that debt owed by the companies Chinese cities use to borrow rose about 14 percent from 2023 to 2025, reaching roughly $10.5 trillion. The rescue of Zhuhai Huafa shows how one city is keeping a cash-strapped borrower afloat by moving assets between state-owned companies and arranging new financing.

Zhuhai Huafa Group is the largest state-owned company in the southern Chinese city of Zhuhai. In late October, it failed to repay two trust products at maturity. It also asked at least three banks to extend its loans and cut interest rates.

The news set off China’s worst credit selloff in two years. The selling spread to Chinese government debt. On Oct. 30, 30-year government bond futures fell 0.94 percent , their largest one-day drop since March 9.

In early November, a senior Zhuhai official said the city had already provided Huafa with more than 40 billion yuan (about $6 billion). The city was coordinating another 70 billion yuan (about $10.5 billion) in financing.

Huafa’s own figures show why investors sold. The group posted its first annual loss in 2025, a consolidated net loss of 16.9 billion yuan (about $2.5 billion).

The net loss attributable to shareholders of the parent company was 11.03 billion yuan (about $1.65 billion). On the same basis, Huafa lost another 6.9 billion yuan (about $1 billion) in the first nine months of 2026.

At the end of September, Huafa held 52.2 billion yuan (about $7.8 billion) in cash. It owed 154 billion yuan (about $23 billion) within a year. Its bond documents listed about 413 billion yuan (about $62 billion) in interest-bearing debt as of March.

Huafa is a local government financing vehicle (LGFV), a type of state-owned company Chinese cities created to borrow on their behalf. In November 2024, Finance Minister Lan Fo’an put local governments’ hidden debt at 14.3 trillion yuan (about $2.1 trillion) at the end of 2023. In September 2025, he reported that it had fallen to 10.5 trillion yuan (about $1.6 trillion) by the end of 2024.

The International Monetary Fund uses a broader measure. It estimated LGFV debt at 64.4 trillion yuan at the end of 2023, 4.5 times Beijing’s hidden-debt figure for the same date. The IMF figure rose to 73.2 trillion yuan (about $10.5 trillion) at the end of 2025. In a statement included in an earlier IMF report, China’s executive director said hidden local debt had been “properly resolved.”

Part of the official decline comes from companies leaving the list Beijing counts. In a November report , the State Council said the number of remaining LGFVs had fallen 92 percent by the end of September 2026. Their outstanding operating financial debt had fallen 79 percent by the end of June 2026. Both declines were measured from the end of March 2023.

Many vehicles left the list through mergers and deregistrations . Others exited after debt swaps converted their hidden debt into official local government bonds. Companies that meet the other exit requirements can leave the list with financial debt still outstanding if creditors holding at least two-thirds of that debt agree.

Analysts found that many companies that left the list still depend mainly on government construction contracts and budget payments for revenue. IMF staff warned that removing companies from the official list could weaken oversight and allow local governments to keep increasing off-budget debt.

People’s Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng put LGFVs’ operating debt to financial institutions at 14.8 trillion yuan (about $2.2 trillion) at the end of 2024.

Local governments also face a backlog of unpaid bills. In February 2025, Tsinghua University economist David Daokui Li, a policy adviser to Beijing, estimated that local governments owed 10 trillion yuan (about $1.5 trillion) to contractors and civil servants. That was about 7 percent of GDP.

Huafa’s urban operations unit shows how these bills pile up inside a city’s own companies. The unit has developed new districts with the city’s authorization since 2009. It paid development costs up front and was to recover them through a share of land-sale proceeds. Caixin reported that the unit was owed tens of billions of yuan.

The land sales that were supposed to repay Huafa have collapsed. Zhuhai’s land-sale revenue fell 94 percent, from 56.3 billion yuan (about $8.4 billion) in 2020 to 3.3 billion yuan (about $490 million) in 2025.

Nationally, local government revenue from land-use rights fell 14.7 percent to 4.15 trillion yuan (about $620 billion) in 2025. It was the fourth straight year of double-digit decline. Revenue was less than half its 2021 peak of 8.7 trillion yuan.

Both Huafa and the city agency that controls it have changed leaders repeatedly. Li Guangning joined Huafa in 1998 and became chairman of its listed property unit in 2014. He led the group’s expansion from Zhuhai into more than 70 cities. Annual property sales topped 100 billion yuan for five straight years.

Trending: Remember the West Point Graduate Who Flashed a Pro-Communism Message in His Hat? You’ll Never Guess What He’s Doing Now

Li left his group posts in 2025 and resigned as chairman of Huafa Properties on May 30. Xie Wei took over as group chairman in January 2025. Guo Jin replaced Xie on Sept. 9, 2026, becoming the group’s fifth chairman since 1980.

Zhuhai’s State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission owns more than 93 percent of Huafa. Its three most recent chiefs, Li Congshan, Wu Aicun and Li Wenji, have come under investigation. The investigation into Li Wenji began in April 2026.

Zhuhai cannot cover Huafa’s debt from its budget. The city’s general budget revenue was 49.4 billion yuan (about $7.4 billion) in 2025.

The rescue has involved moving assets among companies the city already owns. In September, Gree Group, another Zhuhai state-owned company, agreed to pay 4.53 billion yuan (about $676 million) for Huafa’s 96.28 percent stake in Zhuhai Investment Holding. Gree also agreed to pay 3.17 billion yuan (about $473 million) for Huafa’s 23 percent stake in the city’s duty-free group.

In October, Huafa moved to transfer part of its stake in another subsidiary, Huachuang Investment Holding, to Gree Group and Zhuhai Transportation Holding Group.

Huafa paid interest on schedule on two public bonds in early November. China Lianhe Credit Rating kept Huafa’s rating at AAA but placed it on negative watch. Huafa’s onshore bond due in 2029 rebounded 17 percent to 85 yuan after the city announced its support. It had traded at roughly 100 yuan the previous week.

Shenzhen also used a state-owned company to support a struggling developer, China Vanke. State-owned Shenzhen Metro, Vanke’s largest shareholder, provided 31.46 billion yuan (about $4.7 billion) in shareholder loans in 2025. That allowed Vanke to repay 30.49 billion yuan in public debt.

Shenzhen Metro then capped its support, and Vanke asked bondholders for extensions. Shenzhen Metro resumed lending in 2026. By July, Vanke had secured extensions on all of its public bonds due that year.

China’s debt stood at 308.2 percent of GDP at the end of June, according to the National Institution for Finance and Development, a Beijing think tank. The government was the only sector whose debt rose as a share of GDP in the second quarter.

The IMF’s executive board recommended restructuring unsustainable LGFV debt through insolvency frameworks and recognizing losses promptly. Beijing has chosen refinancing. Its 10 trillion yuan (about $1.5 trillion) program, approved in November 2024, converts hidden debt into official local government bonds with longer maturities. IMF staff concluded that the swap does little to improve LGFVs’ ability to service their debt.

The Austrian School of economics holds that business failures, painful as they are, free up capital for more productive uses. Failures also teach lenders to stop financing projects that cannot pay for themselves. Government subsidies keep capital tied up in those same projects. When lenders expect another bailout, they keep extending credit to investments that cannot generate enough income to repay what they already owe.

The CCP treats liquidation as a political threat. In Zhuhai, the city is keeping Huafa in operation through asset transfers and new financing. Huafa has asked banks for more time to repay, and some trust investors are still waiting for overdue payments.

Beijing can shrink its list of local financing vehicles by refinancing some of their debts with government bonds and allowing companies to leave the list with other debts still outstanding. The bills still have to be paid. In Zhuhai, a full year of city budget revenue would cover less than one-eighth of Huafa’s interest-bearing debt.

scraped.h1: WATCH: Hundreds of Georgia Residents Pack Council Meeting to Protest Construction of 20,000-Square-Foot Islamic Center and Mosque in Their Town
scraped.body_text:
Many argued construction had already begun without proper public notice or a council vote.

Dozens spoke during the lengthy meeting, with some people waiting nearly five hours in the parking lot for their turn, according to reports.

WATCH:

Yesterday at the Loganville City Council, residents showed up to speak against the 29,000 sqft Islamic center they’re trying to build. https://t.co/1R65akkvAW

— Everything Georgia (@GAFollowers) November 13, 2026

The proposed facility at 883 Lee Byrd Road would replace a small existing Loganville Islamic Center that has operated out of a house on the five-acre tract since 2023, after the Lawrenceville-based Georgia Islamic Institute of Religious and Social Sciences purchased the property for $630,000.

Residents expressed frustration that construction was underway and that they were only learning about the scale of the project now, with one speaker demanding the city halt work until permits could be verified and another questioning why the project had not gone through normal channels so the community would know what was happening.

“If required permits were never issued, then why hasn’t the city taken enforcement action? We know no permits [were] issued for work being done, and until the city can verify permits are in place, then I’m calling for the construction work to stop,” one resident said, according to a report from Fox 5 .

Councilmember Melanie Long told the crowd the proposal for the building never came before the council and that officials were unsure what would happen next.

City officials have pushed back on claims that the project skipped required steps.

Assistant City Manager Jeff Smith said the center spent 14 months working with the city and submitted plans seven times for engineering, fire safety, and utility reviews before site work was allowed to proceed, and that the property’s zoning permits religious assembly uses on qualifying residential lots of at least three acres without a council vote, the same process used for other churches.

A source told local reporter Cody Alcorn that the center holds proper land disturbance permits and does not need a council vote to proceed, though officials have not publicly confirmed full building permit status.

Dozens spoke against the Loganville Islamic Center’s expansion Thursday, including a group opposed to Islam. A city source says the center has followed requirements since 2023, holds proper land disturbance permits and needs no City Council vote to proceed.

— Cody Alcorn (@CodyAlcorn) November 13, 2026

The project was not on the meeting agenda for a vote.

Speakers at the meeting raised a range of concerns, including traffic, the impact of a large institutional building, flooding outsiders into a small community of roughly 17,000 people, and whether the city had enforced its own rules.

Supporters of the center accused opponents of bigotry.

“I don’t know what we are all here for today. I’ve never felt so much hate, bigotry, [and] racism. I don’t know what your guys’ decision is today, [or] what you guys can decide what we are here for, truly,” another resident said, according to the Fox 5 report.

scraped.h1: DSA Target Schumer, Jeffries as Democratic Leadership Revolt Grows
scraped.body_text:
The Democratic Socialists of America is launching a campaign against the Democratic Party’s top two leaders in Congress, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries.

The group has thrown its support behind efforts to deny Schumer another term as leader. “We do support a challenge to New York Senator Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader,” the DSA told Newsweek. “Senator Schumer has consistently failed to deliver for the working class.”

The DSA is running a letter-writing campaign urging senators to replace Schumer. The letters attack him for his “support from pro-Israel donors,” his “ties to corporate interests” and his “refusal to back abolishing ICE,” and accuse him of going along with “Republican spending bills when Democrats had leverage.”

The push comes after Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced Thursday that he will challenge Schumer. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed have backed Van Hollen. At least six incoming Democratic senators have called for new leadership or said they will not back Schumer.

Senate Democrats will choose their leader by secret ballot on Dec. 1. Van Hollen says he has the support of more than 10 senators, while Schumer insists he has the votes to win.

The DSA also vowed to “continue to run socialist candidates for all levels of local, state, and federal office.” It is already making gains. Six DSA-backed members will join the House in January, bringing the number of DSA-affiliated lawmakers to eight, including Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib.

One DSA member, Ahmed Moor, has announced a 2028 primary challenge against Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman.

Most Americans are not buying what the socialists are selling. An Economist/YouGov poll in October found 51 percent of Americans think capitalism is better, compared with 20 percent for socialism.

scraped.description: The tower’s mechanical arms snagged the ship after a 22-hour flight, though the Super Heavy booster had to ditch in the Gulf.
scraped.h1: SpaceX Makes History by Catching Starship Upper Stage
scraped.body_text:
SpaceX made history Saturday when its launch tower caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket as it returned from orbit, The Daily Wire reported.

Starship Flight 15 lifted off at 5:47 p.m. Eastern on Friday from the company’s Starbase facility in South Texas. At 4:20 p.m. Eastern on Saturday, the tower’s giant mechanical “chopstick” arms caught the upper stage, known as Starship or “Ship,” as it came back to Earth.

“Mechazilla catches Starship! Congratulations to the entire SpaceX team on this incredible achievement!” SpaceX posted on X.

Mechazilla catches Starship! Congratulations to the entire SpaceX team on this incredible achievement! https://t.co/YJzmGUZb2B

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) November 14, 2026

The flight did not go entirely according to plan. The Super Heavy booster, which pushes the ship through the thickest part of the atmosphere, was supposed to fly back to the launch pad. Minutes after liftoff, a low-fuel alarm forced it to abandon its return. The booster corrected course on its own and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico.

The ship kept going. It climbed to roughly 170 miles above Earth, deployed Starlink satellites and circled the planet 14 times over 22 hours before returning to be caught by the tower.

SpaceX has caught Super Heavy boosters before, but catching the upper stage brings the company closer to its biggest goal: a fully reusable rocket that can fly again and again, much like an airplane.

Elon Musk said at a conference in September that Starship is designed for “not just [for] full reusability but also rapid reusability, like an aircraft.”

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman cheered the achievement. “Congrats to @elonmusk and the @SpaceX team!” he wrote on X. “It was almost magic … Making more believers by the day … one step closer to [the moon].”

scraped.h1: FAA Rules Out Cyberattack, Apologizes for Nationwide Ground Stop
scraped.body_text:
The Federal Aviation Administration says there is no sign of foul play behind Friday’s nationwide ground stop, which disrupted travel for more than a million Americans.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters Saturday morning that officials believe they have found the problem. “I do think we’ve identified the fault, and I want to reiterate, we see zero evidence of anything nefarious,” he said, “and zero evidence of anything AI-related.”

Bedford opened with an apology. “First of all, I’d like to start with an apology, a sincere apology to the American traveling public,” he said. He said the stop was ordered “out of an abundance of caution.”

According to Bedford, the system experienced about 45 minutes of instability before officials decided to stop flights. “I think that was the right call, and we stand behind that,” he said.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the trouble appears to have started at a remote FAA site where a contractor was doing routine maintenance. “In at least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire, and they were bringing it over to fiber,” he said.

Duffy said investigators are trying to determine whether the problem was human error by L3Harris, the FAA’s longtime telecommunications provider, or a faulty router. “We haven’t determined what the fault was. Was it the router, or were they not doing great work for us at L3Harris?” he said.

Once the work at that location was isolated, the systems came back online. “So we don’t believe this was cyber at all,” Duffy said. “This was an FAA system that didn’t meet the moment.”

The fallout was severe. As of Saturday, FlightAware showed more than 4,000 U.S. flights canceled and more than 13,000 delayed. Atlanta, Chicago O’Hare, Houston Bush Intercontinental, LaGuardia and Dallas-Fort Worth were among the hardest hit.
