scraped.title: 'Love thy neighbor' is not a socialist manifesto | Blaze Media
scraped.description: Democrats campaigned on Christian compassion. But Christ commanded personal sacrifice, not government-enforced generosity.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: 'Love thy neighbor' is not a socialist manifesto
scraped.body_text:
Democrats campaigned on Christian compassion. But Christ commanded personal sacrifice, not government-enforced generosity.

The 2026 midterm elections brought a new wave of “Christian” voices into Congress. James Talarico in Texas, Adam Hamilton in Kansas, and Sarah Trone Garriott in Iowa were among the Democrats who campaigned on a message rooted in faith, compassion, and the biblical command to “Love t hy n eigh bor . ”

Invoking the words of Christ does not automatically confer His authority upon a political platform.

The Good Samaritan did not petition Rome to pay for the wounded man's care. He opened his own purse.

Christian compassion is not optional. Jesus commanded it. But the tendency to equate biblical love with socialist policies requires closer examination. Before deciding what government should do in the name of love, we must understand what Jesus meant when He commanded it.

On the night before His crucifixion, Jesus gathered with His disciples and gave them a new commandment: "A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another" ( John 13:34 ).

Those words followed an extraordinary demonstration of humility: Jesus, their Lord and teacher, knelt to wash His disciples' feet. The one deserving of service became the servant. His example established that true love demands something of the person offering it.

Later, Jesus made that sacrifice unmistakable: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends" ( John 15:13 ).

Within hours, He would demonstrate those words upon the cross.

Christ's definition of love is neither sentimental nor politically convenient. It demands personal sacrifice, obedience, and fidelity to truth. In John 14:15 , He declared, "If you love me, you will keep my commandments."

Love and obedience are inseparable. Consider the parable of the Good Samaritan. The Samaritan did not merely express concern for suffering. He interrupted his journey, spent his resources, and assumed responsibility for a stranger. His mercy crossed cultural boundaries and required self-denial. It reflected the very love Christ commanded of His disciples.

There is a profound difference between sacrificing what belongs to you and claiming moral virtue by redistributing what belongs to someone else. Christ commanded His followers to give of themselves, not to outsource their obedience to the state.

Yet socialism can offer a counterfeit of Christian love, promising compassion through government power while relieving the individual of personal sacrifice. It is easy to appear generous when the responsibility of sacrifice is placed on someone else.

The Good Samaritan did not petition Rome to pay for the wounded man's care. He opened his own purse. Biblical charity begins with a willing heart and an open hand. Socialism replaces both with political coercion, letting people congratulate themselves on compassion they delegate rather than demonstrate.

History provides sobering reasons to distinguish compassionate government promises from their lived-out consequences.

The Soviet Union promised equality through central planning, forced collectivization, and repression. Millions suffered under policies that subordinated individual lives to state objectives. Chronic shortages and stagnation eventually exposed the system's failures.

Venezuela's experiment with extensive state intervention, nationalization, and price controls, compounded by oil dependence and economic mismanagement, contributed to devastating shortages, inflation, and mass emigration.

Cuba's state-dominated economy has struggled with persistent shortages and limited productivity. Its government also imposed severe restrictions on religious institutions.

China, the communist regime, was responsible for the deaths of tens of millions during the Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution because the collective was treated as more important than the individual. Socialism does not solve class inequality; it simply replaces one hierarchy with another — party officials and connected elites above ordinary citizens.

Some will argue that America is not embracing full-scale socialism, only borrowing certain policies while retaining the safeguards of a constitutional republic. But democracy is not an automatic safeguard against government overreach. Elections determine who exercises political power; constitutional limits determine how far that power can reach.

The danger is not that every government program inevitably leads to communism. It is that each expansion of state authority deserves scrutiny, particularly when it transfers decisions from citizens and independent institutions to political officials. A government does not have to become authoritarian overnight to gradually erode the boundaries that keep its power in check.

History reminds us that the promises of government are no guarantee of its results. It can promise equality while establishing a privileged ruling class. It can promise collective security while depriving citizens of the independence necessary to build their own futures.

That is why compassion cannot be measured merely by political intentions.

Can families afford necessities, pursue opportunity, and build financial security? Can communities flourish, civil liberties survive, and voluntary institutions operate independently? Can churches worship freely, teach Scripture, and serve their neighbors without government coercion?

These are not peripheral concerns. They are essential questions when evaluating policies advanced in the name of government money like grants, tax hikes, and universal health care.

RELATED: The most dangerous evil can look remarkably like good

Amanda Cassingham-Bardwell/Getty Images

In my November 1 article, "America doesn't need a Jesus made in our political image," I examined how James Talarico's interpretation of Scripture concerning Mary and abortion raises serious questions about allowing political commitments to govern biblical interpretation.

Christians must apply that question consistently, regardless of which party invokes the Bible. Communicators must remain free to examine these claims publicly and defend biblical teaching without political intimidation.

Jesus did not merely promise love. He demonstrated it through the ultimate sacrifice.

Political leaders invoking His name should be prepared to defend both their interpretation of Scripture and the real-world consequences of their proposals.

Love is not measured by the generosity of a government's promises, but by whether our neighbors are genuinely helped. Christ commanded us to love one another, not to surrender our judgment to anyone who claims to govern in His name.

Troy A. Miller

scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: The CS Lewis masterpiece almost nobody reads — and why it’s his most Christian novel
scraped.body_text:
Auron MacIntyre and British commentator Nick Dixon explain why Lewis’ retelling of a pagan myth is really a Christian conversion story that mirrors Lewis' own.

With the exception of his children’s series “The Chronicles of Narnia,” C.S. Lewis is best remembered for his nonfiction works of Christian thought, especially “Mere Christianity,” “The Screwtape Letters,” and “The Problem of Pain.” But BlazeTV host Auron MacIntyre believes the world-renowned apologist was also a master of the novel.

On this episode of “The Auron MacIntyre Show,” he is joined by British commentator and C.S. Lewis enthusiast Nick Dixon to dive into what they believe is Lewis’ “most underrated masterpiece”: “Till We Have Faces.”

The novel, which is a retelling of the Greek myth of Cupid and Psyche, has sometimes been called Lewis’ “most pagan book,” but MacIntyre and Dixon contend the opposite, arguing the story mirrors Lewis’ own conversion.

“Lewis, you know, thought about writing this book originally as an atheist and siding with kind of the screed against the gods — you know, the logic, the reason how you're a victim,” MacIntyre explains.

He argues that by the time Lewis finally wrote it, late in life and long after his own conversion, he had come to see himself as “the author of [his] own woes” — and the novel reflects that.

In the novel, Orual and her beloved younger half-sister, Psyche, are raised by the Fox, a Greek tutor who scoffs at the gods and champions pure reason. When Psyche is offered as a sacrifice to a mountain god and claims to be living happily in his invisible palace, Orual, unable to see it, refuses to believe her and destroys her sister’s happiness.

Orual evolves from a woman raging at the gods over her own “victimhood” to recognizing that she was actually “the victimizer” all along, MacIntyre says.

“I think this is one of his most Christian books, because even though he's telling this pagan myth ... this kind of repentance, this touch of the divine is something that is so analogous to his own kind of experience in life when encountering and converting to Christianity,” he adds.

“It redeems the character [Orual] in a way that I don't think you'd see in a Greek myth, right?” he continues. “Like I don't think you'd see this kind of repentance and understanding and coming to reconciliation with the gods.”

Dixon agrees. Even though in the book “Christ isn't named as such … it's clear that it is a Christian conversion story,” he says.

Calling himself “obsessed with these biographical readings” of “Till We Have Faces,” Dixon retells the story of Sept. 19, 1931 — the night J.R.R. Tolkien convinced Lewis that “Christianity is the one true myth,” a turning point that soon ended his years-long journey from atheism to Christianity.

“I think that's kind of mirrored by the end of this book — the way that they've been messing around with paganism until there's this synthesis at the end, and the Fox realizes he was wrong, and Orual realizes she's been wrong, and Psyche, I suppose, has been vindicated really as the kind of Christlike figure,” he says.

To hear the full conversation, watch the episode above.

To enjoy more of this YouTuber and recovering journalist's commentary on culture and politics, subscribe to BlazeTV — the largest multi-platform network of voices who love America, defend the Constitution, and live the American dream.

BlazeTV Staff

scraped.title: Bill Gates is right about cyberattacks. That’s the scary part. | Blaze Media
scraped.description: Americans may not accept drastic digital-security changes until disaster strikes. James Poulos sees a troubling opening for a much larger economic transformation after the shock.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: Bill Gates is right about cyberattacks. That’s the scary part.
scraped.body_text:
Americans may not accept drastic digital-security changes until disaster strikes. James Poulos sees a troubling opening for a much larger economic transformation after the shock.

Bill Gates is roiling the internet again with fresh remarks on the fresh hell that awaits us all because we just won’t listen… to him.

In a sense, Gates is right to complain. He gets to see a lot more under the hood of global tech than regular people anywhere in the world. Undoubtedly, there is a ton of complacency or worse in the normie culture right now.

Gates is right to worry that the public won’t snap to attention unless the fabric of their lived reality splits right before their very eyes.

Many of us feel too powerless, too ignorant, too busy, or just too depressed to bother trying to keep up with the main source of public information about the transformations happening out of plain sight. Gates is right to worry that the public won’t snap to attention unless the fabric of their lived reality splits right before their very eyes.

Unfortunately, Gates doesn’t make the greatest messenger. That’s especially true in our long moment when everyone basically agrees on what’s going on, and disagreement — which switches back and forth depending on which “team” seems to be in power — is restricted to whether what’s happening is a good thing or a bad thing.

People with the inside scoop and their hands on the levers of power can and do flip messages as easily as zonked-out citizoids flip between TV channels or social media clips.

Gates has fallen prey to the flip side of the old joke that “if this is wrong, I don’t want to be right.” It feels so wrong to say Gates is right that even when he is right, he seems wrong.

This unfortunate state of affairs is on stark display in his latest interview , where he sat down with CBS News podcast host Tony Dokoupil. The topic, a familiar one to Gates-heads, was the planetary risk of climate ch— excuse me , of artificial intelligence .

RELATED: Sorry, Bill Gates. We’re sitting out this apocalypse.

BAY ISMOYO/AFP via Getty Images

In the sequence that went viral this week, Gates emphasized that elites preparing to deal with cascading cyberattacks are more or less resigned to the fact that the world’s ordinary people will probably resist any kind of sweeping security-enhancing social restructuring until hackers finally make the pillars of their everyday life shake and crumble.

“If you have a big cyber attack that causes a lot of problems,” he said, “then people will say, OK, they were right. The people who were talking about that were right. So it may be that we have to suffer a few of the negatives before we’ll respond as fully as we should.”

“Fortunately,” he went on, keeping it vague, “those aren’t civilization-ending. They’re bad —”

At which point Dokoupil interjected, immediately getting very, very specific. “If you hack Fidelity or Vanguard,” he suggested, “and much of the world’s trillion-dollar retirement nest egg, that would be a pretty big event.”

Ya think? That’s quite the random example.

“Well,” Gates agreed, “you could create uncertainty in cases like that.” He went on to affirm the wisdom of “being ready” and “trying to make sure we do the things” that might “avoid any negative incidents. But” — yes, there’s a but — “assuming we fall short of that, then when some of the negatives start to emerge, you have very concrete ideas in place, so people say, okay, you’re right, we don’t want that to happen again.”

RELATED: Don’t be fooled by Bernie Sanders — tech won the midterms

Tom Baker/Getty Images

But Bill , Dokoupil might have jumped in, you’re giving me nothing but vague. I’m the one giving concrete suggestions about how to nuke the world reserve of funds ostensibly guaranteed to ensure young people don’t have to provide decades of retirement and end-of-life support to the last generation born at population replacement levels. You’re just talking about “the things” and “the negatives.” What concrete suggestions do you actually have?

Instead, Dokoupil concluded, “what it’s going to take for us as a country and a world to tackle this is not just a 12-page essay from Bill Gates. It could be a catastrophe.”

To which Gates responded: “That’s fair.”

Neither man would state the obvious: Draining the world’s retirement accounts would throw the economic and financial life of the Western world into a tailspin with only one possible way out — a coordinated international switch-flip to mandatory welfare-for-all: universal basic income denominated in a magical new kind of digital-credits currency.

It was left for the beleaguered viewer to understand.

James Poulos

BlazeTV Host

items.title: Portugal’s housing protests escalate, defying police repression
items.summary: Both the CGTP and the Socialist Party-aligned UGT trade union federations rejected appeals from housing activists to join the November 11 general strike in neighbouring Spain.

scraped.title: Portugal’s housing protests escalate, defying police repression
scraped.description: Both the CGTP and the Socialist Party-aligned UGT trade union federations rejected appeals from housing activists to join the November 11 general strike in neighbouring Spain.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
The housing protests sweeping Portugal have become a political confrontation between a growing social movement and a ruling establishment determined to defend the interests of landlords, property developers and financial investors. What began as opposition to soaring rents, evictions and housing speculation has developed into a broader expression of social anger over inequality, low wages and deteriorating living conditions.

The protests were fuelled by the right-wing Social Democratic Party (PSD) government’s introduction of legislation seeking to liberalise the rental market by reducing restrictions on landlords and rent-setting while making evictions easier.

Protests in July escalated into mass demonstrations and protest camps in Lisbon and Porto during October and November, to which Prime Minister Luís Montenegro’s right-wing coalition government responded with escalating repression, deploying the specialist public-order and riot-control unit, the Corpo de Intervenção, to dismantle camps and remove protesters.

According to Público , seven police operations against the encampments resulted in 99 arrests and dozens of injuries. Protesters were struck by rubber bullets, including in the face, while widely circulated footage showed officers charging demonstrators and beating people attempting to retreat.

The scale of the housing crisis is immense. Between 2015 and the end of 2025, house prices rose by approximately 182 percent while wages increased by only around 48 percent, creating one of the widest gaps between housing costs and income growth in Europe. Housing, a basic social necessity, has been transformed into a financial asset whose value rises far beyond the reach of those who depend on wages for survival.

The housing bill advanced through parliament after the far-right Chega abstained at a crucial stage, allowing the legislation to proceed. While seeking to capitalise on widespread anger over housing costs, Chega has been openly hostile to the encampments. Party leader André Ventura condemned a court ruling permitting the camps to continue, claiming it “undermines the authority of law enforcement” and legitimises “violence and anarchy.” Chega has called for new legislation granting police broader powers over public demonstrations.

More than 200 lawyers signed a public letter alleging disproportionate force and unlawful police actions and demanding an investigation. Amnesty International accused the authorities of using “beatings and excessive force” resulting in injuries and hospitalisations.

Such is the concern within ruling circles that class antagonisms will erupt that President António José Seguro demanded explanations from the government regarding police operations and convened the Council of State, a step associated with matters of exceptional significance. A former general secretary of the Socialist Party (PS), Seguro served as opposition leader during the 2011-14 Troika austerity years, opposing aspects of austerity while accepting the framework imposed by Portugal’s international creditors.

The housing crisis is the responsibility of successive governments rather than any single administration. House prices began their steep ascent during the geringonça , the “cobbled-together” arrangement that kept the PS in office between 2015 and 2019 with the support of the pseudo-left Left Bloc (BE) and the Stalinist Portuguese Communist Party (PCP).

Today, the BE and PCP seek to obscure this record through their opposition to the housing law and denunciations of police violence. While criticising Montenegro’s reforms, both parties spent years sustaining PS governments on the claim they could secure more progressive policies. They withdrew support only in 2021, when growing industrial unrest and opposition to austerity made the arrangement politically untenable.

By subordinating social opposition to parliamentary manoeuvres, these organisations helped contain working-class resistance while living standards deteriorated. The resulting disillusionment has fuelled the growth of Chega. Since the May 2025 election, support for the Social Democratic Party (PSD)-led government has declined sharply, while Chega and PS have gained ground and now compete for first place in opinion polls.

The role of the trade unions is equally treacherous. The PCP-aligned CGTP has increasingly linked housing costs to inflation, poor wages and declining public services. Yet both the CGTP and the PS-aligned UGT rejected appeals from housing activists to join the November 11 general strike in neighbouring Spain. That strike emerged from Spain’s own housing movement and from growing anger over evictions, inequality and falling living standards. Millions of workers participated in what became Spain’s first nationwide strike in 14 years, demonstrating the potential for a broader mobilisation of the European working class around common social demands.

The conditions driving Portugal’s protests are not unique. Similar housing crises have developed across Europe as governments prioritise corporate profits and preparations for war over social needs. Housing costs, declining living standards and worsening inequality are provoking growing opposition in country after country.

At the same time, workers across Europe face the same obstacle: trade-union bureaucracies that work to keep struggles divided along national lines. The recent one-day strike in Spain and upcoming ones in France, Italy and Greece have all been organised separately, preventing the emergence of a unified movement capable of challenging governments and employers on a continental scale.

The decisive question facing workers and youth is the international unification of these struggles on a revolutionary perspective. The defence of democratic rights, the fight against unaffordable housing and opposition to falling living standards and the drive to war require the building of rank-and-file committees in workplaces, schools, universities and working-class neighbourhoods, democratically controlled by workers themselves.

This requires a political break with the forces that present themselves as the left but subordinate mobilisations to parliamentary negotiations and the continuation of capitalist governments. The World Socialist Web Site and the International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees (IWA-RFC) advance the program of a coordinated European struggle against war and the capitalist oligarchy: the building of independent rank-and-file committees, the preparation of a European general strike, and the replacement of the European Union by the United Socialist States of Europe.

Get email updates on workers’ struggles and a global perspective from the International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees.

items.title: Jeremy Corbyn’s silence on Europe in revolt
items.summary: An active response among workers and youth in Britain to the protests and strikes sweeping Europe has been blocked by the labour and trade union bureaucracy.

scraped.title: Jeremy Corbyn’s silence on Europe in revolt
scraped.description: An active response among workers and youth in Britain to the protests and strikes sweeping Europe has been blocked by the labour and trade union bureaucracy.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Over the past two months, mass protests and strikes have spread across Europe, involving millions of students and workers. A teachers’ strike over staff shortages at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in Paris on September 17, followed by student-led strikes and protests in the south-eastern suburbs, spread by the first week of October to hundreds of schools, colleges and universities.

By mid-October, striking fuel and public-sector workers joined students, with more than one million demonstrating across France. They were met with violent police repression and mass arrests.

Simultaneously, a protest in Madrid against the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen from her apartment on September 23 led to coordinated demonstrations by October 3 in more than 50 cities, culminating in this week’s Spanish general strike involving more than 3 million workers.

In Germany, 150,000 students in 35 cities joined the Gen Z regelt protests over military conscription, impossible living costs, rearmament and war.

In Albania, a wave of student protests swept the country against cuts to education and financial aid, and poor job prospects. These built on earlier protests over the Sazan Island Resort being developed by Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, in a country where workers’ average annual gross income is just €11,300.

Strikes and protests have also developed in Belgium, Portugal, Italy, Serbia, Greece, Austria and Ireland.

As Alex Lantier, national secretary of the Parti de l’égalité socialiste (PES), wrote on the World Socialist Web Site on October 22, “There is an echo in the present events of 1848, a year of revolutionary upheavals across the continent. This is, of course, an analogy, not a concrete comparison. The world of 2026 is vastly different from that of 1848. But the rapid spread of mass protests from France across Europe and beyond expresses the essentially global character of the movement now unfolding. More fundamentally, its emerging social and political essence is working class and socialist, not bourgeois-democratic.”

In Britain, support for the protests and strikes is widespread. At street campaigns, workplace leafleting and campus literature stalls run by the Socialist Equality Party (UK), workers and young people have expressed admiration for the revolutionary traditions of the French working class and support for their struggle.

Millions can see that youth in Europe are fighting the same problems as in the UK: a severe cost-of-living and housing crisis, brutal austerity, the complicity of governments in genocide, escalating global war, attacks on immigrants and the rise of the far-right.

Statements such as “I wish the same would happen here” are common, as are questions about why this is not the case. This identification with the European protests registers the objective unity of workers and youth across national borders, against the toxic nationalism, xenophobia and wars promoted by capitalist governments.

But while workers and youth in Britain have followed the wave of European protest on social media, posting messages of support, Britain’s labour and trade union bureaucracy, including its “left” wing, has been virtually silent. This goes a long way toward explaining why the protests and strikes in Europe have not yet developed in Britain.

Britain’s labour and trade union bureaucrats have watched with hostility and fear an emerging process of social and political radicalisation in the working class, above all its youngest generation, against governments—whether led by Sanchez, Merz or Macron—which function, in the words of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, as “a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie”.

Fear of the class struggle, and the danger of “contagion” from Europe, is epitomised by the response of Jeremy Corbyn and his co-leaders of Your Party. Likewise, Zack Polanski’s Green Party, Labour’s Socialist Campaign Group, and trade union “lefts” have acted in concert to block British workers and youth from joining a developing pan-European movement against war, austerity and authoritarianism.

In two months, Corbyn has issued not a single tweet in solidarity with the European protests. The train from London St Pancras to Paris Gare de Nord takes two hours and twenty minutes. Yet Corbyn’s response to hundreds of thousands of students and workers protesting just across the Channel was to pretend it wasn’t happening. Addressing 250,000 people at the national rally for Palestine on October 10, Corbyn said nothing of the events sweeping France and Europe. Not even the international dockworkers’ strike against Israel’s genocide in Gaza, the largest coordinated action by port workers in history, was deemed worthy of a tweet by this self-declared champion of the Palestinians.

Corbyn’s Your Party, founded last November and pledged to “internationalism” and “socialism”, has issued no statement supporting the protests and strikes. On October 30, it posted a single message about the international dockworkers’ action against genocide, but made no call on the Trades Union Congress or its affiliated unions for practical measures (strikes, work bans, and emergency aid shipments) to paralyse the Israeli war machine and save Palestinian lives.

Corbyn’s only extended comment was to the independent outlet Breakthrough News (BTN) on October 14, supporting the youth protests and describing them as directed “against the war machine of Europe”. He described Ursula von der Leyen, head of the European Union, as “leading the idea that Europe should become a military alliance itself and should be directly involved in wars in Africa and Ukraine”. A month of silence has followed.

His statements to BTN are, in any case, pro forma. Despite threats of nuclear retaliation, the Burnham Labour government is escalating UK involvement in the NATO-Russia war in Ukraine, declaring that Britain has 1,000 days to prepare for a major military conflict. It has deployed Royal Air Force (RAF) fighter planes to Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen and is providing logistical and military backing for the US-led war on Iran.

If Corbyn were a genuine socialist, he would have seized on the strikes and protests across Europe and called for the broadest political and industrial mobilisation of the working class and youth in Britain against the catastrophic war and austerity policies of the Burnham government, waged as a common struggle with workers and youth across the continent.

Corbyn is no such leader. Instead, his activities have focused on demands for a parliamentary inquiry into British complicity in the Gaza genocide. On October 19, Burnham formally rejected Corbyn’s call for a Chilcot-style inquiry into the UK’s military, economic, and political cooperation with Israel since October 2023. As under Starmer, the Foreign Office stated it “does not believe that the proposed inquiry is necessary”.

Despite Labour’s continued backing for the Gaza genocide, including RAF intelligence and supply missions over Gaza for the Israel Defense Forces, Corbyn has stepped up his futile pleas to the government. Responding to Burnham’s rejection of a public inquiry—whose terms, as under Chilcot, preclude any legally enforceable findings—Corbyn has spent weeks promoting Your Party’s parliamentary petition, gathering more than 100,000 signatures to trigger a parliamentary debate.

Corbyn is a master of doomed-to-fail initiatives, content in his allotted role as a backbench critic. His ineffectual moral hand-wringing is joined to parliamentary cretinism, seeking always to redirect anti-war sentiment behind appeals to the Labour Party and the British state.

Left-wing and anti-capitalist sentiment in Britain was expressed last year through mass support for Zarah Sultana’s announcement of a new left-wing party co-led with Corbyn against Starmer’s Labour Party. She wrote: “Billionaires already have three parties fighting for them. It’s time the rest of us had one”. 850,000 people signed up in support.

The potential for a mass political break by workers and youth from Labour was deliberately sabotaged by Corbyn and his backers. Having blocked the formation of a mass “socialist” party for years, when he could no longer prevent it, Corbyn ensured it would offer no serious challenge to the Labour Party and British capitalism.

Sultana, who spoke repeatedly last year against the “failures of Corbynism”, advances no alternative to Corbyn on Europe or anything else. In two months, her online X account has offered just four words on the mass protests in Europe, posted October 6: “Solidarity with the students!”, alongside a raised-fist and French flag emoji. On October 8, she retweeted Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s post, “The Bastille has been retaken”, showing thousands of students occupying the Place de la République.

This, like Corbyn’s celebration of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s presidential election victory in Brazil, or Sultana’s cheering of the German Left Party’s victory in Berlin, is not “internationalism” but the promotion of pseudo-left politicians devoted to upholding capitalist rule. Mélenchon has responded to the deepest crisis of French capitalism since May-June 1968 not with calls for a general strike to topple Macron and bring to power a workers’ government, but with nationalist calls for a Sixth Republic to be achieved via next year’s presidential elections.

Corbyn and Sultana’s silence mirrors that of Labour’s rump Socialist Campaign Group of Labour MPs, including John McDonnell and Diane Abbott, and the Green Party under Zack Polanski, which has issued no appeal to its many young supporters to take part in a continent-wide struggle against war, austerity, and environmental destruction.

Corbyn, in his appeals to the alleged good conscience of the Labour Party and the parliamentary institutions of the British state, represents the fag end of Fabianism. His exhortations to end war, genocide and oppression, and for a society “of the many, not the few”, are directed not to the working class but to the ruling class and its trusted servants.

Trotsky wrote more than a century ago of Fabianism as a “mental junk shop” whose advocacy of evolutionary socialism (via parliamentary and municipal reform), liberalism and religion was directed against the class struggle. The early Fabians (Sidney and Beatrice Webb, George Bernard Shaw, Ramsay MacDonald) regarded the struggle between capital and labour as a positive evil, because its outcome, as Marx predicted, was socialist revolution and the abolition of class society.

For the Fabians, social change would be introduced from above, by the high-minded representatives of the propertied classes. Trotsky observed, “Throughout the whole history of the British Labour movement there has been pressure by the bourgeoisie upon the proletariat through the agency of radicals, intellectuals, drawing-room and church socialists and Owenites who reject the class struggle and advocate the principle of social solidarity, preach collaboration with the bourgeoisie, bridle, enfeeble and politically debase the proletariat.”

Driven by the third major breakdown of the global capitalist system since 1914, the working class across Europe is stirring. Mass student strikes and youth protests anticipate a new period of revolutionary struggle, one that the working class in Britain will inevitably join. The urgent task facing humanity is the resolution of the crisis of working class leadership. In Britain, this means a conscious political break with the pro-Labour, pseudo-reformist politics of Corbynism and the building of the Socialist Equality Party, based on the strategy of the United Socialist States of Europe and the world.

items.title: Sri Lankan migrant worker speaks out against Labour government’s attack on residency rights
items.summary: A Sri Lankan chef on a Skilled Worker visa describes the insecurity created by the Labour government’s retrospective doubling of the wait for permanent residency from five to 10 years, and the exploitation that employer sponsorship makes possible.

scraped.title: Sri Lankan migrant worker speaks out against Labour government’s attack on residency rights
scraped.description: A Sri Lankan chef on a Skilled Worker visa describes the insecurity created by the Labour government’s retrospective doubling of the wait for permanent residency from five to 10 years, and the exploitation that employer sponsorship makes possible.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
“We deserve fairness. We deserve dignity. We deserve a future”

The World Socialist Web Site (WSWS) is publishing the following letter it has received from a Sri Lankan migrant working in the UK. We have changed their name to Ravi for protection. “Ravi”, a qualified chef employed in the hospitality sector, describes the profound uncertainty created by the Labour government’s retrospective extension of the qualifying period for Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR) from five to ten years. Having come to Britain on a Skilled Worker visa and built a life here expecting to qualify for permanent residency after five years, they explain the devastating personal consequences of changing the rules after migrants have made enormous sacrifices to work and contribute to society. Their letter also highlights how the threat to migrants’ immigration status leaves sponsored workers vulnerable to exploitation and intimidation by employers.

****

Dear WSWS,

We listened to Shabana Mahmood’s speech announcing the proposed changes to Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR) for migrant workers with disbelief and profound frustration. She began by declaring that the policy would be “guided above all by fairness”. But where is the fairness in promising migrants the prospect of settlement after five years when they came to the UK, only to extend that qualifying period to ten years after they have built their lives here, worked, paid taxes and contributed to society?

What was particularly hurtful was not simply the severity of these proposed changes, but the dismissive and prejudicial way in which Mahmood spoke about migrants’ skills, worth and contribution. Her remarks demeaned people whose labour keeps essential sectors of the UK economy functioning.

With one stroke, the government proposes doubling the ILR qualifying period from five to ten years for tens of thousands of migrant workers outside social care, including those earning between £25,000 and £50,000 a year and working in often insecure, demanding conditions across hospitality, agriculture and other sectors. These are workers who have organised their lives around the rules and assurances under which they migrated, only to find the goalposts being moved after their arrival.

I am a fully qualified chef with extensive professional experience, yet I earn around £30,000 a year. My spouse and I both work full-time in the hospitality sector. By the government's own definition, we are net contributors to the economy. We work, pay taxes and contribute to the communities in which we live. Yet the government's proposals would treat our years of work and contribution as though they count for less simply because our earnings fall below an arbitrary threshold.

I came to the UK approximately two and a half years ago through the Skilled Worker visa route. Like thousands of other migrant workers, I came here with genuine hopes, dreams and expectations. We made significant sacrifices, invested our savings, left our families and homes behind, and built our futures around the immigration rules that existed when we made the decision to come.

The five-year ILR route was an important part of that decision. Now, suddenly changing those expectations and extending the settlement period to ten years is deeply unfair. We cannot simply be expected to accept that the terms on which we built our futures can be changed after we have made enormous personal and financial sacrifices.

Why, then, are we talking only about care workers? What about the thousands of other Skilled Worker visa holders whose futures are equally threatened?

There are thousands of other migrant workers employed in restaurants, hotels, hospitality and other industries who are facing similar difficulties. We are also contributing to the British economy, paying taxes, working in businesses and filling essential vacancies that employers struggle to fill.

Many of us work extremely long hours, sometimes 15–18 hours a day, under enormous pressure. Unfortunately, some sponsored workers, like us, experience exploitation and poor working conditions. We often feel unable to speak up about our rights because our employers hold significant power over our sponsorship and immigration status.

If we complain about unreasonable working hours, unfair treatment or violations of our employment rights, we may fear losing our jobs and sponsorship. This creates a situation in which vulnerable migrant workers feel trapped, powerless and unable to defend themselves. The threat of losing our right to remain in the country can become a powerful weapon in the hands of unscrupulous employers.

We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for fairness, dignity, consistency and respect for the commitments and expectations under which we came to this country.

It is particularly concerning that immigration policy changes can have such a significant impact on people who have already spent years building their lives in the UK. Extending the ILR qualifying period without adequate protection for existing visa holders raises serious questions about fairness, legitimate expectations and the security of people's futures.

Furthermore, we are concerned about the disproportionate impact these changes could have on migrant workers from Asian and other non-European countries. Everyone who works in this country deserves to be treated fairly, regardless of their nationality or background.

This is not simply an issue affecting care workers. It concerns all of us who came to Britain through the Skilled Worker visa route. Chefs, restaurant and hotel workers, agricultural workers and thousands of others must recognise that our concerns are shared. Dividing migrant workers by occupation will only weaken our ability to defend our common interests.

We must speak out collectively against these proposals. We should not remain silent out of fear or assume that the changes will affect somebody else. If one group of workers can have its settlement expectations taken away today, others can face the same treatment tomorrow.

We must come together across occupations, workplaces and nationalities to demand:

- An end to the proposed extension of the ILR qualifying period from five to ten years.

- Protection of existing Skilled Worker visa holders against retrospective changes to their settlement expectations.

- Recognition that these changes affect workers across all Skilled Worker occupations, not just care workers.

- An end to the exploitation of sponsored workers and the use of immigration status as a weapon of intimidation by employers.

- The right to secure settlement, dignity and equal treatment, without arbitrary salary thresholds, discriminatory conditions or ever-changing immigration rules.

As the government refuses to listen to the legitimate concerns of migrant workers, we must raise our voices collectively through lawful and peaceful democratic action, public campaigns and protests.

We deserve fairness. We deserve dignity. We deserve a future.

To all Skilled Worker visa holders, whatever your occupation or nationality: this concerns you. Do not remain silent. Stand together, support one another and make your voices heard. Our rights and our futures are worth defending.

***

Dear Ravi,

Your call for a mobilisation of working people against the stripping away of residency rights for migrant workers at the stroke of a pen gives a powerful voice to the broad-based opposition to the Labour government’s reactionary measures.

Both skilled workers and care workers have been caught up in the Labour government’s anti-migrant dragnet. As the WSWS article explains , many care workers and their families who arrived before May 2025 have been disqualified from the limited reprieve that allowed them to apply after five years for Indefinite Leave to Remain, and have been told they must start the process again.

The wedge which has been driven between migrant workers by the Burnham government has the backing of the trade union bureaucracy, with UNISON claiming the “worst aspects” of the tearing up of migrant’s rights to residency have been stopped. No section of the trade union bureaucracy can be entrusted to conduct a principled fight.

The continued scapegoating of migrants and refugees for the collapse of public services is enabled by the union bureaucracy and their partnership with the government. The Trades Union Congress and its affiliated unions are suppressing any mobilisation of the working class against the savage cuts and austerity being enforced by the Burnham government.

To oppose this, rank-and-file committees must be established to unite every section of the working class against the employers, the Labour government and the capitalist system. Migrant and British-born workers face the same attacks: declining wages, insecure employment, deteriorating public services and the erosion of democratic rights.

The attempt to divide workers through immigration controls, differential residency rights and the threat of deportation weakens the collective strength of the entire working class and gives employers a means of driving down conditions for all. The answer is not to appeal to the government or the trade union bureaucracy, but to organise independently across workplaces, industries and neighbourhoods, in defence of every worker's right to live and work free from super-exploitation and the constant threat of deportation.

The fight for full citizenship and equal democratic rights for all is inseparable from the struggle for decent wages, secure employment, housing, healthcare and education. Defending one section of the working class is inseparable from defending the rights and conditions of the entire class.

Fraternally,

Tony Robson

WSWS UK Industrial Editor

scraped.title: France After November 5: Don’t Ditch the Unions, Outflank Them and Build the General Strike - Left Voice
scraped.description: To recapture the spirit of the October 17 mobilizations across France, workers must be drawn into the fight, bureaucracies bypassed from below, and cross-industry assemblies built to organize a general strike.
scraped.author: Leon Bengochea
scraped.body_text:
To recapture the spirit of the October 17 mobilizations across France, workers must be drawn into the fight, bureaucracies bypassed from below, and cross-industry assemblies built to organize a general strike. Leon Bengochea The strike on November 5 was paradoxical. On the one hand, it marked a significant step forward in uniting the labor movement with the youth revolt that began in early October. Not only did the day mobilize more than 1 million people, but it also saw high strike participation in parts of the SNCF (the national railway) and in secondary education, as well as mobilizations in sectors such as energy, petrochemicals, and the civil service. On the other hand, the strike was far from “active.” On the contrary, union leaders did everything they could to turn it into a routine day of action. Worse still, they attempted to use this occasion to co-opt the movement and position themselves as the government’s negotiating partners, in order to bargain at young people’s expense. And this came after they waited nearly a month following the start of the high school students’ revolt to call a strike, despite the brutal repression being unleashed against it. On October 24 and 31, they even vouched for protest routes that skirted city centers and were far more tightly controlled and policed than on October 17. The betrayal came quickly: the CFDT and FO, two of France’s major union confederations, stopped calling for strikes after the government granted them a 5-euro increase in the minimum wage. A real slap in the face for the mobilized youth and for all the workers who can no longer make ends meet. The CGT, for its part, is more responsive to pressure from the movement’s rank and file. It remains in the fight and is calling for a new day of mobilization in both the public and private sectors on November 17, but it is making no serious effort to build a genuine, open-ended general strike. This situation fuels perfectly legitimate anger against the union bureaucracy and sparks a broad debate on social media. Several leading figures in the movement are therefore calling for the unions to stay out of the upcoming days of mobilization. However, this view overlooks the contradictions inherent in the days of revolt — even the most powerful ones — and the potential of the labor movement. Admittedly, union leaderships have long been co-opted by the regime, which tolerates and subsidizes them only on condition that they help keep it stable by keeping workers from becoming too radical. But at the rank-and-file level, they continue to organize the workers who keep the refineries, ports, power and telecommunications networks, logistics warehouses, and factories running, and even the data centers of the operators that the government is asking to stand ready to suspend TikTok. Trade unions therefore hold the labor movement’s strategic positions. And without these battalions of workers joining the struggle, it is impossible to envision a victory against those in power. Furthermore, the workers’ struggles of the past 10 years are full of examples of highly progressive stances taken by rank-and-file union members. In recent weeks alone, think of the union members and education workers who defended high school students against the police in Le Havre, Saint-Denis, Paris, Toulouse, and Saint-Avold, to name just a few examples. To win, we must rally the vast majority of union members and workers to break with their own bureaucratic leaderships — including the rank and file of the CFDT and FO — by showing them that their leaders have betrayed their interests. October 17: A Show of Force and Its Limits October 17 was a “historic, independent action” by the masses that shook the powers that be. Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators — the vast majority of whom were young people, high school students, college students, and workers — converged on the seats of power and partly broke through police lines. A massive surge that surprised and terrified the ruling classes . They were quick to launch a media campaign against the “dangerous classes,” while the government barricaded itself behind the army and deployed unprecedented repressive forces against the young protesters. Nevertheless, October 17 also revealed the limits of weekly days of action, even when they take a very radical turn. Mobilizing such energy comes at a cost — particularly in terms of repression — and it is difficult to maintain the same level of mobilization from one week to the next, especially now that the element of surprise that played a role that day is gone. Between days of action, the authorities have plenty of time to reorganize. The protesters, for their part, must return to work, where they face harassment from their bosses and low wages that barely cover the cost of the gas needed to get to work. In short, a large part of their time is still devoted to work and commuting. As early as October 17, a pressing problem therefore arose: to strengthen the movement, it must first be extended to new sectors, particularly in the workplace. Next, a general strike must be organized — one capable of paralyzing both the government and the economy while freeing up a great deal of time for mobilized workers. But as the past few days have shown, a general strike will not fall from the sky; it must be organized and prepared. The movement is thus reaching the limits of what Anton Jäger calls “hyperpolitics.” With this concept, Jäger describes a situation marked by massive and radical repoliticization, which makes it possible “to rapidly mobilize a large number of people” , but faces significant difficulties in “crystallizing this energy into sustainable structures capable of acting over the long term and transforming the mobilization into effective political decisions.” For class struggle, this observation helps explain the emergence of movements as powerful as the Yellow Vests, Black Lives Matter in the United States, or the October 17 movement in France, but also their lack of structure, in contrast with the revolutionary labor movement of the last century. This lack of organization means that even very radical outbursts can easily run out of steam and be co-opted by those in power. Bringing the Labor Movement into the Fray Is the Decisive Issue The sequence of events that began on November 5 offers a valuable opportunity to reflect on these strategic questions. Even if only partially so far, the labor movement has begun to enter the fray, with a march of 1.6 million people, making the movement even more unprecedented. This is no longer just a massive youth movement, a “revolt” like the Yellow Vests, Gen Z edition. This dynamic is now joined by hundreds of thousands of striking workers. This combination has no precedent in any struggle of the past decade. By entering the fray, union leaderships have also forced the government to open negotiations, notably by breaking the “taboo” surrounding wage increases. Now, across the country — including far from the urban centers and among workers who felt no connection to the youth movement and did not march on November 5 — people are beginning to discuss the possibility of winning wage increases. Everyone is struggling with the high cost of living. Before October 17, some had in fact expected an even broader movement, but it ultimately remained limited to young people, albeit mobilized on a massive scale. We therefore need demands that speak to all segments of the working class, not just the most politicized and radical sectors of the Left. Even among the working-class base of the far-right National Rally, workers have every reason to strike for wage increases, even though Marine Le Pen opposes them . If these workers joined the struggle while Gen Z is mobilizing, it would be a major opportunity to develop their political and class consciousness — and to permanently weaken the party that threatens to take power. In short, taking into account the uneven pace of such a process, current conditions could allow the radicalism of youth to spread to the labor movement. Restoring the working class as a whole to its status as a “dangerous class” to those in power — as it was for more than two centuries — is a central challenge. Today, it has been transformed. Its older members were raised on legalism and the idea that you shouldn’t get too political, that you should settle for case-by-case negotiations and politely ask for raises. But Gen Z’s courage and its demand for a future — coupled with the firm conviction that those running society are condemning them to a life without a future — can restore the labor movement’s prestige. This is all the more true given that young people make up the vast majority of workers in precarious jobs, including in certain sectors with large workforces, such as logistics. Developing Demands and Cross-Industry Assemblies to Broaden the Struggle Initially, the highly subversive movement of young people and certain more politicized sectors of the workforce may coexist with more limited, economic strikes. This was the case in other intense episodes of class struggle, such as the Russian Revolution of 1905. Lenin noted at the time the coexistence of political strikes — particularly in the metalworking industry, a more politicized and better-off sector — and economic strikes, which were especially prevalent in the textile industry, a more exploited and politically less advanced sector:
In the first quarter of 1905, for instance, economic strikes noticeably predominated over political strikes […] In the last quarter of 1905, however, the ratio was reversed […]. This means that in the early stage of the movement many workers put the economic struggle first, while at the height of the movement it was the other way round. But all the time there was a connection between the economic and the political strike. Without such a connection, we repeat, it is impossible to have a really great movement, one that achieves great aims.
But to develop these tendencies, a proactive strategy is needed to mobilize the entire working class, along with a policy to unify the most politically active and radical sectors with those who are entering the struggle for limited demands — and whom union leaderships seek to keep apart from the broader movement. This begins with promoting ambitious wage demands on a mass scale: for example, a 400-euro raise for everyone, as proposed by the cross-industry assembly in Toulouse , which brought together several hundred workers from various sectors, as well as college and high school students. These demands must be linked to those of the youth, such as the repeal of Parcoursup (the national university admissions platform), more funding for education and healthcare rather than the military, and the dropping of all legal and disciplinary action against those who have taken part in the protests. The weapon for waging this struggle is bringing different sectors together in assemblies, in order to reach workers who have not yet joined the movement and rank-and-file union members, to set demands without ceding control to union bureaucracies, and to organize actions that break with legalistic routine. This is precisely what the dozens of cross-industry assemblies currently beginning to meet across the country — such as in Lyon , Bordeaux , Toulouse , the Île-de-France region, and Strasbourg — are doing. All of them have a mixed membership, bringing together college students, high school students, and workers. They aim to propose frameworks that bring together all the perspectives within the movement, so that participants can discuss strategy together: how to build and expand the strike, fight repression, and solidify the common ground between young people and workers. Though still in their early stages, they have already helped organize the November 5 strike — something the union leaderships failed to do — as well as actions on the day itself, such as spontaneous demonstrations at train stations, in front of the Ministry of the Interior, and in the streets of Saint-Denis. In Paris, the cross-industry assemblies gathered several thousand demonstrators at the head of the march. If the movement grows, these assemblies could develop into mass bodies, with delegates from numerous companies, neighborhoods, and educational institutions. They could thus begin to become genuine centers of counter-power and realize what V2 called for during his press conference at Paris Cité University , in preparation for October 24: “Students and workers alike, we’re all united; we’re all the ones keeping France running, so we can govern ourselves.” The development of such organizations is a response not only to attempts by union leaderships to regain control, but also to similar attempts by the reformist Left, which deserves at least as much suspicion as the leaders of the CFDT, the CGT, or FO. Neither Union Bureaucracy nor Mere Electoralism: Building a Revolutionary Perspective From this perspective, it is surprising that certain figures in the movement who present themselves as the most “radical” opponents of union legalism are, at the same time, openly campaigning for Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of La France Insoumise. Yet Mélenchon is a fervent defender of the “republican order” and expressed outrage over police understaffing on October 17. La France Insoumise’s strategy is based on taking over institutions and striking a compromise with big business, by persuading them to accept a few concessions in exchange for peace in the streets. Mélenchon regularly acknowledges this. In August 2025, during the party’s Amfis summer conference, he noted, for example, that a far-right government would lead to resistance and “barricades,” before concluding: “For the sake of public order, it’s better to elect La France Insoumise.” To achieve such pacification, they would rely heavily on the complicity of union leaderships and their expertise in “appeasement.” So yes, we must “recapture the spirit of the 17th,” but with a hundred times more firepower. It is precisely for this reason that we must draw the labor movement and its organizations into the battle and push them to move beyond legalistic routine. For it is clear that the bosses do not feel threatened by the “merguez” marches (named for the sausage stands that follow union processions) between Place de la République and Place de la Nation. What they do understand is hard-hitting strikes, workplace occupations, and joint radical actions between students and workers. Transforming the labor movement so that it reconnects with the best of its tradition is the historic task of the segment of Gen Z that claims to be revolutionary. This involves sustaining the youth movement, particularly in the high schools. Since the start of the school year, contradictions have been growing: the pressure of the baccalaureate is weighing on some students, and the difficulty of winning people over is fueling attempts to “harden the movement” in response to its shrinking ranks. To tackle this strategic problem, we need frameworks that allow these issues to be discussed, that seek to bring along the lagging sectors, that close ranks against repression, and that thus keep the vanguard from detaching from the mass of high school students. At the universities too, as general assemblies grow, convincing students that victory is possible is a central challenge. It must go hand in hand with strengthening coordination bodies, which keep the union bureaucracy from taking control of the movement, and with organizing actions that break out of the established limits, as when the banned demonstrations in Paris were held anyway. All of this helps influence the world of work positively. But this also requires building an organization that sets itself long-term goals beyond immediate struggles: a major revolutionary party. Spontaneity alone will not suffice; it will eventually be dispersed or derailed. We need a party with a presence in thousands of workplaces and schools, spokespeople, and worker and youth activists from all sectors who are used to working together; a media network capable of disseminating ideas on a mass scale; and a resolute strategy to carry through the overthrow of the capitalist order and its institutions. This is the proposal that Révolution Permanente puts forward to all those who truly want to end Macronism and the Far Right, but also imperialism and the capitalists’ power over our lives. To all those who want to fight for a social revolution, to expropriate those who exploit us and ravage the planet: join us. Révolution Permanente organizes open meetings in every city where we are active, in order to bring together all those who share our political vision. We want this movement to serve as a springboard for building an organization with thousands of members. We also want to use Anasse Kazib’s candidacy in the 2027 presidential election to advance this goal — so that revolt bursts into the presidential race and these elections do not offer a respite to the regime, which hopes to see anger leave the streets and be channeled into “calm debates.” We refuse to let bourgeois politicians calmly debate how we will be devoured. Who better to spoil the party than Anasse Kazib, a railroad worker from the Paris suburbs and a central figure in all the major struggles of recent decades? Originally published in French on November 12 in Révolution Permanente France General Strike Protests Unions Spain’s first general strike in 14 years shut down car plants, ports, and highways. Electricity demand dropped almost 10 percent, and employers estimate more than 2 billion euros in lost output. Santiago Lupe goes through the data to show where the strike hit hardest, how it compares to the strikes in 2010 and 2012, and why linking labor demands to housing could open a new phase of struggle. Santiago Lupe November 5 brought 1.6 million to the streets in France and high strike rates on the railways and in education, confirming workers are joining the youth movement. While the government seeks to channel discontent through negotiations, we need a plan of action for a general strike. Damien Bernard The Berlin Left Party's state convention is likely to approve the coalition talks on Saturday. But the fight against expropriation and solidarity with Palestine must continue. Ari Aalto October 17 opened a pre-revolutionary period in France. The question now is whether the students and their working class allies can expand, organize themselves, and win the political independence required to fight for its own way out of the crisis. Juan Chingo As tensions rise in the region, Trump, weakened by the midterms, has decided to postpone the launch of a new offensive. But the situation remains highly unstable, while the status quo — with neither war nor an agreement — is at risk of deteriorating. Enzo Tresso The midterms exposed an important contradiction: millions want a break with the status quo, yet the elections strengthened the grip of the Democratic Party on U.S. politics. AOC 2028 makes DSA's choice immediate: mobilize behind the Democrats and negotiate a platform acceptable to them, or build an independent organization to resist the Right and fight for all of our demands? scraped.title: War in Iran: Weakened by the Midterms, Trump Takes a Wait-and-See Approach - Left Voice
scraped.description: As tensions rise in the region, Trump, weakened by the midterms, has decided to postpone the launch of a new offensive. But the situation remains highly unstable, while the status quo — with neither war nor an agreement — is at risk of deteriorating.
scraped.author: Enzo Tresso
scraped.body_text:
As tensions rise in the region, Trump, weakened by the midterms, has decided to postpone the launch of a new offensive. But the situation remains highly unstable, while the status quo — with neither war nor an agreement — is at risk of deteriorating.

Enzo Tresso

“I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I’ll have to. You will know soon enough,” Donald Trump warned on Friday. Within days, his tone has changed radically: on Monday, the U.S. president said that “Iran, militarily, is effectively over,” noting that he saw “positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict.” In Tehran, officials say Washington is “manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks” and that Iran’s conditions remain unchanged.

Nevertheless, this change in tone marks yet another retreat by Trump, who has just suffered a crushing defeat in the midterms, as the U.S. electorate overwhelmingly punished the economic consequences of the war. While a resumption of the imperialist war would have run head-on into prevailing U.S. public opinion, Trump has chosen to strengthen the imperialist blockade. The Republicans’ debacle appears to have isolated those within the Trump administration who favor resuming a high-intensity war .

While Hegseth faces the threat of impeachment and spent most of his Pentagon press briefing — his first in six months — trying to defend himself, Admiral Brad Cooper, head of Central Command, faces opposition from the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and Marco Rubio, who believe that a new military campaign will not yield different results from previous ones, even if the United States were to significantly expand the scope of its targets. While the Secretary of State and the military leadership want to maintain the economic blockade and stick with the status quo — no war and no agreement — the faction led by Vice President JD Vance would like to finally turn the page on the debacle in Iran and sign an agreement with Tehran. For the vice president, this is undoubtedly a matter of preparing for the post-Trump era and distancing himself from this strategic fiasco.

For now, it appears that the faction led by Rubio has prevailed. On Saturday, CENTCOM announced the creation of Task Force Iron Gate, charged with gathering intelligence on overland flows of weapons and hydrocarbons at Iran’s borders. While Trump stated the following day that this was an extension of the naval blockade onto land — reinstated on July 14 — this announcement has all the hallmarks of a major rebuff to imperialism.

Far from ensuring that “very little gets into, or out of, Iran,” as Trump claims, this task force of about twenty people is primarily tasked with gathering information. It is possible that this intelligence will be used to pressure Iran’s neighbors diplomatically to close border crossings, or even to carry out military operations. But in reality, it has no means of taking action on its own . In the Caspian Sea, for example, the United States has no military assets capable of intervening against targets identified by the task force. Above all, it is unlikely that Iraq or Azerbaijan — the former out of fear of an escalation in Iranian militia activity, the latter due to Russia’s probable opposition to any military operation on its doorstep — would take the risk of collaborating with the United States or serving as its proxies.

Moreover, Trump’s imaginary land blockade starkly highlights the ineffectiveness of the naval blockade in place since July. While there is no doubt that Iran’s economic situation is deteriorating, that workers and the working classes are bearing the full brunt of imperialist sanctions, and that the regime is suffering significant revenue losses, the Iranian economy has for half a century been built almost entirely on circumventing crushing sanctions and has other avenues available.

However, we cannot rule out that Trump’s announcements are yet another ploy. At present, a third carrier strike group, led by the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt, and a second amphibious group — comprising the USS Makin Island, the USS Anchorage, the USS John P. Murtha, and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit (13th MEU) — are en route to the Arabian Sea .

On the one hand, Trump’s defeat in the midterms does not automatically reverse the trend toward the resumption of a large-scale imperialist war: Trump, who has already suffered a defeat in the class struggle in Minneapolis, a crushing military defeat in Iran, a defeat in Brazil with the chaotic exile of Flavio Bolsonaro, and a major electoral defeat, may seek to avoid another diplomatic defeat by signing an agreement that would ratify his strategic and military failure. On the domestic front, Trump has already made decisions that run counter to the lessons of the election: while ICE raids have alienated certain segments of the electorate that had turned to Trump in 2024 and caused significant vote shifts toward the Democrats, the White House has just appointed the deeply racist Stephen Miller — architect of the mass deportation policy and a white supremacist ideologue — as the president’s chief of staff.

On the other hand, maintaining the status quo — which allows Trump to avoid taking a stance for now — is unlikely to suit Iran. As Vali Nasr summarizes ,

Trump has been weighing three options, war, deal or blockade which means continue with current no war and no deal status quo and hope Iran will cave. He is claiming GCC is asking for this but in reality he has been sitting in war plans he asked for past few weeks, not comfortable with giving the order to attack. despite letting Vance step up diplomatic efforts Trump is not ready to make concessions that would get a deal.

That leaves him with the option favored by in Rubio and Bessent, settle for economic pressure. But this is at best a stop-gap policy. And it is now up to Iran to accept the status quo and it has said (most recently in Supreme Leader’s statement) that it will not. Which means Iran will try to break the blockade which could escalate into more war. The question will be when.

In a recent article, we identified two other trends that threaten to disrupt the current balance . Netanyahu has more reason than ever to seek a new war in order to remain in power — now that Israeli President Isaac Herzog has tasked Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new government — while the Saudi offensive currently being prepared in Yemen could set the powder keg ablaze.

U.S. imperialism thus remains in a complete impasse: the strategy of economic coercion can only intensify Iran’s determination to break the blockade and thus return to war; judging by the latest U.S. offensives, a new campaign would likely end in failure, while Iran could strike far harder at strategic economic infrastructure across the region and disrupt not only the Strait of Hormuz but also the Bab el-Mandeb Strait; the opening of a new round of negotiations would undoubtedly result in tougher Iranian demands and could only lead to an agreement amounting to a U.S. capitulation. Faced with this impasse, Trump might thus opt for adventurism — whether through a ground deployment or even the use of a tactical nuclear weapon — to escape the consequences of defeat in Iran, which is accelerating the decline of U.S. hegemony .

The situation therefore remains uncertain. Nevertheless, this new phase poses an existential threat to the peoples of the region, starting with the workers and the working classes of Iran, whose living conditions continue to deteriorate as a result of the imperialist offensive. In this context, it is more important than ever to denounce the ongoing imperialist war and build a solidarity movement that firmly advocates for the defeat of the United States, while maintaining complete political independence from the Iranian regime.

Originally published in French on November 10 in Révolution Permanente .

Iran

U.S. Imperialism

Nathaniel Flakin

Speaking before the UN General Assembly, Donald Trump bluntly reaffirmed his imperialist ambitions, issuing a series of threats against Iran and Cuba. In response, we need an international campaign against U.S. imperialism.

This is part of the broader economic war waged by U.S. imperialism against Irantargeting the working class and youth. Duolingo must restore access immediately and we must fight sanctions and oppose imperialist war against Iran.

Maryam Alaniz

AOC 2028 makes DSA's choice immediate: mobilize behind the Democrats and negotiate a platform acceptable to them, or build an independent organization to resist the Right and fight for all of our demands?
