scraped.title: Hibernation is Just the Tip of the Iceberg
scraped.description: Overview: Wildlife relies on remarkable physiological adaptations, from hibernation and torpor to brumation and regional heterothermy, to survive extreme cold, while domesticated animals depend on humans for protection from harsh weather. Guest Opinion As temperatures drop and days and nights become colder, wildlife must adapt quickly to survive. Hibernation helps bears sustain themselves through a […]
scraped.author: Professor Victoria Sutton
scraped.h1: Hibernation is Just the Tip of the Iceberg
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Wildlife relies on remarkable physiological adaptations, from hibernation and torpor to brumation and regional heterothermy, to survive extreme cold, while domesticated animals depend on humans for protection from harsh weather.

As temperatures drop and days and nights become colder, wildlife must adapt quickly to survive. Hibernation helps bears sustain themselves through a long winter, but how does other wildlife survive these extreme conditions?

When food becomes scarce and caloric needs increase, we are familiar with the bears’ hibernation strategy. However, when temperatures suddenly drop at any time of the year, without a season of preparation through eating berries and other foods, some mammals can enter another physiological state called torpor.

Torpor can occur at any time of the year, lasting for short or prolonged periods in response to a sudden drop in temperature and the increased caloric demands of maintaining body heat. Hibernation, by comparison, is a winter process preceded by months of feeding in preparation for the long period of dormancy. (There are also two types of hibernation — facultative and obligate — but those distinctions are not essential to this discussion.)

Further, torpor can look a lot like hypothermia. However, it is the combination of reduced body temperature and a reduced metabolic rate that identifies the condition as torpor rather than hypothermia.

The alligator has an amazing adaptation, making it one of the more cold-tolerant reptiles. It can survive beneath frozen ice and tolerate temperatures as low as 40 degrees below zero. It must poke its nose through the ice to breathe, but otherwise remains in this dormant state. Here is an alligator at North Carolina’s Shallotte River Swamp Park.

Brumation in reptiles differs from hibernation in mammals. Alligators in brumation enter a state of suspended animation, but they experience periods of activity and continue to drink water to avoid dehydration, although they do not eat. Hibernation, by comparison, involves a much deeper state of dormancy.

Ducks, geese and gulls can stand on ice for long periods because they are able to keep their core body temperatures warm while their feet remain nearly frozen. They accomplish this through a physiological process called regional heterothermy.

Your contribution is appreciated.

This process allows birds to conserve heat in their core without expending additional energy to warm their feet. The heat-exchange system is designed with veins surrounding arteries in the feet. Blood returning from the feet is warmed through this exchange, conserving most of the body’s heat for the core.

The legs of birds consist primarily of bones and tendons rather than the muscles and nerves that require more energy to keep warm.

This begs for a diagram, so here is a graphic description of how this process works (from Khan Academy):

Whether an invasive species arrives in a new habitat on its own or is released or introduced by humans, it may not have the adaptations needed to survive extreme weather events such as a polar vortex.

In Florida, during a period of extreme cold, spectacled caimans (an invasive crocodilian species) disappeared completely following the 2010 freeze because they could not adapt to the cold, while native alligators survived.

The manatee is notoriously poor at adapting to cold weather and can die if water temperatures drop below 68 degrees. Despite its appearance, it actually has very little insulating fat to keep it warm. When exposed to cold temperatures, its physiological response appears to trigger a weakened immune system, causing it to become ill quickly. This entire process is well documented and is called manatee cold stress syndrome .

The opossum is another species that does not adapt well to the extreme cold associated with polar vortex conditions. While opossums can survive normal cold winters, their hairless tails and ears make them vulnerable to frostbite. Following extreme cold periods, such as a polar vortex, opossums may be seen with missing tails or ears that appear tattered from frostbite injuries.

Most states and local governments have ordinances and laws requiring animals to have adequate shelter during extreme weather events. In Texas, for example, the care of dogs requires shelter and humane tethering practices during extreme weather, which is defined as:

“Inclement weather” includes rain, hail, sleet, snow, high winds, extreme low temperatures, or extreme high temperatures.

Livestock care during extreme cold is regulated by individual states, where failure to provide adequate care may constitute animal cruelty. There is no federal law specifically regulating the care of cattle during cold weather, but the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) does provide recommendations.

Calves are particularly vulnerable. Their legs are susceptible to freezing, and severe injuries may require euthanasia. Providing shelter and plenty of roughage, such as hay, is recommended to help livestock withstand cold weather.

Most livestock owners want nothing more than to protect their animals, but doing so also means being prepared for extreme cold events. In Texas in 2016, 15,000 dairy cows froze to death during a snowstorm. During the Great Texas Freeze of 2021, livestock losses reached $228 million.

Wildlife have developed adaptations to withstand extreme cold, whereas domesticated animals have been displaced from their original habitats and, unfortunately, must rely on humans to ensure their safety.

Looking ahead, researchers are considering how humans might benefit from these same mammalian processes. Medical research has observed that mammals capable of entering a state of torpor may have an advantage over humans, who are homeotherms. Their tissues appear better able to avoid potentially damaging organs during medical emergencies such as a stroke or cardiac arrest.

The potential use of torpor in space travel is another area of research. Inducing a torpor-like state could make journeys possible that might otherwise exceed the normal human life span.

Winter will take its toll on older, infirm and sick wildlife, but over time, these incredible physiological responses to survive the cold have proven remarkably effective.

During the Great Texas Freeze of 2021, fish along the coast were devastated by the cold and have taken years to recover. Texas Parks and Wildlife (TPWD) reported that 3.8 million fish representing 60 species succumbed to the cold along the Texas coast. Sea turtles were also “cold stunned” and unable to navigate to warmer waters, requiring extensive rescue efforts to try to save them.

Yet, remarkably, wildlife has developed physiological responses to extreme weather events that are unique to each animal classification and habitat. Domesticated animals make humans morally, and sometimes legally, responsible for protecting them from extreme cold.

These physiological mechanisms for withstanding extreme weather events may even inform the future survival of humans, whether on Earth, during space travel or on otherwise uninhabitable planets.

To read more articles by Professor Sutton go to: https://profvictoria.substack. com/

Professor Victoria Sutton (Lumbee) is a law professor on the faculty of Texas Tech University. In 2005, Sutton became a founding member of the National Congress of American Indians , Policy Advisory Board to the NCAI Policy Center, positioning the Native American community to act and lead on policy issues affecting Indigenous communities in the United States.

Guest Opinion “Thank you for your service.” It’s a simple nod of respect and the least we can do. We say […]
scraped.author: Chuck Hoskin Jr
scraped.h1: Our Military Veterans Deserve Our Thanks and a Place to Call Home
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Cherokee Nation Principal Chief Chuck Hoskin Jr. emphasizes that honoring veterans must extend beyond words to meaningful action, highlighting initiatives to expand housing, healthcare, food security and mental health services for Cherokee veterans.

“Thank you for your service.”

It’s a simple nod of respect and the least we can do. We say it often — maybe too often — which shifts the meaning to a simple greeting rather than a true commitment. At the Cherokee Nation, we are determined to honor those words as a promise for action every day, not just on Veterans Day.

Cherokees have served this country since its founding, and that legacy was on full display at our recent annual Veterans Summits , held in Vinita and Roland. We gathered to celebrate and to recommit ourselves to being worthy of the sacrifice our brave military men and women made and continue to make.

Your contribution is appreciated.

Honoring patriotic service demands action, not just appreciation. It demands that no veteran who defended this country comes home to face housing insecurity, inadequate healthcare, or silent struggles with their mental health. If we allow those gaps to persist, then neither the United States of America, nor the Cherokee Nation, can rightly call itself worthy of its veterans.

We have made real progress. When the VA clinic in Vinita faced closure, Cherokee Nation stepped in to keep it open , and it now operates within our world-class health system. It continues to operate and serve generations of veterans. We’ve expanded food security for elders, including veterans, and recently extended additional utility assistance to our lowest-income elders as rising costs strain monthly budgets. We are also investing in programs to address veteran suicide prevention, working to bring struggles out of the shadows and into the light.

Housing remains an area where we must do more. That is why Deputy Chief Bryan Warner and I are launching a new work group, spearheaded by Secretary of Veterans Affairs S. Joe Crittenden, that will explore ways to expand housing opportunities for Cherokee veterans. This group will pursue two federal resources that remain underused in the Cherokee Nation: the Native American Direct Loan program, which helps veterans build homes on trust land, and the HUD-VASH program, which provides rental assistance to veterans facing housing insecurity. We intend to bring these services directly to our citizens rather than waiting on federal agencies to deliver them.

We already know what success looks like. We built our Mige Glory Military Housing Addition in Tahlequah, in partnership with the U.S. Department of Defense, to provide 21 in-demand homes for Cherokee veterans. That’s proof that when we commit our land, resources and purposeful intention, we can deliver real stability.

Additionally, we are preserving the stories behind military service. Our new Cherokee Nation Circle of Honor, launched in partnership with the Library of Congress’ Veterans History Project, will give citizens who received the Cherokee Nation Medal of Patriotism a platform to share their stories. These powerful stories will be on display on our Cherokee.gov website and will be available for generations to come to read and learn more about the heroic acts by our veterans.

This is Gadugi in action.

Our veterans answered the call when the nation needed them. They’ve protected our rights and liberties. Now, it is our responsibility to protect them and show our gratitude with a place to call home.

Chuck Hoskin, Jr. is the principal chief of the Cherokee Nation.

scraped.description: Lawsuit argues unequal commission districts dilutes Native American votes
scraped.author: Daily Montanan
scraped.h1: Fort Belknap tribal members allege Blaine County commission elections discriminatory
scraped.body_text:
ICT

This story was originally published by Daily Montanan.

Micah Drew Daily Montanan

A new federal lawsuit alleges Blaine County dilutes the relative strength of Native American voters in elections for Board of Commissioners.

In the complaint, three tribal members of the Fort Belknap Indian Community are suing the county, the commissioners, the clerk and recorder, and election manager alleging the three commission districts were unlawfully drawn.

The plaintiffs want the U.S. District Court Billings Division to find Blaine County’s three commissioner districts don’t comply with the Fourteenth Amendment, which guarantees a “one person, one vote” doctrine, by creating districts of unequal population.

They also want the court to implement a redistricting plan that equalizes the population between the three districts.

In a statement provided by Upper Seven Law, one of two groups representing the plaintiffs, litigation director Molly Danahy said “the right to vote is the starting premise of our free society — it ensures that we, the people, can hold our government accountable to the rule of law.

“Districts that violate the basic principle that every vote should count the same are unconstitutional. Blaine County’s Commissioner map must distribute power equally among its voters.”

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

The UCLA Voting Rights Project is also representing the plaintiffs.

The Blaine County Attorney did not immediately respond to questions sent on Monday afternoon.

The complaint alleges that the three commission districts have an unequal distribution of voters, which ultimately diminishes the voting power of Native American residents.

The county redistricted last in 2024, and the redistricting resolution stated that the county was required “to maintain commissioner districts having essentially the same population percentages” as in previous years. The three districts were described as being “majority American Indian,” “Majority Non-American Indian,” and “Mix District.”

While the districts were originally created in 2013 and remained the same through the 2024 redistricting resolution, “the court documented disproportionate population changes within the districts,” according to the suit.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

Using numbers cited by the county, the lawsuit shows that District 1, the majority Native American district, has a total population of 2,777; while District 2, the majority non-Native district, has a population of 2,098 — a discrepancy of 28.41 percent.

An ideal population split would have equal districts of around 2,390.

The districts are “presumptively unconstitutional because its population deviation exceeds 10 percent,” the suit argues.

It also argued the county did not provide a “good faith basis” for the excessive population deviations because of the racial makeup targets.

District 1 is around 95 percent American Indian, and attorneys for the plaintiffs argue that it takes “approximately 1.32 people voting in District 1, the most populous district, to have the same effect as 1 person voting in District 2, the least populous,” and most non-Native district.

The county as a whole is roughly 51.4 percent Native American according to the 2020 census.

“​​There is no legitimate justification for the commissioners’ failure to equalize population,” the complaint states.

“The weight of a person’s vote should not depend on which side of a district line they live on,” said Sonni Waknin, senior voting rights counsel at the Voting Rights Project. “Blaine County’s map goes against the principles of our representative government. We are asking the Court to enforce the Constitution and require districts that give voters an equal voice in their county government.”

scraped.author: Associated Press
scraped.h1: Peru’s move to reconsider protections for uncontacted Mashco Piro raises fears of Amazon logging
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Steven Grattan Associated Press

MEXICO CITY — Indigenous leaders in Peru are warning that a government decision to reconsider protections for one of the world’s largest uncontacted Indigenous groups could expose more of their Amazon rainforest territory to logging, raising fears of violent encounters and the spread of life-threatening diseases.

The Mashco Piro, who live deep in the forests of southeastern Peru and avoid contact with outsiders to preserve their traditional way of life, have increasingly been spotted near encroaching logging concessions in recent years, highlighting growing pressure on their ancestral lands.

Eusebio Rios Iviche, vice president of the Indigenous organization FENAMAD, told The Associated Press on Monday the decision threatens to reverse years of efforts to protect the Mashco Piro, exposing them to greater risks of encounters with outsiders and diseases to which they have little immunity.

The controversy centers on a 2016 government study that recommended expanding the Madre de Dios Territorial Reserve, a protected area established in 2002 for the Mashco Piro and other Indigenous peoples living in isolation.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

A government commission responsible for protecting isolated Indigenous peoples decided last week to revisit that study rather than proceed with the proposed expansion, according to Indigenous organizations and the advocacy group Survival International.

The move has raised concerns that logging concessions overlapping with the proposed expansion could continue operating in areas Indigenous organizations say are essential to the Mashco Piro’s survival.

Peru’s Ministry of Culture, which oversees protections for Indigenous peoples living in isolation, did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.

Ramon Rivero, who headed the Peruvian government office responsible for protecting isolated Indigenous peoples in 2014, questioned the decision, saying authorities should complete the reserve’s expansion rather than revisit studies already approved. He said the government should also consider compensation for logging companies whose concessions could be affected.

Growing pressure on isolated communities

Images released by Survival International in 2024 showed dozens of Mashco Piro people near logging concessions in Madre de Dios, a region bordering Brazil and Bolivia.

That same year, violent encounters involving the Mashco Piro and loggers left at least two loggers dead. It remains unclear whether any Mashco Piro were killed or injured.

Following the confrontations, the Forest Stewardship Council, an international organization that certifies responsibly managed forests, suspended certification for Maderera Canales Tahuamanu, a logging company operating in the area. The certification was withdrawn permanently in 2025.

Survival International says logging has continued in the region despite the loss of certification.

Caroline Pearce, the organization’s executive director, condemned the government’s decision, saying it effectively put the Mashco Piro’s territory up for sale and prioritized commercial interests over Indigenous lives.

The dispute comes as Peru faces increasing scrutiny over its protection of Indigenous peoples in isolation.

In September, FENAMAD and the environmental legal organization EarthRights International brought a case before the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, accusing Peru of failing to protect the Mashco Piro’s ancestral territory and their right to remain isolated.

Rios Iviche urged the government to honor the 2016 agreement, expand the reserve and remove overlapping logging concessions.

“The lives and survival of the Mashco Piro people must not come second to economic interests,” he said.

scraped.title: Mahershala Ali tells Black actors not to chase Academy validation on ‘7PM in Brooklyn’
scraped.description: Mahershala Ali says debate over whether Black Oscar winners are A-list “doesn’t translate to anything real,” urging actors to focus on great
scraped.author: Bolarinwa Oladeji
scraped.h1: Mahershala Ali tells Black actors not to chase Academy validation on ‘7PM in Brooklyn’
scraped.body_text:
Mahershala Ali says debate over whether Black Oscar winners are A-list “doesn’t translate to anything real,” urging actors to focus on great material.

Mahershala Ali has two Oscars on his shelf. He still doesn’t think Black actors should measure themselves by them.

The actor appeared on the Nov. 13 episode of “7PM in Brooklyn with Carmelo Anthony ,” where co-host Kazeem “Kaz” Famuyide raised a familiar question, does winning an Academy Award make a Black actor A-list? Complex reported that Ali dismissed the premise almost immediately.

“It’s kind of just talk. It doesn’t translate to anything real,” Ali said. He compared the argument to the endless barbershop debate over LeBron James versus Michael Jordan , a question he suggested matters far less than the obvious point that both are great.

Ali speaks from rare experience. He won Best Supporting Actor for “Moonlight” in 2017 and won the same category again two years later for “Green Book.” Still, he argued that an Oscar means something different for each generation. The industry Sidney Poitier navigated when he won, he said, is not the same one Halle Berry or Viola Davis faced, and a trophy alone does not settle a career’s trajectory.

His larger concern was the climate behind the camera. Ali said recent political shifts have trickled into hiring practices, with DEI now treated as “this bad word.” That environment, he argued, has removed whatever healthy pressure studios once felt to greenlight projects that could be perceived as diverse.

His solution was not to lean into that label. Black actors, Ali said, don’t want to be folded into a “diversity project.” They want to do great material.

The comments carry extra weight given his own history with major studios. In 2019, Marvel announced Ali would lead a new version of “Blade,” but the project fell apart before reaching the screen.

The more recent cancellation of Marvel’s “Wonder Man” has added to fan speculation that Black-led films and series are being quietly deprioritized, a question the studio has not directly addressed.

Ali has since found his footing elsewhere. He reunited with Bassam Tariq, the filmmaker originally hired to direct “Blade,” on “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” which was released in September.

His message for younger actors was simple, the work matters more than the hardware. In an industry that keeps changing the rules about whose stories get made, Ali seems less interested in arguing over who has made it and more focused on choosing material that lasts.

scraped.title: Katt Williams explains what Kevin Hart said that made him finally forgive their years-long feud
scraped.description: Katt Williams explains how Kevin Hart's private apology helped end their feud, paving the way for their reconciliation and Netflix
scraped.author: Bolarinwa Oladeji
scraped.h1: Katt Williams explains what Kevin Hart said that made him finally forgive their years-long feud
scraped.body_text:
Katt Williams explains how Kevin Hart's private apology helped end their feud, paving the way for their reconciliation and Netflix collaboration.

Katt Williams says his reconciliation with Kevin Hart came down to something more personal than a Hollywood collaboration: an apology that addressed the issues behind their years of tension.

According to Complex , the comedian opened up about the relationship during an appearance on “Listen and Laugh,” the podcast hosted by Ice Cube and Mike Epps. In the episode released Nov. 13, Williams explained that although he had genuine reasons for disliking Hart, a private conversation eventually changed his position.

“I didn’t like the guy, and I had reasons that I felt that way,” Williams admitted. He recalled that when Hart reached out, he already had a mental list of things the comedian would need to address before they could move forward.

According to Williams, Hart delivered what he needed to hear.

“He said everything I needed to hear him say,” Williams explained, giving Hart credit for offering an apology he considered “worthy of [him] being forgiven.”

The distinction is important. Williams suggested that their conversation was not about negotiating a professional arrangement or agreeing to work together for financial reasons. He said the personal issues had to be resolved first.

“So there was no working involved in the conversation that we were having,” he added. “But then once that was behind us, now we can do whatever the work is.”

That distinction helps explain how two comedians who had spent years trading public criticism eventually found themselves working on the same project.

Their disagreement became a major entertainment talking point in January 2024, when Williams appeared on Shannon Sharpe’s “ Club Shay Shay ” podcast and questioned Hart’s rise in Hollywood, describing him as an “industry plant.”

The comments reignited older tensions between the two, including Williams’ previous claims that Hart had benefited from opportunities he believed should have gone to him.

But the relationship had begun changing well before their public reunion. During a May 2026 appearance on “The Breakfast Club,” Hart revealed that he and Williams had privately spoken roughly eight months earlier and agreed to find a way to work together.

The public confirmation came during Netflix’s “ The Roast of Kevin Hart ” on May 10, when Williams made a surprise appearance. After the comedian’s set, Hart offered him an olive branch, telling him he wanted to move beyond their differences. The two shook hands and embraced.

Their professional relationship has since extended to Netflix’s comedy film “72 Hours,” which also features Mike Epps. TheGrio previously examined Williams’ appearance in the film, noting that the collaboration suggested their relationship had improved before the public reconciliation at the roast.

On the new podcast, Epps also joked about his own complicated relationship with Hart, teasing that he had joined the film’s cast despite still having issues with the comedian.

Williams’ latest comments, however, provide the clearest account yet of what changed his mind. For him, forgiveness came after Hart acknowledged the issues between them, not simply because an opportunity to work together presented itself.

scraped.body_text:
Ciara, Russell Wilson, A$AP Rocky, Rosalía and other stars make appearances at holiday celebrations, fashion launches and major entertainment events.

From holiday celebrations in New York to high-profile entertainment gatherings in Los Angeles and Las Vegas, celebrities had plenty of reasons to make public appearances this week. Among the familiar faces drawing attention were Ciara , Russell Wilson, A$AP Rocky , Nicky Hilton, Matt Damon and Rosalía.

The latest edition of PEOPLE’s Star Tracks , published Saturday, Nov. 14, captured a cross-section of celebrity life between Nov. 8 and 13, with appearances spanning family outings, fashion events, film promotions and major industry celebrations.

One of the more family-focused moments came in New York, where Ciara and her husband, NFL quarterback Russell Wilson, attended the unveiling of Macy’s Santaland experience at Herald Square with their daughters, Amora and Sienna. The couple joined the holiday event as the department store began bringing its seasonal attractions to shoppers.

They were not the only familiar faces at the celebration. Hotel heiress Nicky Hilton also attended with her daughters, Teddy and Lily-Grace, adding another celebrity family appearance to the festive occasion.

Elsewhere in New York, A$AP Rocky stepped out for the launch of his collaboration with PUMA, centred on the Suede ’94 sneaker. The appearance offered another glimpse of the rapper’s growing presence in fashion, where his creative work increasingly intersects with his music career.

Los Angeles, meanwhile, hosted some of the week’s biggest entertainment gatherings. The GQ Men of the Year celebration brought together actors, musicians and other influential figures at the Chateau Marmont. Matt Damon, Chris Rock, Andrew Garfield, Ayo Edebiri, Joshua Jackson and Shaboozey were among those photographed at the event.

The Museum of Modern Art’s annual film benefit in New York also attracted an impressive guest list. Robert De Niro, Cate Blanchett, Martin Scorsese, Emily Blunt, John Krasinski, Steve Martin and Martin Short were among the personalities who attended the Nov. 12 gathering.

Music had its own defining moment in Las Vegas, where the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards brought together some of the biggest names in Latin entertainment. Rosalía emerged as one of the evening’s major winners, taking home five awards, including Album of the Year for “Lux.”

The week also featured premieres, screenings and promotional appearances connected to upcoming entertainment projects, including “The Hunting Wives,” “ The Odyssey ” and “Blade Runner 2099.”

items.title: Scott Colom Introduces His Beautiful Family After Historic Senate Victory
items.summary: From his politically active parents to his twin brother, wife and daughters, meet the family behind Scott Colom, Mississippi's history-making Black senator.Read more...

scraped.title: Scott Colom Introduces His Beautiful Family After Historic Senate Victory – The Root
scraped.h1: Scott Colom Introduces His Beautiful Family After Historic Senate Victory
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

From his politically active parents to his twin brother, wife and daughters, meet the family behind Scott Colom, Mississippi’s history-making Black senator.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

TUPELO, MISSISSIPPI – OCTOBER 30: Democratic Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom is joined by his daughters after speaking to voters during a midterm campaign rally on October 30, 2026 in Tupelo, Mississippi. Colom is running against Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Photo by Brad Vest/Getty Images)

Mississippi is getting a new U.S. senator, but the bigger story might be the beautiful Black family standing behind him. When Scott Colom makes his way to Washington, D.C., he’ll carry the hopes of Mississippi voters and a family legacy generations in the making. From his trailblazing parents to his identical twin brother, Andrew, and his wife, Nadia, and their two daughters, the people closest to Colom helped make his historic victory possible.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

Here’s what to know about the Coloms and the family power behind this historic win.

Politics and public service are nothing new to the Coloms. Scott is a seventh-generation Mississippian whose family history is deeply connected to the state’s legal and political landscape.

We previously told you that his mother, Dorothy Colom, is a retired judge who made history as the first African American elected to Mississippi’s 14th Chancery District. His father, Wilbur Colom, is an attorney and founding partner of the Colom Law Firm . He also has a history of political involvement, including working with former President Ronald Reagan.

Bet you didn’t know that Colom has an identical twin brother who was also involved in the campaign. A Detroit-based developer, Andrew helped with campaign advertisements, including a playful parody inspired by Ryan Coogler’s “Sinners,” which featured the brothers together.

RELATED : WATCH: This Scott Colom Protein Ad was More Popular Than His Obama Endorsement

Andrew also celebrated his brother’s victory publicly. Speaking to CNN, he described how Mississippi’s voters embraced Scott. “The state of Mississippi was pouring into my brother,” he said. “My brother was receiving all their love, all their ideas, all their excitement, all their needs.”

And here’s another fun fact: Scott will be the fourth identical twin in the Democratic caucus, joining lawmakers Patty Murray, Brian Schatz and Mark Kelly, who also have identical twin siblings.

If there was one person who helped keep the Colom household together while Scott chased his Senate dream, it was his wife, Nadia Dale Colom. The couple married in 2014. Nadia, a Jackson State University graduate with a master’s degree from New York University, has worked in youth development and nonprofit leadership and is now a realtor and property manager, according to her social media.

During the campaign, she helped organize a campaign food truck that visited college campuses, participated in campaign events and moderated panels. Scott made sure to acknowledge her sacrifices during his victory speech.

“She made that dream possible for me. She’s been the love of my life,” he said, adding that he could never lose an election because he had already won the most important one.

And speaking of winning, the couple shares two daughters, Gwendolyn “Luci” Lucille and Brooklyn “Madi” Madison. The girls are growing up in a family where public service and Mississippi history are more than dinner-table conversation. They are part of their own inheritance. Scott also praised his daughters during his victory speech, saying he was proud of how they handled the difficult circumstances.

THANK YOU, MISSISSIPPI! This victory belongs to all of us and I am honored to be your new senator-elect. pic.twitter.com/J2oy1oUVDz

Let’s be clear: Scott Colom’s election is monumental.

Mississippi has a painful history of racial exclusion, voter suppression and violence against Black people fighting for political representation. So, there’s something especially meaningful about seeing an entire Black family share in that achievement. It also sends a message to Black children growing up in Mississippi: Your family history does not have to determine the limits of your future.

Colom captured that collective spirit in his victory speech, telling supporters: “It’s not something that I did, it’s something we did.“

scraped.h1: 15 Photos of Black Celeb Kids Who Look Like Their Parents’ Twins at the Same Age
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

It is easy to see the similarities between celebrity kids and their parents, but things become even more striking when you realize how identical they look at the same age. From Jermaine and Jaafar Jackson to Jada Pinkett Smith and Jaden Smith, here are celebrity kids who are identical to their parents.

By

Mahalia Otshudy

Published

Getty Images, L, Jermaine Jackson, 1984 (Photo by Raymond Boyd/Getty Images); R, Jaafar Jackson, 2026 (Photo by Chad Salvador/Variety via Getty Images)

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

O’Shea Jackson Jr. and Zoë Kravitz are constantly being compared to their celebrity parents, to whom they look identical. Yet while it is easy to see the similarities now, things become even more striking when you compare celebrity children with photos of their parents at the same age. If you do not believe us, we have proof: Here are some famous kids who look exactly like their parents did at their age.

At the start of 2004, Ice Cube was 34, and his film career was taking off; now his son is the same age with similar career aspirations. Placing them side by side, it is like stepping into a time machine.

Other than Damon Wayans Jr. choosing to grow a fuller beard than his dad and still having a full head of hair, the pair are identical at the age of 43.

There is nothing else to say about Jaafar Jackson at 30 years old other than that he is his dad’s identical twin. All he needs to do is grow his hair out, add a Jheri curl, and fans will genuinely get confused between the two.

Related: Then and Now: Iconic Black Stars and Their Mini-Mes, From Babies to All Grown Up

Now 37, Zoë Kravitz looks like an identical copy of her mom at the same age she was in 2006. We are starting to think Lisa Bonet cloned herself.

At 54, Tracee Ellis Ross has the same gorgeous smile her mom, Diana Ross, had at the same age in 1998. We are obsessed.

While Erykah Badu was breaking out as the hottest new musician on the scene in 1997 at the age of 26, her daughter, Puma Sabti Curry, looked just like her in 2022, slaying on red carpets at the same age.

Lauryn Hill’s “MTV Unplugged” performance, which she did at 26 in 2001, is still an iconic album played today. Who would have imagined that only 24 years later, in 2025, Selah Marley would be the very picture of her mom during that performance?

In 1994, Thandiwe Newton was a burgeoning actress still making a name for herself in Hollywood, and as a 21-year-old, Nico Parker is doing the same thing her mom did in the ’90s.

Jaden Smith, 28, looks like his mom, Jada Pinkett Smith, did in 1999, when she rocked red carpets and was a fashion icon. It is no wonder that Jaden Smith is the stylist he is today.

At 26 years old, Willow Smith is the female copy of her dad at the same age, with the same dazzling smiles and low-key swag.

In 2006, LeBron James was just starting his NBA career, making headlines at 22. Now the family legacy has continued with Bronny James, who is making big moves just like his dad did at his age.

Although Jillian Hervey has opted for bolder glam looks than her mom did at 37, the uncanny resemblance is undeniable. They could honestly be twins.

scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Ever find yourself scrolling through Apple TV+ with no idea what to watch? Don’t worry, we’ve rounded up 15 shows worth adding to your watchlist.

By

B.Kadijat Towolawi

Published

Anthony Mackie “12 12 12” | Apple TV+

This fall, Apple TV+ has built an impressive lineup of original programming that’s frankly too good not to binge watch in one sitting.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

From the latest releases, including Anthony ’s “12 12 12,” to the laugh-out-loud comedy “Your Friends and Neighbors,” and gripping crime dramas and mind-bending thrillers like “Severance,” there’s something for every viewer.

So if you’re looking to dive into a new series or just need a show that’s worth adding to your watchlist , these Apple TV+ selections should keep you comfortably locked in this season.

Starring Anthony Mackie as a disgraced FBI agent, the show follows Mackie’s pursuit of a crew responsible for an elaborate bank heist, centering on three timelines: the 12 months leading up to the robbery, the 12 hours it takes to execute the plan, and the 12 days that follow. As a game of cat and mouse unfolds across Europe, the stakes become increasingly dangerous and the viewer is along for the ride.

Set in London, “Criminal Record” follows two detectives, June Lenker (Cush Jumbo) and Daniel Hegarty (Peter Capaldi), as their professional paths collide when a murder investigation raises questions about a past conviction. As the detectives work to uncover the truth, their conflicting approaches put their careers on the line. With two seasons in, there’s a lot to catch up on.

As one of Apple TV’s new features, “Nocturne” is already the most-watched thriller on the platform. A quiet Pennsylvania town becomes the center of a terrifying murder investigation when a series of brutal killings leaves residents unsure of who to trust. FBI agent (Zazie Beetz) work to find the killer, they discover secrets that suggest the danger may be closer than anyone could imagine.

After losing his high-powered finance job and going through a divorce, Andrew Cooper (Jon Hamm) turns to robbing his wealthy neighbors to maintain his lifestyle. But as he uncovers the secrets and scandals behind their picture-perfect lives, his criminal activities lead to some very close calls. With the return of the second season, this dark comedy-drama delivers plenty of suburban drama, deception, and unexpected twists.

Related content: 15 TV Dramas We Can’t Wait to Watch This Fall

Brian Tyree Henry stars as Ray, one of two longtime friends who pose as DEA agents to rob drug dealers in Philadelphia. But when their latest heist leads them into a much larger criminal operation, the pair find themselves in over their heads. As things spiral out of control, they must find a way to escape the mess they’ve created.

Imagine waking up to a life that looks like yours, but isn’t quite. In “Dark Matter,” physicist Jason Dessen is thrown into an alternate reality and must find a way back to his wife and son. This mind-bending thriller explores how the choices we make can shape our lives.

Molly Wells (Maya Rudolph) finds herself broke after her billionaire husband leaves their marriage until she discovers a massive fortune she never knew she had. Now a newly single billionaire, she sets out to rebuild her life while learning the ropes of running her charitable foundation. If you are looking for a laugh-out -loud moment, this show is for you.

If you woke up one day with no memory of your life outside of work, what will you do? In “Severance,” Mark Scout leads a team of employees who undergo a procedure that separates their work memories from their personal lives. But when a former employee appears outside the office and strange events begin to happen, Mark and his coworkers start questioning what their company is really hiding and the meaning behind the procedure.

When a flight from Dubai to London is hijacked, professional negotiator Sam Nelson (Idris Elba) uses his skills to save the passengers before the crisis turns deadly. As he races against time, every decision could result in life or death.

Based on a true story, “The Big Cigar” follows Black Panther Party co-founder Huey Newton as he goes on the run and turns to an unlikely ally in Hollywood to help him escape to Cuba. Together, they create a plan that uses a fake film production as cover for his daring getaway.

Behind the pristine smiles and breaking news, the power struggles and personal drama live. “The Morning Show” stars Jennifer Aniston and Reese Witherspoon as two journalists navigating the cutthroat world of morning television. The series pulls back the curtains on what happens when people delivering the news become the story.

Have you ever wondered how you’d react if your therapist told you exactly what was on their mind? In “Shrinking,” Jason Segel stars as Jimmy, a therapist who takes an unconventional approach to helping others while struggling to rebuild his own life. This hilarious series offers a fresh perspective on what happens when the people who help others need a little help themselves.

“Silo” follows the life of an engineer living in an underground community where the truth about the outside world is a secret. When she begins investigating a mysterious death, she uncovers secrets that could change everything the residents believe about their home.

“Lady in the Lake” is a murder mystery set in 1960s Baltimore, following a housewife who leaves her marriage to become a journalist. When she investigates the death of a Black mother, she is drawn into a world of secrets, corruption, and racial tension. As the two cases unfold, her search for answers exposes the hidden struggles of a city divided by race and class.

Starring Octavia Spencer, this crime drama follows Poppy Parnell, an investigative journalist turned true-crime podcaster who reopens a murder case that once made her famous. As new evidence surfaces, Poppy must confront the possibility that her reporting helped put an innocent man behind bars.

scraped.title: Walmart Shopper Says Customer Made Racist Comments to Cashier, Sending Her Into Mama Bear Mode
scraped.description: A woman’s fiery defense of a young Black Walmart cashier after an alleged racist encounter has viewers cheering her on.
scraped.author: Grace Jidoun
scraped.h1: Walmart Shopper Says Customer Made Racist Comments to Cashier, Sending Her Into Mama Bear Mode
scraped.body_text:
A woman’s fiery defense of a young Black Walmart cashier after an alleged racist encounter has viewers cheering her on.

A Walmart shopper stood up for a young Black cashier over an alleged racist remark made by another customer.

The woman, identified only as Mercedes, tore into the man on camera, and the internet is here for it.

The Oct. 17 video quickly went viral, with thousands of viewers cheering her on. “I’m sorry you had to go through that today,” she told AJ, the cashier, “but this Black sister is going to stand up, baby.”

The confrontation happened on October 10 at the Walmart Neighborhood Market in Cape Coral, Florida. She accused the customer of telling AJ he “didn’t belong here.”

In a follow-up on Instagram, Mercedes said, “Oh, honey, he said to me, my boyfriend, and AJ while talking to all of us, ”’We don’t belong here.’ His family has been here over six hundred years… we need to go back to where we came from.”

She also explained what prompted the prickly interaction.

Mercedes says she struck up a conversation with AJ while checking out, and then the man walked up to their line and told them to “hurry up!”

After they exchanged words, she and her brood moved aside and kept chatting with AJ while he attended to the man. She said that was when he made the alleged racist remarks.

“I went from zero to a hundred real quick,” she quipped.

In the viral video, Mercedes did not hold back.

“He’s just being nasty. He don’t deserve this guy’s customer service,” she told a manager.

She then turned to the man again and told him: “You want someone that’s Black to ring you up, but we don’t belong here? How dare you say that in front of my kids! I literally have chills on my body. My hair is standing up…I’ll have no one disrespect me like that.”

The manager, however, declined to kick the man out of the store.

Instagram commenters were shocked by her decision.

“How dare the manager make that cashier ring him up after comments such as this,” wrote one person.

Another pointed to Walmart’s policy prohibiting racial discrimination and harassment. Its Code of Conduct specifically classifies verbal, written, or graphic material that ridicules, insults, or shows hostility toward someone based on a protected status as unacceptable.

The commenter added, “This baby was not protected.”

Another person heaped praise on Mercedes: “On behalf of all the Black women with Black sons…Thank you. We can’t be around 24/7 to protect them the way we would like, but with people like you, they will be protected.”

Mercedes said she had reached out to Walmart management but had not heard back. She has not shared any further updates.

A post shared by Mercedes Cherry 🍒 (@mercedes__cherry)

scraped.title: Trump Gives Black Senator Rare Credit for Move That Helped Flip a Red State — and Walks Straight Into the Awkward Truth He’s Been Dodging
scraped.description: President Donald Trump rarely hands out praise to Democrats, but he gave Mississippi’s newly elected Black senator credit for a campaign move that helped him pull off a stunning upset.
scraped.author: Shelby Erdman
scraped.h1: Trump Gives Black Senator Rare Credit for Move That Helped Flip a Red State — and Walks Straight Into the Awkward Truth He’s Been Dodging
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump rarely hands out praise to Democrats, but he gave Mississippi’s newly elected Black senator credit for a campaign move that helped him pull off a stunning upset.

President Donald Trump just did something he rarely ever does. He complimented a newly elected Black U.S. senator on his campaign strategy.

Sen.-elect Scott Colom beat incredible odds and stunningly made history in deep-red Mississippi when he ousted career politician Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

On Thursday, during an interview with sports analyst and political commentator Stephen A. Smith at the White House, Trump credited Colom with appealing to Republican voters.

Colom’s victory marks the first time Mississippi residents have elected a Black senator by a popular vote since the Reconstruction era.

In the final weeks of the midterm campaign, Trump tried to rally uninspired MAGA supporters and other GOP voters in Republican states that he had won by wide margins in the 2024 presidential election. That included a campaign rally in Corinth, Mississippi, for Hyde-Smith.

During the interview with Smith, Trump doubled down, attributing Republicans’ massive losses across the country to his absence on the ballot, even though at his rallies he implored his supporters to pretend that he was on the ballot.

When Smith asked about Colom’s win, Trump praised the new senator even as he tried to steal some of his thunder.

“I don’t know the gentleman, but I give him credit,” Trump told Smith.

“And you know what he did? He campaigned on lines, I give him a lot of credit for this, he campaigned on lines,” Trump continued.

“I had a rally there, and we had lines that went 10 miles long, and he campaigned on that line, telling everybody in the line what a good job he did,” Trump said before adding, “I give him a lot of credit for that.”

Colom did indeed show up at Trump’s rally in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26. He talked with voters standing in line waiting to get in to see Trump.

He asked them what their top concerns were and what issues were making the biggest impact on their lives.

Many told him prices, including groceries and gas, the unapproved and deadly war in Iran, data centers, and even “honesty.”

Colom posted the video on social media a few days later, and so far, it’s received almost three million views.

He sent a message, too.

“I walked the Trump rally line to listen, not make assumptions. I talked with voters, asked questions and heard what matters to them. When I’m elected, I’ll represent all 82 counties and every Mississippian, no matter who they voted for. That’s what being your senator means,” he wrote.

Hyde-Smith finally conceded the race on Wednesday, more than a week after Election Day.

In an interview on MS Now Friday morning, Colom elaborated on walking the Trump lines and talking to voters.

Colom said he talked with voters on the streets in Mississippi “for months and months and months.”

“My campaign team would tell you I was doing that even when the cameras weren’t rolling. I was always asking voters what mattered to them and listening,” he explained.

Colom said that when he talked to Trump supporters, he heard the same things as he did from others in the bluest areas of the state.

“Gas, groceries, concerned about the war in Iran, concerned about Flock cameras, just very common-sense stuff,” he said.

Colom offered some advice to politicians and even Trump.

“To be a real leader you have to learn how to listen,” he stated.

He went on to explain how his mom was a judge and that when he was young she always told him, “Scott, if you talk too much your ears will shrink, and if they shrink too much you won’t be able to hear, and she was telling me you gotta listen.”

Well, Colom listened all the way to the U.S. Senate.

Colom also has a history with Hyde-Smith, according to The Hill .

Former President Joe Biden nominated Colom for a federal judgeship in 2023, but the now-outgoing Republican blocked a confirmation hearing for him.

In an ironic twist, if she had allowed a hearing for Colom three years ago, she might not have lost her Senate seat in the midterms.

scraped.title: Tye Tribbett Draws the Line on Gospel Artists Working with Rappers After Kirk Franklin Teams Up with GloRilla
scraped.description: Tye Tribbett faces backlash over his criticism of Kirk Franklin’s GloRilla collaboration as fans question his own history of working with hip-hop artists.
scraped.author: Nicole Duncan-Smith
scraped.h1: Tye Tribbett Draws the Line on Gospel Artists Working with Rappers After Kirk Franklin Teams Up with GloRilla
scraped.body_text:
Tye Tribbett faces backlash over his criticism of Kirk Franklin’s GloRilla collaboration as fans question his own history of working with hip-hop artists.

Kirk Franklin is no stranger to controversy in the gospel world.

And he seems to have no regrets about tapping the hottest artists climbing the charts for his latest album, “I Am What I AM.” His recent collaboration with Memphis rapper GloRilla has stirred up another debate about mixing sacred music with secular artists.

Now, fellow gospel artist Tye Tribbett has weighed in with an opinion that some fans believe deserves a closer look.

Tribbett recently explained why he would have made a different choice when it comes to his music. However, his comments have brought renewed attention to his own history of working with mainstream artists.

Some fans are wondering whether the rules change depending on who’s holding the microphone.

The Grammy-winning singer appeared on “The Breakfast Club” on Nov. 11 to promote “Victory B20,” marking the 20th anniversary of his breakthrough project, “Victory.”

During the interview, DJ Envy asked about the backlash Franklin received for featuring GloRilla on a remix.

“I think Kirk Franklin has been Kirk Franklin since he’s been Kirk Franklin,” Tribbett responded. “So I don’t know why people are surprised at Kirk Franklin.”

However, when Envy pressed him about secular artists entering gospel music, Tribbett acknowledged that he would have approached the collaboration differently.

“I love Glo,” he said, adding that Franklin could have given another artist the opportunity. “He did not have to go the GloRilla route.”

Tribbett argued that gospel artists should be mindful of maintaining boundaries between sacred and secular music.

“Christ was in the world. Christ walked the streets. He wasn’t in church all the time, but he never did the things the world did to try to win the world,” he explained.

His comments, however, divided Threads users.

“I think the most profound part of what he said is that Christ didn’t do the things of the world by trying to win the world and he is correct,” one wrote.

Another questioned the effectiveness of such collaborations: “I agree with Ty. Because also what did having Nicki on a gospel song really do as well. Does this really lead people to Christ or to the church?”

Others saw a double standard, pointing to Tribbett’s past collaborations.

“Tye has been jealous with everyone and he came behind him, so with that being said he wouldn’t be in this genre for younger generations but he did try his wasn’t received like Kirk Franklin Tye there was J Moss Fred Hammond stop lying Tye!!!” said one person.

Another asked, “Wasn’t Tye on Snoops album though…?”

The fan was referring to Tribbett’s appearance on Snoop Dogg’s 2018 gospel album, “Bible of Love.”

Tribbett performed on the song “You” and later joined Snoop and Jamie Foxx to perform it at the BET Awards that year.

There is, however, a key difference Tribbet was trying to point out, between that collaboration and Franklin’s decision to feature GloRilla.

Tribbett was invited onto a rapper’s gospel project, while Franklin invited a rapper onto his own gospel recording.

Snoop’s “Bible of Love” represented a departure from the rapper’s mainstream catalog, which frequently references marijuana, sex and street life.

Tribbett was participating in a project specifically devoted to gospel music. In essence, he was bringing the gospel message to Snoop’s audience, not introducing Snoop and his mainstream musical identity to Tribbett’s Christian fan base.

Tribbett’s musical history extends well beyond the gospel industry. Through his group, Greater Anointing (G.A.), he worked with Common, The Roots and Will Smith. He also earned vocal credits on Justin Timberlake’s hit “Cry Me a River.”

His early career also included performances with Jill Scott and tours with country stars Faith Hill and her husband, Tim McGraw.

Just a week before his Breakfast Club appearance, Tribbett told HipHopWired that he would consider recording with rapper Lil Baby.

“We have not, and I would be open to it,” he said. “It’s all about the message to me. As long as the message is legit, we could do it.”

Lil Baby and GloRilla are both mainstream rappers whose catalogs include explicit lyrics about relationships, sex and street life.

“It’s always the gospel artist that’s so critical. If you take the words GOD or Jesus out of his songs, they sound like an R&B song,” one Threads user argued.

Another added, “I understand it. However, if we’re going to be this critical then gospel artist should no longer be present at any other awards show outside of Gospel award shows.”

Franklin has weathered similar criticism for decades. His 1997 crossover hit “Stomp,” featuring Salt of Salt-N-Pepa, upset traditional gospel audiences. Salt recently recalled that some radio stations removed her verse.

The backlash resurfaced when Franklin collaborated with GloRilla on “Rain Down on Me” from her 2024 album “Glorious.” Their subsequent musical partnership revived questions about whether the rapper’s explicit catalog conflicts with gospel’s message.

However, Salt, John P. Kee and Da Brat have defended Franklin. They argue that his collaborations introduce gospel music to audiences who might never enter a church.

Franklin and Tribbett also share a lengthy professional relationship, sharing the same stages on tours and collaborating on “Could’ve Been” from Franklin’s 2005 album “Hero.”

Still, their differing approaches to incorporating mainstream artists and sounds into gospel music reflect an ongoing debate within the genre about tradition, artistic expression and the boundaries of contemporary gospel.

During Franklin’s “Den of Kings,” rapper T.I. questioned the church’s business practices, expressing skepticism about its motives and criticizing pastors who pressure congregants for money.

“I don’t think it’s real. I think it’s a business, just like anything else,” he said, criticizing pastors who pressure congregants for money.

Tribbett previously faced his own backlash after calling the church’s religious structure “wack” during a 2024 “Breakfast Club” interview, arguing that the church had lost sight of its responsibility to serve and love people.

Pastor Mike McClure Jr. publicly challenged him.

“How can you go on a national platform and totally throw under the bus the very institution that made you who you are?” McClure asked.

Meanwhile, the GloRilla debate continued on Threads.

“Her mama named her Glorious… SHE WAS SUPPOSED TO BE ON THAT SONG,” one person joked.

For Franklin and Tribbett, the disagreement highlights a familiar question within gospel music: How far should artists go to reach people outside the church?

scraped.title: Targeted by al-Shabaab for defending Kenya's ecosystems: Foundation founder gets award
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.author: Malavika Vyawhare
scraped.h1: Targeted by al-Shabaab for defending Kenya’s ecosystems: Foundation founder gets award
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

Conservation is rarely conflict-free. On Kenya’s northern coastline, in Lamu and Tana River counties — a biodiversity hotspot where the nation’s longest river meets the Indian Ocean — the work of protecting marine and terrestrial habitats often takes a willingness to challenge industrial fishing and extractive industries.

For Raabia Hawa, defending nature against these activities has meant operating in areas largely neglected by official conservation bodies. A former broadcast journalist and Montessori teacher turned environmental defender, Hawa founded the Ulinzi Africa Foundation (“Ulinzi” means the defenders in Swahili) in 2014 to provide frontline ranger patrols against elephant poaching and wildlife crime. Her work has since expanded beyond anti-poaching to combat illegal industrial bottom-trawling and empower local communities resisting extractive mining concessions.

Operating near the Somali border comes with high political insecurity. Hawa’s vocal stance against environmental destruction has come at a personal risk, including death threats and being designated a target by the militant group al-Shabaab. Despite these perils, Ulinzi has continued to operate on a shoestring, powered by volunteer family support. In London to receive the 2026 Tusk Award for Conservation in Africa — which provides Ulinzi with three years of critical funding — Hawa spoke with Mongabay about the realities of countering industrial fishing and mobilizing rural women against mining giants, highlighting the disconnect between global biodiversity targets and the daily battles frontline nature defenders fight on the ground.

Raabia dedicates the award to her father, Abdul Kadir Hawa, who she credits for her success. “He really believed in allowing me to find my path and walk my path, and he just empowered me every day,” she says.

The interview was edited for length and clarity.

Mongabay: Congratulations on your award. Can you take us into the everyday reality of your work?

Raabia Hawa: We work in a quite a difficult situation because it’s a high security area, a little bit different from some other conservation spaces. I have an anti-poaching team, which is the frontline defense or rapid response unit. Our marine program is the newest — we discovered that there’s actually quite a lot of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, because we are close to the Somali border, in the LAPSSET Corridor.

In 2021, there were all these reports of dead dolphins, dead turtles — every day. So, I went to check with my rangers. We documented two dead dolphins [and] 15 dead turtles. And then we saw the trawler. We actually mounted the trawler for an inspection. What we found on board was just a total massacre. They had 48 endangered species on board — shark, rays and guitarfish, which are meant to be protected species. We then were instructed to arrest the boat captain, and the trawler was instructed to anchor. What they did instead was they fled the waters after we left.

I realized that fisheries is actually a very dirty, corrupt industry. I got calls from the owner of the vessel; I got calls offering money, saying we will fund your conservation work if you just leave this alone. And I wasn’t entertaining that. It resulted in the first spate of threats and intimidation against me. The first being, I was notified that I was a named target of an al-Shabaab attack, which usually around these parts is used to just disappear you.

Mongabay: How did you evade that threat?

Raabia Hawa: I realized it was just a tactic to intimidate me into not pursuing the case. But I did not relent. I continued to write letters to the DPP [Director of Public Prosecutions]. The Kenya Coast Guard put together a thorough investigative report for prosecution. The DPP has still not prosecuted that case.

I started teaching some of the community how to gather evidence and make a strong letter. Because before, they would just do a march to the chief’s office, or write a letter to the fisheries department. The fisheries department never gave [them] any attention. So, I said maybe we need to try a new tactic here: Because it’s affecting turtles, and turtles are protected by the Wildlife Act, let’s instead write to the Ministry of Wildlife. What that resulted in was the Minister of Wildlife responding in writing and committing to keeping Kipini, which is the name of the landing site area there, a trawling-free zone.

Mongabay: Did that make a difference?

Raabia Hawa: It was really such a win. Between 2023 and 2025, we recorded a notable decline in the death of turtles as a result of trawling. In 2025, they tried to bring in a trawler under research purposes; and this year there has been a trawler: We’ve already recorded 20 turtle deaths. Because of a lack of enforcement, [and] a lot of ambiguity with our fisheries regulations, and the fact that the Ministry of Fisheries and Blue Economy [The Ministry of Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs] is prioritizing fisheries over the health of the ocean — despite making pledges at our ocean conference last year to really do everything possible to stop illegal fisheries.

Mongabay: What gives you the motivation to devote yourself to this fight against the odds, against threats?

Raabia Hawa: I’ve always loved wildlife. But there’s loving wildlife, and then really dedicating your life to making sure they’re safe. For me, it was difficult to get into conservation — I didn’t really know how. I ended up becoming a teacher instead. During the time that I was teaching, I was [also] working on radio. Media was really who I was.

By [that] time I had worked with rangers for some years, I had lost some friends to poachers, and it was very difficult for me. So, I wanted to see how I could leverage my media work to change that. I wanted to do a big awareness campaign. I did a cross-country trek called “Walk with Rangers from Arusha in Tanzania to Nairobi in Kenya through the bush.” Interest peaked on social media. I ended up having 71 people from all over the world join me on Walk with Rangers. I had an online fundraiser going, and raised enough money to purchase a Land Cruiser — that vehicle is what we [still] use today.

I never planned to have an organization or do projects of my own, but then I realized that this particular ecosystem really needed somebody. And at the time, nobody was willing to come here. There was a lot of insecurity because of al-Shabaab, no tourism. I decided, maybe I’ll just try and do it myself.

Mongabay: You mentioned losing friends to poachers, threats to yourself and the overall security situation — can you tell me what’s creating this climate?

Raabia Hawa: At the moment things are difficult. We are facing new threats. I think one of the most dangerous things that Kenya has done is combine the ministry functions of mining and blue economy, and combine the ministerial functions of tourism and wildlife. Because wildlife now is seen as a commodity, all the focus goes to tourism, and no [remotely sufficient] budget is allocated towards conservation. Mining and [the] blue economy are just being used for exploitation all over the country, and this is affecting us here on the ground.

Mongabay: Can you give me an example?

Raabia Hawa: We’ve recently had a lot of interest from the titanium mining industry. In 2024, there were applications for mining prospecting from Base Titanium, [which has] an Australian [parent] company. They wanted to take over entire blocks of land, including the environmentally significant area. I was able to put together a coalition. We successfully wrote memorandums in objection to this.

I also tried to sensitized the community [at Kipini village]. I found [out] that the mining company was taking the community for excursions to the mining site — showing them how they built schools, a clinic, how this was going to transform their lives. It was like a massive greenwashing campaign. Members from this very marginalized community bought into it. I spoke about my concerns [at a women’s meeting]. And that just lit a spark. They all said: “We don’t want the mining, but how do we stop this?” I said, “Well, we can write a letter of objection because the minister has said he’s calling for public comments.”

We [also] made a lot of information open source. We were able to map the mining blocks and hold a training session for the farming community and the women to enable them to access Google Maps — when they’re at their homestead, or at their farm, or at their grandfather’s graveyard, [to] put your live location and see if this is within the mining site and if you’re going to lose your land. That really helped to shift the perspective. They pushed back against the company, and Base Titanium pulled out their interest in mining in this area.

Mongabay: Who funds your work, and how did you build that capacity?

Raabia Hawa: All of the capacity that we brought as Ulinzi, no one’s funding it. Our advocacy program is completely unfunded, with the exception of one which we recently got funding for, to fight against bottom trawling and industrial scale fishing. The stuff on mining has all been pro bono, and actually, with the support of my brother: He did a course on GIS mapping and open-source data, and so he was able to bring that skill set [in], again, pro bono at the time. My sister is a lawyer, so she’s been doing all the legal stuff for Ulinzi pro bono —checking MOUs, going through affidavits, that kind of thing.

This is one of the reasons why I’m so excited about Tusk [and the award], because for the first time, Ulinzi has got a donor who is giving us sustained funding for three years. I can’t tell you what a lifeline this is for us. The thing is, our rangers are the beating heart of Ulinzi: This is our core program, and as long as my rangers get paid, honestly, I’ll do everything else for free.

( Banner Image: Raabia Hawa receives The Tusk Award for Conservation in Africa from William, Prince of Wales, at a ceremony in London on Nov. 11. Image courtesy of Chris Jackson/Getty Images for the Tusk Conservation Awards 2026.)

Mongabay’s Spoorthy Raman examines how this change is playing out: conservationists welcome the wolves’ return, ranchers vilify them due to livestock losses, and others seek coexistence at a time when wolf numbers are growing.
